How UK AISI and EvalEval Are Making Benchmark Results Reproducible

📅 22 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (800 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.
  • In a recent development, AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema.
  • As AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly notable sources of evidence about model and system performance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

In a recent development, AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

As AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly notable sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

This builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

Recent findings suggest that transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this new phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:.

These results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

Recent findings suggest that performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve shows the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

Industry observers note that when results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

Sources indicate that the EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

Sources indicate that the coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Recent findings suggest that the UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

It has been revealed that reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.

📅 28 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1132 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that reinforcement Learning environments give new capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents.
  • An environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome.
  • An RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that highlights up in the new RL Environments filter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that reinforcement Learning environments give new capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents. Therefore, Hugging Face Hub now has a special place for RL Environments.

An environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome. The resulting rewards can measure an agent's performance during evaluation or provide a learning signal during training. For an introduction to this interaction loop, see our blogpost on environments. Within the environment, the agent will perform a set of tasks that are represented as datasets. Therefore, environments can be split into broadly two parts: tasksets and runtimes. In this release, we are focusing on the tasksets.

An RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that highlights up in the new RL Environments filter. The Use this dataset button gives you the command to run it in that framework. There is no new repo type, no registry, and no sign-up. There are already environments in Harbor, Verifiers, and NVIDIA NeMo Gym.

Every RL paper or framework uses its own way to find environments. Custom hubs, runtime registries, independent task datasets, or a GitHub list of tasks with a custom loader. This means that many of the published environments are siloed: if you publish an environment for one framework, owners of the other three can’t load it. If you want to train on an environment from another framework or a newly introduced paper, you’ll need to port it by hand.

We think this is the wrong shape. An environment is tasks, tests, containers, and a reward rule, which are data with a runtime on top. The Hub already stores data, versions it, gates it, previews it, and serves it to millions of people. It does not need a second system to hold environments. It needs a way to say "this data is an environment, and here is how you run it.".

The frameworks keep doing what they are good at. The Hub does what it is good at, which is hosting, discovery, and versioning. Nobody has to own the catalogue. In fact, catalogues can run on other platforms too, powered by the hub.

Recent findings suggest that the dataset repository hosts your environment files. The framework runs them locally or on a supported cloud backend. Hugging Face Jobs can run cloud workloads, and Hugging Face Sandboxes, built on Jobs, provide interactive command execution. The tags describe compatibility and generate loading commands; adding a tag does not start a job or sandbox.

The RL Environments filter. Go to huggingface.co/datasets?other=rl-environment. Every dataset with the rl-environment tag appears there, whatever framework it works with.

Framework tags. Four environment frameworks are registered as dataset libraries:.

Each framework tag puts the framework's icon on the dataset page and adds a generated snippet to Use this dataset.

A dataset can carry more than one framework tag. That is the point. Tags describe compatibility, and compatibility is not exclusive. Each listed framework must support the files in the repository; adding a tag does not convert them.

Choose the example for your framework and run it in a separate Python environment with the prerequisites listed below.

Recent findings suggest that harbor can load task directories from a Hub repository. The oracle agent runs the task's reference solution, then the verifier scores the result. It does not call a model.

Industry observers note that the viewer indicates the task's reward, verifier output, and logs. This checks the task and its reference solution before you try a model agent.

It has been revealed that the Harbor integration of verifiers v1 can run the same task directories in different runtimes, such as Docker. It also supports different harnesses, including a minimal bash harness.

Here repo is the full Hugging Face Git URL, while dataset is the name and version in that repo's registry.json. This loader uses Harbor's registry conventions, so a bare Hub repo ID cannot replace both values.

OpenEnv's Harbor integration can run the same task directories with an agent such as OpenCode and return the verifier's reward alongside the agent's trace.

It has been revealed that the command downloads the dataset's tasks/ directories, runs one task in Docker, and writes the result. The default connection uses a temporary Gradio tunnel so the sandboxed agent can reach OpenEnv's model proxy. Read the verifier result and the number of model calls:.

According to recent reports, A reward of None means no verifier reward was produced; inspect error before interpreting the run as a model failure. This path expects Harbor task directories.

In a recent development, neMo Gym supports evaluation and RL training: its environments collect trajectories and compute rewards, while a training framework updates model weights. For example, the Structured Outputs dataset pairs prompts with JSON schemas. Its verifier rewards schema adherence; it does not check whether the generated content is factually correct.

It has been revealed that the best part is that this gives one repo and one discussion tab where people report broken tasks from all major frameworks. So when an author fixes a bad test, every framework gets the fix on the next pull.

Open your dataset card and add this to the YAML header:.

In a recent development, that is the whole integration. Keep rl-environment, then list every framework that can load your files. If your environment works with a framework we have not registered yet, open a PR to the list of supported libraries.

The docs have the full reference.

Sources indicate that we opened PRs to tag some of the environments people already train on. If you maintain one of these, merge the PR and your environment reveals up in the filter.

The first version generates one default snippet per framework. Per-config snippets are next, so a repo with several task sets can show the right command for each. After that we will look at structural detection for frameworks with strict layouts. It would also be really cool build custom task UIs, we’ve been experimenting with this here:.

Recent findings suggest that the bigger goal is for framework tagging to be automatic everywhere. OpenEnv already does it on upload. If you maintain Harbor, Verifiers, Nemo Gym, or any other environment framework, add the tags in your push path. It is a few lines, and every environment your users publish becomes visible to everyone else.

Industry observers note that if you train agents, go browse the filter. If you build environments, publish and tag them, whether they cover coding, tool use, games, robotics, or another task. Include the files, a working run command, and the rule that produces the reward so others can use them. If your framework is missing, contribute it to the list of supported libraries.

#23427. Breaking: Before You Scale AI Agents, Ask What They Don’t Know

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1270 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Unite ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Before You Scale AI Agents, Ask What They Don’t Know

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1270 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, picture this: A CFO is getting ready for a meeting with a major institutional investor.
  • Recent findings suggest that the tool confidently states that the investor owns 2.5 million shares.
  • In a recent development, but there’s a catch: The AI pulled the figure from a Form 13F filing, which reports holdings as of the previous quarter-end.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, picture this: A CFO is getting ready for a meeting with a major institutional investor. To help with prep, the investor relations (IR) team asks an AI tool to pull some background—the date of the last meeting with that firm, priorities expressed, number of shares held, and so on.

Recent findings suggest that the tool confidently states that the investor owns 2.5 million shares. No one bats an eye, and the CFO continues preparing for this important conversation, full speed ahead.

In a recent development, but there’s a catch: The AI pulled the figure from a Form 13F filing, which reports holdings as of the previous quarter-end. The information was accurate back when it was reported… but now, it’s months old. In the meantime, the investor has quietly sold 2 million shares, reducing their position significantly. The meeting agenda (and potentially the meeting itself!) no longer seems relevant.

What went wrong? In this scenario, the AI didn’t hallucinate or fabricate a number. It retrieved legitimate information but failed to qualify it or explain the limitations.

While in this case, the consequences might be an awkward conversation or missed opportunity, in other situations, a similarly definitive answer that lacks critical context can carry even greater risks.

Sources indicate that foundational models are getting better and better. So, why does it seem like confident-but-wrong answers are popping up more and more—something businesses across industries are grappling with?

For starters, generative AI (GenAI) has become completely pervasive. According to McKinsey’s The State of AI in 2026 report, nearly 9 in 10 business professionals say their organizations regularly use AI in at least one business function.

And as organizations move beyond experimentation—increasingly relying on AI for everyday business tasks and decisions— they’re also encountering the limitations of what these tools know and understand.

A recent industry survey reveals what’s often at the root of it: In the past six months alone, nearly 6 in 10 businesses (57%) traced a confident-but-wrong AI agent answer to missing or incomplete business context.

It has been revealed that with all the data available to AI, this may come as a surprise. But there’s an important distinction to be made: Context isn’t the same thing as data.

Context can encompass institutional knowledge, exceptions to the rules, relationships, processes and expectations around how work gets done—nuances that are often unique to each firm.

Sources indicate that in my work with investor relations teams, I see just how vital these distinctions can be. Consider a few seemingly straightforward examples:.

Given all this, it’s no surprise that the same underlying model can deliver very different results at different companies, depending on the context and specialized knowledge available to it.

Recent findings suggest that purpose-built, industry-specific (or “vertical”) AI can help bridge some of these gaps, recognizing the specialized knowledge, workflows and nuances of a given sector. But even the most sophisticated technology can’t capture everything an organization knows, which is why humans have a part to play too.

In a recent development, but humans don’t stick around forever. Consider what happens when an experienced investor relations officer (IRO) leaves their tech giant after, say, five years. They’ve likely spent their time identifying and targeting prospective investors, analyzing shareholder activity, cultivating relationships, preparing for earnings, prepping execs… and a whole lot more.

The tech giant retains the earnings scripts, presentations, and other files. But the institutional knowledge behind them? Much of that walks out the door too, especially when you consider that nearly eight in 10 IROs (78%) don’t have a successor identified for their roles.

That’s why organizations need to put in the work to preserve knowledge and understanding in a way that AI systems can use. Simply connecting an AI agent to a shared drive often isn’t enough.

Having a way to systematically capture key knowledge and workflows—like the reasoning behind key decisions, the history of relationships, and other mission-critical information that never made it into a formal document—is notable to businesses across industries.

In a recent development, and powering such a knowledge base requires people: both for recording information and applying judgment around it. AI can help organize knowledge, but it’s employees who provide the key context that technology often misses.

It has been revealed that we’ve discussed what happens when AI gets an answer wrong. But sometimes, an AI agent can retrieve information that’s right—it’s accurate, current and relevant—and still create problems by sharing it under the wrong circumstances.

In highly regulated industries, those missteps are especially costly.

Sources indicate that in investor relations, for instance, sharing material nonpublic information (MNPI), such as unreleased financial results, with an analyst or investor can violate the U.S. SEC’s Regulation Fair Disclosure (Reg FD)—potentially resulting in financial penalties and reputational damage.

Other industries like healthcare, financial services, and legal services face similar regulatory risks, highlighting the need for guardrails when AI agents are privy to sensitive information.

Industry observers note that this also indicates why humans remain crucial—an essential part of reviewing and approving what gets communicated. Companies may consider making the level of human review proportionate to the stakes, with different types of AI workflows operating with different levels of autonomy.

Industry observers note that we’ve probably all encountered situations, in work or life in general, where we don’t know what we don’t know. Sometimes the ramifications aren’t consequential; other times they’re more serious.

With such massive datasets available to AI today, AI models know a lot more… but still need to “speak up” when holes exist. So, as businesses use AI to tackle more strategic priorities and workflows, it’s important to ask these questions before scaling:.

Recent findings suggest that I want to be clear: I’m bullish on AI. I use it daily in my role, see the current and future benefits, and think that—in many ways—we’re just scratching the surface of AI’s potential. I have no doubt that companies that avoid AI, and those that fail to implement it in an organized, effective way, run a real risk of falling behind.

But adopting AI doesn’t mean giving a general-purpose model access to enterprise data and letting it operate willy-nilly.

Sources indicate that right now, and as far as I can see, fully autonomous AI isn’t appropriate for every business task or decision. Organizations need to understand where AI can operate independently, where it needs additional context, and where human judgment is non-negotiable.

According to recent reports, so, before asking what an AI agent knows, ask what it doesn’t. The answers shape how you deploy it, what you trust it to do, and how you set it up for success.

Dror Nadler is Chief Product Officer at Q4 Inc., where he leads product strategy and innovation, helping investor relations teams harness AI, data and technology to work more effectively. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that holo4 is our new series of agentic models.
  • Holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs.
  • Holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that holo4 is our new series of agentic models. It comes in two sizes: 27B dense and 35B-A3B Mixture of Experts. Both are available on the H Models API. We are also releasing an updated version of Holotron 3: Holotron4 Nano.

Holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs. It scores well on academic benchmarks, but we built it for real business workflows. It was trained through supervised and reinforcement learning on a large set of environments and tasks, including those generated by our Agentic Task Factory.

Holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools. It uses whichever fits the task. Most agentic models are trained for one interface only: GUI-focused models are blind without a screen, while models that prefer tool calling are stuck in front of an application that has no API. Real work is not siloed that way, and a single business task can require combining these different approaches.

Industry observers note that holo4 runs on desktops, on the web, on Android, in a code sandbox and against business APIs. It is the same model in each case and it is called the same way. You do not need to select a different model for each platform.

Holo4 models improve significantly over their Qwen base. Holo4 trails only the strongest closed models on long workflows: on OSWorld 2.0, Holo4 27B scores 61.7% against 81.8% for Opus 5.5, and Holo4 35B-A3B reaches 30.9%. However, it does so with orders of magnitude fewer parameters and at a much lower cost. We open-source every trajectory behind our scores on public benchmarks: replay each step at trajectories.hcompany.ai or download them from Hugging Face.

On the hardest academic benchmarks for desktop control (OSWorld 2.0) and API use (AutomationBench), Holo4 competes with frontier models at a much lower cost per task.

According to recent reports, our internal set of agentic pipelines builds interactive environments and verifiable tasks from documentation alone, such as screenshots of real websites or open-source software. So far it has produced about 10,000 tasks across web apps, MCP servers and desktop environments, including hybrid environments that expose the same state through a GUI and MCP.

Alongside training, we rebuilt our harness, the loop that executes the model's actions and manages its context over hundreds of steps, using feedback from agentic performance on OSWorld 2.0. Agents tagged why each task failed and engineers reviewed their fixes. The largest changes were giving the agent a reliable memory that can keep track of hundreds of steps, and a shell on the desktop machine itself.

Opus 5 (70.2%) and GPT-5.6 Sol (66.2%) use max-effort partial rewards on the v2026.08.08 offline set from OpenAI's launch chart, as in the cost-performance plot. Other reference scores come from model cards and the official leaderboard. Task releases, subsets and harnesses vary.

Industry observers note that our post-training stack is designed to adapt to new foundation models and produce agents that generalize across interfaces and environments. As a member of the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition, we applied our latest stack to the Nemotron 3 Nano Omni model as a follow-up to Holotron 3.

The same recipe turns Nemotron 3 Nano Omni into Holotron4 Nano, a generalist agentic model that significantly improves over the base model on GUI workflows and in environments exposing MCP, APIs or coding sandboxes.

Gains are absolute percentage-point improvements over Nemotron 3 Nano Omni.

It has been revealed that these gains show that our recipe transfers well and can turn a generalist model into an agentic expert. Nothing in it is size-specific.

In a recent development, both sizes are available today on the H Models API. Weights are on Hugging Face in BF16, FP8, NVFP4 and 4-bit GGUF, next to our small model, Holotron4 Nano.

We will release optimized DSpark drafter checkpoints in the coming days to further accelerate inference.

The planned research foundation includes more than a decade of records from over 5 million patients, following their care over time.

The platform is still to be developed, with its research and AI functions described as intended capabilities. The work is designed to convert information generated during clinical care into research-ready data across therapeutic, diagnostic and surgical areas, giving investigators a common basis for analyzing records across disparate and unstructured formats.

nference will architect the system with federated software designed to protect patient privacy and harmonize data from different clinical formats. Longitudinal curation, the organization of records as patient care unfolds, will include physician adjudication, bringing doctor review into the process of preparing data for research.

In a recent development, the de-identified inputs will include clinical notes, laboratory results, medications and diagnostic reports, alongside radiology and pathology images, genomic information, electrophysiology waveforms, vital signs and flowsheet measurements. Biospecimens collected with patient consent will also be included.

According to recent reports, frequent data refreshes will add new information as routine care progresses. nference envisions this continually updated resource helping researchers gain finer-grained insight into how diseases begin and progress, an intended benefit rather than a demonstrated research outcome.

In a recent development, the platform is intended to support investigator-led studies, grant-funded research, education and quality improvement, as well as collaborations with life-science industry partners. It will also provide a foundation for Cedars-Sinai researchers and affiliated innovators to develop and evaluate new AI models.

Drug discovery, clinical-trial design and future diagnostics are potential downstream uses identified by the companies. Those applications depend on the studies and model evaluations the platform is meant to enable; they are not outcomes unveiled as already achieved.

Sumeet Chugh, vice dean and chief artificial intelligence health research officer at Cedars-Sinai, said the institution expects the collaboration to help clinicians and scientists learn from collective patient-care experience, validate scientific hypotheses and accelerate biomedical discovery.

Industry observers note that the collaboration’s immediate deliverable is research infrastructure: a privacy-focused, regularly refreshed environment that joins clinical curation with AI model development and evaluation. Its broader significance will depend on whether those combined data and curation mechanisms help investigators validate hypotheses and produce useful models across the many kinds of patient information the platform is designed to connect.

#23421. Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

📅 29 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1818 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

📅 29 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1818 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage.
  • Our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap.
  • According to recent reports, consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this blueprint includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage. Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an agent can call a search tool, inspect a structured patient or account record, query a database, and pull metadata, then weave all of it into one answer. That m aakes the usual question of factuality more subtle than it looks. Most of the systems built to check LLM answers, from RAGAS faithfulness to fine-grained checkers like MiniCheck, AlignScore, and SummaC, ask whether a claim is supported by the available evidence once that evidence has been pooled together. In their usual form, they do not tell us which MCP tool output supports each claim, or whether that is the source the answer names.

Our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap. The failure mode we care about is one we call cross-source conflation: a claim that is true somewhere in the evidence, but attributed to the wrong source. A source-blind verifier may pass it, because the fact does exist in the pool. A source-aware verifier should not.

According to recent reports, consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this blueprint includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to. Pool the two together and the claim looks supported. Keep them separate and the attribution is wrong, and in a data-sensitive setting a wrong attribution can be as damaging as a wrong fact. The same pattern demonstrates up in a clinical agent, where a patient-specific medication detail taken from a patient-history tool becomes misleading the moment the answer presents it as a finding from the medical literature.

A claim can be supported by one MCP source while the answer attributes it to another. Source-blind scoring sees support in the pooled evidence and passes it; ProvenanceGuard separately checks whether the supporting source matches the one the answer states or implies. Source: paper Figure 1.

This is why faithfulness scores, useful as they are, are not enough for MCP agents. An answer carries provenance, sometimes explicitly ("according to the account record") and sometimes implicitly. ProvenanceGuard keeps that connection between claim and source available for inspection.

Sources indicate that provenanceGuard is a post-generation verification layer that sits on top of a black-box MCP agent. It runs after an agent produces an answer, and never collapses the evidence into one anonymous context. Instead it carries the source identity all the way through the pipeline. It reads the captured MCP trace, including the tool outputs and their source IDs, without retraining the agent. Then it does five things in sequence: it breaks the answer into specific claims, finds the source most relevant to each one, checks whether that source actually supports it, compares the source with the one the answer names or implies, and finally emits both a per-claim source verdict and a global, answer-level allow or block decision.

The verification flow. Source identity is preserved through decomposition, routing, support scoring, attribution checking, and repair, rather than being pooled. Blocked answers can go through RARR-style repair and be re-verified. Source: paper Figure 2.

A few of the design choices are worth calling out. For the experiments in our paper, we used local models so the captured traces could be processed in a controlled, offline setup: MiniLM helps find the relevant source, a DeBERTa NLI verifier model checks whether that source supports the claim, and a local language model helps break answers into claims. The verifier also checks literal values closely: a number, date, or identifier absent from the source cannot pass merely because the sentence sounds plausible. A calibrated decision step combines these signals. If an answer is blocked, a RARR-style repair step can try a source-grounded revision or a safe fallback, which the verifier then checks again.

Those named models are the setup we evaluated, not a requirement of ProvenanceGuard. The same claim, source, and decision steps can be adapted to hosted models where a team prefers cloud services; a latest setup would need its own testing and calibration. Our reported results come from the local configuration. Its conservative decision policy suits data-sensitive review, where getting the source right matters more than producing the fastest possible answer.

Recent findings suggest that we tested ProvenanceGuard on answers from a medical agent that had used patient records, research articles, and other tools. This gave us 281 real traces to study. Medicine is a useful test because a fact from a patient's record and a fact from general research cannot be treated as the same source. The method can also be used in other fields when an agent keeps a record of its tool outputs and source IDs. For the main test, human experts checked 361 claims from 40 answers set aside from the data used to develop the system.

The most direct result is this: experts said 139 claims should not pass, and ProvenanceGuard caught 138 of them. It let one through. It also held 67 claims that the experts considered supported, sending them for review or repair. This reflects the cautious setting we tested: it favors a second look at some supported claims over letting unsupported ones through. For claims with an identifiable source, it also picked the right source about 86% of the time in this test.

We ran four other support checkers on the same claims. ProvenanceGuard scored highest on the paper's measure of how well a system catches claims that should be blocked while avoiding unnecessary blocks. The other checkers in this comparison did not tell us which tool output supported each claim. ProvenanceGuard records that connection, so a reviewer can see the source checked for each claim and the decision it produced.

Industry observers note that binary support metrics on the same held-out claim packet. ProvenanceGuard matches or beats the source-blind baselines on blocking while also producing per-claim source verdicts. Source: paper abstract and Table III.

Industry observers note that in a separate, harder test with several similar sources, ProvenanceGuard scored 0.846 F1 for deciding which claims to block, but identified the exact source correctly in 50.3% of claims. Telling similar sources apart remains an notable area for improvement.

Industry observers note that we also ran a controlled test focused on wrong attribution: we changed the named source in 50 cases while leaving the supporting evidence intact. ProvenanceGuard caught all 50 swaps. This shows it can detect a clear source error, while the harder test shows the challenge of choosing among many plausible sources.

Blocking is only useful if there is something to do with a blocked answer. Wired to the RARR-style repair loop, the full-trace run resolved all 173 blocked answers, though 144 of them ended in fallback text rather than a substantive rewrite, which is the system choosing to avoid an unverifiable answer rather than manufacture one. On reconstructed multi-source test traces, a fresh repair run resolved all 59 initially blocked answers with only two terminal fallbacks. As an offline gate the overhead is modest, roughly half a second per answer on the reported local configuration, with the NLI and routing calls themselves in the tens of milliseconds.

As agents move from single-passage RAG to multi-tool MCP setups, the question of which source a fact actually came from stops being a footnote and becomes part of what factuality means. ProvenanceGuard makes that source connection visible claim by claim. For Multiverse Computing, that means a way to check existing agents while keeping sensitive traces in a controlled environment when needed. The medical study is one use case; the same approach can be adapted wherever an agent's trace preserves its tools and sources.

Industry observers note that that adaptation is already visible in NVIDIA NVFlow, which merged an optional grounding-verification stage for its finance agent. It checks completed answers against the SEC excerpts the agent retrieved and saves separate decisions without changing the original rollout or training data. The NVFlow contribution uses ProvenanceGuard's source-aware verification approach; the repair loop discussed above belongs to the broader research system.

ProvenanceGuard was also presented as a poster at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 at UC Berkeley.

Recent findings suggest that want the full technical details, including the routing and NLI derivations, the calibration ablations, the multi-source stress slices, and the complete results tables? Read the full paper on Hugging Face, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying source-aware verification to your own agents.

The failure mode that matters for MCP agents is quieter than "hallucination": a claim that is true somewhere in the pooled tool outputs, attributed to the wrong source.

Source-blind faithfulness can still go green in that case — the fact exists in the soup. Source-aware verification is the contract upgrade: keep tool/source IDs through claim decomposition, support check, and attribution check, then allow/block with a per-claim source verdict a reviewer can actually inspect.

Sources indicate that practical ask for teams wiring MCP: when your eval indicates "grounded," does it mean supported-by-any-tool-output, or supported-by-the-source-the-answer-named? Those are different release gates. In multi-tool setups the second one is the one that catches cross-source conflation before a human trusts the citation.

Hi, thank you for your comment. You’ve captured the issue well. For ProvenanceGuard, when a claim is “grounded” it means it is supported by the source the answer names or implies. Finding the fact somewhere else in the tool outputs isn’t enough. In the refund-window example, the policy supports the fact, but the answer credits the account record, so we flag the mismatch and show the source verdict.

I had a brief read on the paper, but I could not find any comparison with cheaper llm agent for source aware judge. Like this is my reading of the paper;.

It has been revealed that like, it seems (2 - 5) can be done via basic prompts in lifecycle, if you own the executing agent. If not, this can also be done via hooks in harness as plugin. Do you have any comparison on this. Basically, how much of random forest, and all of these eng/plumbing is buying, vs second llm call over traces+ans?

Hi, fair question. A source-aware LLM judge could do these checks, and we don’t report a direct comparison with a cheaper one in the paper.

In a recent development, however, part of our motivation is that introducing an LLM judge can itself give inconsistent verdicts or confuse sources (the same kinds of errors we’re trying to catch). A second LLM call can therefore introduce latest errors of its own. ProvenanceGuard uses explicit source tracking and calibrated support checks to reduce reliance on another generative judgment. The comparison you suggest would indeed be a useful further study to quantify the benefit in accuracy, latency and cost.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: The Future of Apache Iceberg.

Nov 20, 2026 3 min read.

Apache Iceberg V4 proposes a redesign of table metadata to improve scalability and support more frequent writes, alongside new capabilities for data management and schema evolution. Daniel Weeks, co-creator of Apache Iceberg and member of technical staff at Databricks, presented a session at QCon San Francisco on the fourth version of the Apache Iceberg open table format specification.

Iceberg V4 will address the limitations of managing very large tables while expanding the format to support new data types and workloads. The speaker described the new version as a major reimagining of the table format rather than an incremental step, with changes including a new metadata tree, more efficient commits, typed column statistics, relative file paths, and support for file and vector data types. While earlier versions left most of the metadata structure intact, V4 addresses problems that emerge at large scale and adds support for new use cases. Weeks told the audience in San Francisco:.

V4 is a major reimagining of a table format. We didn't get everything right in V3 and prior, so now we're taking the opportunity to fix some of the biggest things that are challenges as we scale up to even larger data sets and we bring on new use cases.

Industry observers note that apache Iceberg is an open table format for managing large analytical datasets across different data processing engines. Originally developed at Netflix in 2017, it was open-sourced in 2018 and became an Apache top-level project in 2020. The main alternatives among open table formats are Delta Lake, created by Databricks and now a Linux Foundation project, Apache Hudi, originally developed at Uber, and Apache Paimon, which grew out of the Flink community and gained adoption for streaming-oriented workloads. However, interoperability tools are increasingly blurring the lines between them.

In his talk, Weeks covered three areas of the proposed Iceberg V4 changes: metadata and scalability, including the Adaptive Metadata Tree, single-file commits, improved column statistics, relative paths, and column-level updates; new table features, such as expression-based default values and constraints; and new data types, particularly file and vector types, which support additional workloads such as AI and search. Regarding faster commits, Weeks explained:.

In a recent development, this gets us into use cases where we can stream data much faster. We can do commits at the 2nd level or subsecond level, where right now we largely recommend that you don't do commits under 2 minutes.

In V3, adding a data file requires at least four I/O operations, including manifest creation and rewriting. V4 simplifies this process by allowing the metadata tree's root to point directly to data files, reducing the operation to a single metadata write. According to Weeks, this could enable commits every second or even at subsecond intervals, compared with the current recommendation of at least two minutes between commits. Iceberg V3, introduced in 2024, added deletion vectors, row lineage, latest data types, encryption, and default values.

According to recent reports, V4 replaces V3's binary column statistics with structured, typed statistics, improving projection and schema evolution. Furthermore, V4 introduces expression-based default values, check, unique, and primary key constraints, and statistics-only fields that support partitioning, sorting, and filtering without storing additional data. It will also track constraint validation status, allowing engines to determine when further checks are needed.

In August, Weeks started an initial V4 scope discussion on the Apache Iceberg developer mailing list, with Steven Wu suggesting adding monotonic snapshot and row-level patch timestamps, while Manu Zhang discussed efficient column updates and the removal of equality deletes.

It has been revealed that during the Q&A, Weeks explicitly confirmed that V4 metadata will not be backward compatible with older readers. Existing V3 metadata can remain in place during an upgrade, but older readers cannot consume the new representation.

  • Industry observers note that commvault SHIFT — Nashville, Tenn.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An organization's ability to promptly recover from a business disruption will be a competitive advantage in an era of AI-driven threats and business enablement.

Industry observers note that commvault SHIFT — Nashville, Tenn. — Enterprise data recovery practices must evolve from a last-resort response to a continuous operational discipline focused on minimizing business disruption and containing the blast radius of cyber incidents as quickly as possible.

That was the central message at Commvault's SHIFT 2026 conference this week, where security executives highlighted the growing importance of making operational resilience a business priority as AI-driven threats and increasingly autonomous business processes complicate the task of maintaining continuity.

Sources indicate that "AI is changing the durable advantage you have built for your business, your brand, your supply chain, your data," said Sanjay Mirchandani, president and CEO of Commvault, in a keynote address at the event. "In the AI era, resilience will be your newly introduced competitive advantage.".

Industry observers note that two developments are driving the trend. On the threat side, AI is giving attackers the ability to automate and accelerate reconnaissance, exploit development, social engineering, and lateral movement. The trend has compressed the time organizations have to detect and contain an intrusion, Mirchandani and other executives at the event noted.

Related:What We Missed: Nvidia CEO Scandal Rocks AI Industry.

At the same time, enterprises are increasingly embedding AI into business processes, workflows and decision-making, creating upcoming dependencies on data, applications and autonomous systems.

The result is a more complex operating environment in which a disruption can have wider and faster consequences, making the ability to contain incidents, preserve trusted operations and recover without derailing business activity more notable than ever.

Attackers these days are able to move faster with a level of automation not available before, noted Rajeev Kottomtharayil, chief products officer at Commvault. Increasingly, recovery is becoming not just about speed but bringing back clean data. "If everything is under attack, how do we know what to trust? The real goal is to have a clean, safe space to recover even if everything around you has been compromised," Kottomtharayil remarked.

Business innovation and enablement are also driving the need for greater operational resilience. Resilient operations give organizations the confidence to experiment with AI and put it to work across the business, while ensuring they can recover swiftly when something goes wrong, said Pragnesh Dave, head of generative AI and ML sales at AWS. "AI is collapsing the amount of time it takes to move from an idea to an outcome," he said during a keynote session. As a result, the competitive advantage will come not simply from how quickly organizations can turn intelligence into action, but from how quickly they can do so while managing the risks and consequences when those actions sometimes prove wrong.

Related:Qwen Incidents Show Self-Hosted AI Models Need Stronger Steering.

Dave pointed to the operations model at Amazon that emphasizes the notion of the "door swinging both ways" when teams try to innovate. It is an approach that has enabled teams at Amazon to code more than four times faster than before, he noted.

"The question for everyone is not if something is going to break," he stated. Rather, it is about what the blast radius is and the time it takes from when something breaks to recovering to the prior trusted state. "If something goes wrong, you need to be able to recover rapidly. You should be able to walk back a decision. Think of your recovery time as your innovation project.".

Continuous detection and continuous recovery are going to become a baseline requirement for organizations, argued Peter Diamandis, futurist, entrepreneur, and founder and chairman of the XPRIZE Foundation. Over the next few years, he foresees all organizations harnessing AI to migrate a significant workload to the "digital edge" with humans providing judgement, taste, and oversight. "AI gives us all access to capabilities that were once scarce." The qualities that matter the most will be the speed at which an organization can innovate and that requires standing up capabilities to recover quickly when failures do occur, he said during a keynote address.

Related:Strike Graph Rolls out Integration AI to Automate Continuous Compliance Evidence Using Any Existing Tool.

At the same time, recovery is not becoming a substitute for prevention, says Bill O'Connell, chief security officer at Commvault. Both are equally key. But "building the highest walls and the deepest moat" to keep threats out alone is no longer enough. Organizations have to equally focus on building an ability to recover quickly to a trusted state regardless of the reason for a disruption and to thoroughly test that ability before it becomes necessary.

It has been revealed that the key to keep in mind is that while AI has dramatically accelerated the pace of change it hasn’t altered the need for traditional, and long-familiar, IT governance and controls around their assets, identities, access, authentication and authentication, O'Connell indicates. "The IT maintenance and housekeeping elements still matter." When organizations have supercharged tools which they are not entirely sure how to govern, they need to make sure those fundamentals remain in place.

Industry observers note that in enabling better resilience, organizations should also evaluate what impact third parties could have on their ability to quickly restore operations, O'Connell says. For years, organizations have used questionnaires and external vendor risk-scoring services to try and assess third-party risk. In the AI era, security teams need to go a step further with their most critical suppliers, he adds. O'Connell suggested organizations have their technical architects work with their counterparts at third-party suppliers to understand how critical services are actually configured and what would happen if a provider experienced a breach or a disruption.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) remarked on November 19, 2026 that it will help develop a know-your-agent protocol for financial services and reposition its SGD Testnet as the SG Digital Ledger, an operational settlement utility, as part of prepares to expand agentic transactions and tokenised finance.

Managing Director Chia Der Jiun set out the aims at the Singapore FinTech Festival. Some payment service providers and financial institutions are building agent interfaces, but many institutions have yet to establish terms or channels for agent access. The initiatives address that access gap alongside the settlement infrastructure needed for tokenised markets.

Chia stated some consumers are giving agents their financial-account login credentials and advised against the practice because safety assurance is insufficient. Institutions also lack certainty over whether the customer fully authorised the agent, whether it is transacting within its mandate and instructions, and who bears responsibility if it acts incorrectly or exceeds those instructions.

Recent findings suggest that MAS will facilitate development of a protocol for trusted information exchange between customer agents and financial institutions. It would convey who an agent is and whom it represents, what authority it has received, what mandate it operates under, and what assurance exists about its provenance and reliability. Institutions could use that information to set the terms and scope permitted to each agent and establish a dedicated secure channel for access.

The protocol remains under development, with MAS planning industry collaboration on common approaches. The announcement therefore concerns development work toward a shared access mechanism, rather than the deployment of a finished standard.

It has been revealed that the work builds on Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime (SAFR), a framework published on July 3, 2026 and jointly developed by financial-industry participants under MAS’s BuildFin.ai initiative. It addresses how agent actions are authorised, how human oversight is activated and what is recorded at each decision.

Recent findings suggest that the first phase produced four lessons: agents need bounded autonomy; identity and authority must be established; mandates must specify permissible actions, limits and conditions; and controls should strengthen as an agent’s discretion and potential impact increase. Those principles now carry into the proposed exchange of identity, authority and mandate information.

The protocol work will sit alongside an Agentic Money Sandbox, separately announced by MAS and the Future of Finance Institute on November 18, 2026. The controlled environment allows financial institutions to develop and test agents transacting with digital money within defined authority, limits and safeguards before live deployment. It combines AI agents with programmable money, initially in agent-initiated payments and corporate treasury management.

For corporate treasury, an agent could monitor liquidity positions and due payments, decide when and where funds should move, and use tokenised deposits for permitted actions. The corporate would set the mandate, while participating banks would establish controls and the terms for accepting each instruction. In payments, banks and payment service providers would verify an agent’s identity and authority and apply risk controls before executing transactions using digital money such as tokenised deposits or stablecoins.

Recent findings suggest that the SG Digital Ledger extends the same scale-up agenda to settlement. As an operational utility, it is intended to support settlement across institutions, tokenised assets, different forms of digital money and separate ledgers. The existing testnet has supported interbank settlement and MAS Bill issuance. Chia noted $100 million of MAS Bills was issued and settled against a Singapore dollar central bank digital currency in November 2026, and that market demand would determine how widely the utility is adopted.

Two publications released alongside the keynote address other parts of that infrastructure. The Guardian Tokenised Collateral Framework, developed by industry workgroup members, sets operational requirements across collateral eligibility, custody, valuation, return and enforcement. Collateral is central to derivatives, secured funding and liquidity management, making those operational arrangements vital to potential adoption.

Industry observers note that the BLOOM Field Guide to Extending Settlement Capabilities examines functions, structure, connectivity and controls across end-to-end digital money transactions in different institutional, technical and jurisdictional settings. BLOOM brings together 24 industry members and policymakers from the region. MAS sees tokenised bank deposits, regulated stablecoins and wholesale central bank digital currency as possible forms of settlement money.

It has been revealed that chia said agents could lower search and information costs, support continuous comparison or negotiation, automate procurement and enable more dynamic pricing. These are potential economic consequences of broader agent adoption, rather than measured outcomes of the new initiatives.

In a recent development, alongside those potential benefits, Chia cited emerging studies in simulated environments suggesting that agents could collude without instructions to do so and that more capable agents could secure better prices and terms. Such outcomes would raise concerns about competition and unequal access to capable models. Faster agent-directed movement of money and asset allocation could also lead financial institutions to consider transaction limits and regulators to assess financial-stability implications.

Sources indicate that chia’s stated boundary for adoption was that consumers and businesses retain meaningful control over agents’ objectives, mandates and actions, with bounded autonomy and accountability for actions and outcomes. That principle connects the protocol, sandbox and ledger: broader use depends on making authority and control operational as agents gain the ability to move money more quickly.

In the proposed productivity track, participants will use Alibaba’s MuleRun agent platform to build AI-assisted workflows. In the creative track, they will use Alibaba Cloud’s WonderClip video-creation platform to develop original visual stories, storyboards or short videos.

#23415. Open TTS Leaderboard: Scalable Evaluation for Multilingual Text-to-Speech and Voice Cloning

📅 30 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1390 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Open TTS Leaderboard: Scalable Evaluation for Multilingual Text-to-Speech and Voice Cloning

📅 30 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1390 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The pace of open-source text-to-speech (TTS) model releases has been incredible.
  • Evaluation, however, hasn't kept pace: it remains fragmented and unstandardized.
  • These arenas compare models by presenting users with TTS outputs from two models, and asking them to choose one over the other.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The pace of open-source text-to-speech (TTS) model releases has been incredible. On the Hugging Face Hub (as of Sep 30, 2026) there are more than 8K TTS models available 🚀.

Evaluation, however, hasn't kept pace: it remains fragmented and unstandardized. The gold standard is human preference scores such as MOS or MUSHRA (more on metrics). To this end, several arena-based leaderboards have established themselves as useful reference points for the community:.

These arenas compare models by presenting users with TTS outputs from two models, and asking them to choose one over the other. After collecting a sufficient number of votes, an Elo score is computed to rank models, typically with the Bradley–Terry model (see Voice Arena methodology).

Industry observers note that while human preference is the ultimate decider, arenas cannot scale to keep up with the pace of TTS releases. This may partly explain why open-source models are underrepresented on arena-style leaderboards: as of Sep 30, 2026, only 16 of the 92 models on Artificial Analysis are open-weights, with a similar skew on Voice Arena. This likely reflects practical factors: adding an API model requires little more than an API key, whereas an open model must be hosted and served by the arena operator, and commercial providers have more reason to seek placement than open-source authors. Another limitation with arena-style evaluation is voter consistency: no arena can ensure that the same voters with the same criteria of “better” can consistently evaluate models over time. Even the preferences of a single person change over time (“A man cannot step into the same river twice” as famously remarked by Heraclitus).

To this end, we've built the Open TTS Leaderboard, which uses objective metrics to evaluate models on complementary aspects of performance:.

By relying on objective metrics evaluating a model drops from a couple weeks (for collecting votes) to a couple hours ⚡.

Sources indicate that importantly, the Open TTS Leaderboard does not replace human preference ranking. ASR-based WER provides a proxy for intelligibility, while speaker similarity estimates voice identity preservation. Neither directly measures naturalness, expressiveness, or listener preference. Nevertheless, they can even inform voting-based leaderboards which models to include in their evaluations.

Our intention with this leaderboard is for it to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. The next few sections give an overview of main features of the Open TTS Leaderboard.

From the default view of the leaderboard, models are ranked by macro-average WER on the English splits of Seed TTS Eval (paper) and CV3 Eval (zero shot) (paper).

hexgrad/Kokoro-82M, Supertone/supertonic-3, and fishaudio/s2-pro lead the pack on English WER when averaged on these two splits, while the Pareto plots visualize which models strike a good balance between WER, batched inference (RTFx), and size.

Industry observers note that english performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

k2-fsa/OmniVoice, fishaudio/s2-pro, and FunAudioLLM/Fun-CosyVoice3-0.5B-2512 are strong multilingual models.

By toggling “Voice cloning”, the models that support this functionality (on the selected languages) can be compared.

Moreover, a SIM column for speaker similarity now appears in the table, as well as two more Pareto plots for visualizing the tradeoff between SIM, batched inference, and size.

The average WER of some models, such as bosonai/higgs-tts-3-4b and openbmb/VoxCPM2, improve under voice cloning, namely when a reference audio is provided.

According to recent reports, numbers only tell part of the story, and as mentioned earlier human preference is the ultimate decider. From the “Listen” tab, you can compare the generated outputs that are behind the metrics, to find which model(s) you prefer!

Pick the language/dataset you're interested in, whether you want to compare voice cloning, and optionally pick the models or listen to outputs from a random selection.

The “Listen” tab fills an vital gap in existing TTS leaderboards: a space to explore model outputs of various models.

Sources indicate that you can even give feedback on the generated outputs. As we collect more votes from the community, we may include this data on the leaderboard. So vote! But please login with your HF account to help us weed out spam/bots.

The “Streaming” tab compares the streaming capabilities. Models are ranked by TTFA (time-to-first-audio), which quantifies how long a user waits after probing a model in order to obtain audio that can be played. This is vital for voice agents and other interactive apps.

For streaming models (✅ under “Streaming API”) it's the time until the first audio chunk arrives. For non-streaming models, it's the time until the whole utterance is generated, because playback can't start any earlier. Every model runs one audio at a time (batch size 1), on the same 50 English prompts from CV3-Eval, on the same hardware and in its default voice. We drop the first 3 runs as warm-up and report the median TTFA across the rest.

It has been revealed that the default view compares performance on an H200 GPU. Results are also available for CPU for a small (but growing) set of models!

kyutai/pocket-tts is a great model for streaming on both GPU and CPU!

The goal of the Open TTS Leaderboard is not only to keep up with the incredible pace of TTS model releases, but to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. Let us know which datasets, models, and metrics you want to see!

Industry observers note that we will soon open-source the evaluation scripts, much like the Open ASR Leaderboard repo, so that you can directly provide your feedback and suggestions via GitHub Issues and PRs! Let's shape TTS evaluations together 🤗.

Glad this board splits multilingual TTS quality from voice-cloning identity instead of one aggregate green.

The check I'd keep reading: whether the ranking still holds when you hold language/domain fixed versus when cloning is the axis. Otherwise teams optimize the easier subscale and still call the result "SOTA TTS.".

According to recent reports, english performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has movie box audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

Open TTS Leaderboard is an open evaluation platform designed to make multilingual text-to-speech and voice-cloning models easier to compare at scale. Traditional TTS arenas usually let users listen to outputs from two models and choose the one they prefer. Those votes can then be used to calculate an Elo-style score, often through approaches such as the Bradley–Terry model, giving users a simple way to understand how different systems perform based on human preference.

Sources indicate that human feedback remains an vital part of evaluating speech quality, but relying only on arena-style voting can be difficult as newly introduced TTS models are released at a rapid pace. Open-source models can also face practical barriers because they generally need to be hosted and served by the evaluation platform, while API-based commercial models can be added more easily. This can result in open-weight systems being less visible on public leaderboards. Another challenge is consistency: people's preferences and listening criteria can change over time, meaning that votes collected months apart may not always represent exactly the same standards.

According to recent reports, open TTS Leaderboard aims to address these challenges by providing a scalable and transparent space for evaluating multilingual TTS and voice-cloning systems. The goal is to make comparisons easier to reproduce, expand coverage of open models, and provide useful evaluation signals alongside human preference. By bringing together scalable testing and community feedback, the project can help researchers, developers, and users better understand how speech models perform across different languages, voices, and use cases.

Sources indicate that gitHub repo with the eval scripts is public! https://github.com/huggingface/open-tts-leaderboard.

Recent findings suggest that meredith Whittaker announced on November 20, 2026 that the encrypted messaging app is restricting screenshots on iOS 27 and on Android when it detects an AI assistant trying to read the screen, seeking to prevent operating-system agents from capturing private chats. The protections are incomplete, and Signal cannot reliably block screenshots on macOS.

On iOS 27, the announcement shows an enabled Block Siri AI setting. Android uses a conditional approach: Signal automatically enables Screen security when an AI assistant attempts to access the screen, rather than applying one screenshot rule across every Android distribution. Customers can disable the protection to retain screenshots, though Signal warns that doing so can expose their own and their contacts’ content and break its privacy guarantees.

Industry observers note that signal’s concern is at the endpoint, where private content becomes visible on a screen. Operating-system agents can scan that visible information to answer questions or carry out tasks. Signal states the resulting captures can be stored in a local database or on a remote server used by the agent, outside its control, potentially exposing every participant in a conversation. Application encryption therefore cannot determine what happens to content after the operating system captures it.

Apple said on September 14, 2026 that Siri AI was beginning to roll out in English beta with its 2027 software releases, including onscreen awareness to answer questions or take actions related to content on a user’s screen. Google’s Gemini documentation claims screen actions can upload information visible on the screen or in a file for context, while Intelligent Screen Context can use currently visible content to answer a chat request in English.

It has been revealed that signal’s Android design reflects differences across vendor distributions. On many of them, the company cannot reliably detect a screenshot attempt when screenshots are already disabled. It chose assistant-access detection to avoid screenshots simply stopping without explanation, but that approach also leaves some Android devices without coverage.

Blocking screenshots leaves other routes open as well, including retrieval of content already present on a device through the filesystem. The gap is larger on macOS 27: Signal cannot reliably block screenshots there and cannot apply the available continuous-capture protections to the screenshots most agentic systems use.

Industry observers note that for macOS 27, Signal recommends adding the app under System Settings > Siri > Excluded Apps to protect message content from proactive access by Siri AI. On iPhones, the Electronic Frontier Foundation documented Apple’s iOS 27.2 Excluded Apps control on October 28, 2026. Excluding an app prevents Siri AI from accessing its contents but also disables features such as onscreen awareness for that app. That feature loss illustrates the trade-off behind Signal’s request for exclusions that do not undermine an app’s core utility.

According to recent reports, signal is asking Apple, Google, and Microsoft for a documented way to opt apps out of AI access and processing across screen reading, filesystem access, notifications, APIs, and other operating-system frameworks without undermining core utility. The request also covers accurate technical documentation of how agents access and process data.

Industry observers note that signal argues that confidential-computing approaches are not a complete answer because providers still control the extent of any privacy guarantees. The same concern applies to third-party agents such as Meta’s Muse when deep setup permissions and accessibility settings intended to help people use apps provide broad access to application data.

Signal has used a version of this defense before. On May 21, 2025, it enabled Screen security by default on Windows 11, using a digital rights management window flag so screenshots of Signal Desktop appear blank and Microsoft Recall cannot capture their contents. The Windows control was local to each computer, required a warning and confirmation to disable, and could interfere with accessibility software such as screen readers and magnification tools.

It has been revealed that signal said it is discussing standardized approaches for privacy-sensitive apps with Google and Apple and is cautiously optimistic about further changes. The result is right now a partial defense: Signal can obstruct screenshot capture in certain environments, but the comprehensive privacy boundary it wants still depends on controls and documentation that operating-system providers have not supplied.
