Latest Update: AutoSynthData: Generating Training Data for Enterprise Agents

📅 02 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2016 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments.
  • Industry observers note that the difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data.
  • At ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments. The work they ask these agents to do is shaped by the systems they use, the rules they follow, and the state of their data. A model may be broadly capable and still struggle with a particular environment: a workflow it handles poorly, a combination of tools it misuses, or a constraint it fails to respect. Those are the weaknesses an enterprise needs to improve.

Industry observers note that the difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data. An individual failure tells us something, but training a model requires many new tasks that exercise the same capability in different situations. Those tasks must also be possible to complete in the environment, resemble work someone would actually request, and have a reliable way to check whether the agent succeeded.

At ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data. It uses a target model’s failures and a stronger teacher’s successes to decide what the model should learn next, then generates and validates new tasks that exercise those capabilities. As the model improves, the curriculum shifts toward what it still finds difficult. We illustrate the pipeline with EnterpriseOps Gym (Malay et al., 2026), using the released dataset. We begin by describing the environment an agent operates in and what makes a task useful for training.

An agentic environment defines the world in which an agent operates: the state it can observe and modify, the tools and APIs it can invoke, and the state transitions produced by its actions.

Sources indicate that A task is instantiated within this environment. We use the following abstraction:.

The system specification defines the constraints under which the agent operates, including system instructions, environment policies, and, when applicable, task-specific initialization such as a seeded database state or a set of knowledge articles.

The specification must be compatible with the environment’s tools, state, and supported actions. Its instructions should be clear and avoid arbitrary constraints introduced solely to manufacture difficulty.

Recent findings suggest that the user prompt specifies what the user wants the agent to accomplish, together with any user-level constraints. A generated task should satisfy three properties.

Feasibility. There should exist at least one trajectory in the current environment that satisfies the user prompt while respecting the system specification. This rules out tasks that depend on unavailable tools, inaccessible knowledge, impossible state transitions, or actions prohibited by policy.

Realism. The user prompt should resemble something a user would plausibly ask in the target environment. The space of executable behaviors is usually much larger than the space of realistic workflows.

Difficulty. For training, the task should expose a weakness of the current agent. Tasks that are already solved reliably provide little new training signal. The useful region is therefore tasks that are feasible and realistic, but not yet consistently solved.

Industry observers note that the verifier determines whether the resulting trajectory successfully completes the task. It should satisfy three properties.

Recent findings suggest that consistency. It should agree with the user prompt, the system specification, and the task-specific environment state.

According to recent reports, soundness. It should reject trajectories that fail to satisfy the task or violate relevant constraints.

Completeness. It should accept valid solutions rather than encode one particular reference trajectory.

These properties matter directly during training. A lax verifier can reward incorrect behavior, while an overly restrictive verifier can penalize valid solutions.

Industry observers note that given an environment and a target model, AutoSynthData generates training tasks consisting of a system specification, user prompt, and verifier. The generated tasks are grounded in the environment and selected to provide useful training signal for the current model.

AutoSynthData first evaluates the target model in the environment using diagnostic tasks and identifies patterns in the tasks it struggles to complete. A stronger teacher helps characterize which of those tasks are solvable and what successful behavior looks like. AutoSynthData turns the resulting capability gaps into fresh executable tasks, checks each task in the environment, and uses accepted samples for post-training. Evaluating the updated model reveals which gaps remain and can guide the next round of generation.

AutoSynthData uses evaluation runs in the target environment to identify what the model needs to learn next. In our EnterpriseOps Gym experiment, we run both the target model and a stronger teacher on the evaluation tasks. We examine those runs to identify:.

Recent findings suggest that we distill these findings into sanitized capability specification cards. The evaluation tasks guide what the model should learn, but the generator does not receive their original prompts, entities, trajectories, or verifier details. It receives the cards and uses them to create upcoming tasks with different prompts, states, and solution paths.

Identifying a capability gap tells us what to teach, but training requires many varied tasks that exercise it. AutoSynthData uses the specification card to generate those tasks.

Suppose the target model struggles with tasks that require the following workflow:.

The generator creates fresh tasks that exercise this workflow, varying the entities, initial environment state, workflow composition, tool combinations, wording, and difficulty. The stronger teacher then demonstrates a successful trajectory for each task. For supervised fine-tuning (SFT), these demonstrations teach the target model how to apply the capability in new situations.

AutoSynthData builds the dataset in two phases: first generating and validating core samples, then expanding them into novel variants.

Industry observers note that the target phase creates the core set of training samples from the capability specifications. Workers generate independent tasks in parallel, picking up a new target when they finish. Each candidate goes through validation, execution, solver evaluation, and repair before acceptance. The result is a batch of vetted examples built around what the target model needs to learn.

The multiply phase expands the dataset by creating novel variants of accepted target samples. Each variant has its own user request, environment state, entity configuration, reference trajectory, and verifier, and must pass the same validation and execution checks. A multiplied sample cannot seed another multiplied sample. This anchors expansion to the vetted target set and limits drift across generations.

To support both phases, AutoSynthData separates generation control from environment-specific execution. A shared controller coordinates generation, quality control, coverage, and dataset construction, while an adapter handles environment execution, task and state management, reference replay, deterministic verification, solver execution, and task profiling.

Together, parallel target generation and multiplication provide a path to training-scale datasets. Their usefulness depends on the checks applied to every candidate: the task must be executable, the solution must work, and the verifier must distinguish success from failure.

Sources indicate that generating a plausible request is not enough to produce useful training data. A task may be impossible in the target environment, its reference solution may fail when executed, or its verifier may reward the wrong final state. AutoSynthData checks these properties before accepting a task for training.

AutoSynthData reviews quality at two levels: individual candidates must pass verification, and batches must provide useful coverage and diversity.

In a recent development, each candidate must clear a quality-control loop before entering the training dataset. We begin with solver evaluation to measure difficulty. In the configuration used here, we favor tasks the target model solves on no more than one of three trials and the stronger solver solves on at least two of three trials. Candidates also undergo positive and negative verification and a bounded repair process.

The positive gate asks: Does the intended solution solve the generated task?

The pipeline executes the reference trajectory in the target environment and checks the resulting state against the candidate’s verifier. This reveals mismatches among the prompt, initial state, solution, and success criteria.

The negative gate asks: Do relevant incorrect outcomes fail?

In a recent development, for example, it can mutate parts of the expected outcome and confirm that those states no longer pass verification. This catches weak verifiers that award success without requiring the intended behavior.

Industry observers note that failed candidates go to a critic before being discarded. The critic examines the sample and its failure, looking for inconsistent state, impossible workflows, incorrect task construction, bad reference trajectories, weak verifier logic, or a mismatch with the intended capability. The critic’s findings guide repairs, with a fixed limit on retries:.

A repaired task must pass the relevant checks again. The diagnosis guides repairs to the existing candidate rather than requiring generation to start over.

Passing these checks makes a sample eligible for training, but individually valid samples can still form a repetitive or unbalanced dataset. AutoSynthData therefore also reviews generation at the batch level.

A batch may overrepresent a few easy task families, miss a capability, or reflect too much generation effort spent on a low-yield pattern.

Recent findings suggest that A meta-review examines accepted samples, rejected samples, and generation behavior across each batch. It asks:.

The controller tracks coverage in the accepted dataset, reduces generation in overrepresented regions, and directs more work toward gaps. When a region repeatedly produces poor candidates, critiques and meta-review guide changes to the generation strategy. These adjustments balance useful learning signal, task quality, coverage, diversity, and low redundancy within the available generation budget and dataset size requirements.

Together, these feedback loops improve both individual tasks and the dataset they form: sample-level checks guide candidate repair, while batch-level review guides future generation.

The useful training distribution changes as the model improves. AutoSynthData treats synthetic data generation as a search for tasks near the target model's capability boundary: difficult enough to expose weaknesses, but solvable enough for the teacher to provide reliable demonstrations.

Sources indicate that after post-training, we evaluate the updated model in the same environment. Tasks it now solves reliably are less useful for the next training round; persistent failures point to capabilities that still need attention. Those results can guide the next generation round.

Our experiments focus on SFT, but the same mechanism could support reinforcement learning (RL): generate tasks that challenge the current policy and provide reliable learning signal, train, then move the generation target with the updated policy. We strategy to test this moving, difficulty-calibrated frontier beyond SFT.

We use EnterpriseOps Gym to test whether this approach improves a model on tasks in a stateful enterprise environment. We generate training tasks in the Gym’s Hybrid and ITSM environments, fine-tune the target model on accepted samples, and evaluate the resulting checkpoints.

We tested the pipeline on the Hybrid domain of EnterpriseOps Gym using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and Qwen3.8-27B as the teacher.

According to recent reports, autoSynthData generated 2,000 synthetic training samples in about 18 hours. We fine-tuned Gemma on this dataset and evaluated the resulting checkpoints on the benchmark. The best checkpoint was epoch 5.

Industry observers note that the synthetic SFT checkpoint improves mean Pass@1 by 7.2 percentage points, a 35% relative improvement, and raises verifier success from 63.01% to 68.55%. It closes 59% of the original Pass@1 gap between Gemma and the reference model.

It has been revealed that the training tasks were newly generated from capability specifications; the generator did not receive the original evaluation tasks. The result demonstrates improvement in EnterpriseOps Gym Hybrid, the environment used for this experiment.

We also applied AutoSynthData to the ITSM domain of EnterpriseOps Gym, using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash as the teacher. AutoSynthData generated 1,994 synthetic training samples in 66 hours. Generation took longer than in the subsequent Hybrid run described above, primarily because the ITSM run used a larger teacher model and preceded pipeline optimizations that improved throughput.

On ITSM, synthetic SFT raises mean Pass@1 from 18.77% to 27.18%, showing that the approach also improves performance in a second domain.

According to recent reports, the tasks most useful for training depend on both the environment and the model working in it. AutoSynthData uses the model’s failures to choose what to generate, validates latest tasks against the environment, and makes those tasks available for post-training. Our EnterpriseOps Gym results show the value of that approach in a controlled setting. As the model changes, the same process can focus on the gaps that remain.

Best Supporting Agent: Why Agentic AI in the Contact Centre Still Needs a Human Lead

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, agentic AI is moving fast from answering customer questions to taking action on their behalf.
  • But giving software permission to act also raises the question of what happens when a customer needs an exception, or when an automated decision is technically correct but plainly unfair.
  • Sources indicate that the opportunity is substantial, provided contact centres are deliberate about which decisions AI can make and when human lead is required.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, agentic AI is moving fast from answering customer questions to taking action on their behalf. It can retrieve account records and move a request forward without waiting for an agent’s input. For contact centres under pressure to handle more conversations with limited resources, that is an appealing prospect.

But giving software permission to act also raises the question of what happens when a customer needs an exception, or when an automated decision is technically correct but plainly unfair. These are everyday realities of customer service, and also moments when trust is won or lost.

Sources indicate that the opportunity is substantial, provided contact centres are deliberate about which decisions AI can make and when human lead is required. A strong option for contact centres is to use automation for routine tasks while giving agents the authority to resolve complex customer problems.

In a recent development, traditional contact-centre automation could only do so much. Customers were often stuck navigating phone menus or choosing from a limited set of options, and anything more complicated usually meant waiting to speak with an agent. Agentic systems can go further, and given the right permissions, they can follow a customer’s request across multiple systems and carry out approved steps. A request to change an appointment, for example, might involve checking eligibility and updating the booking.

That changes the role of the human agent. Instead of spending the first few minutes hunting for information, an agent can enter the conversation with a clear picture of what has already happened. A well-designed assistant can surface and summarize previous interactions before the agent has to ask another question.

Industry observers note that AI can make a real difference in customer service. A study on customer support agents involving more than 5,000 workers found that agents using AI assistance resolved about 15% more customer problems per hour. The biggest improvements came from less experienced agents, who benefited from having helpful suggestions available while handling customer requests.

According to recent reports, these findings are encouraging, but there’s an crucial detail to be considered. The AI was helping agents do their jobs, with people still making the decisions. That leaves an important question for contact centres exploring agentic AI: how much responsibility should these systems have when working directly with customers?

Speed is certainly part of good service, but customers also expect accurate answers and fair treatment. An AI agent might resolve a billing inquiry in seconds, but if it misunderstands the customer’s situation or applies the wrong policy, that quick resolution could turn into another complaint. Contact centres need to look beyond how promptly an glitch is closed and consider whether the customer actually received the help they needed.

Even with access to customer records, AI doesn’t always have the full picture. Take a billing dispute, for example. The AI checks the account and confirms that a charge matches the contract. However, the customer was previously promised a credit during a service outage, and that information was never added to the billing system. The AI may give an answer based on the available records, but an experienced agent can recognize that something is missing and investigate further.

It has been revealed that in 2026, Alibaba’s customer service operations revealed that AI shortened conversations but received lower customer ratings in AI-eligible interactions. The research also showed that the effectiveness of human intervention depended on when agents stepped in and what had gone wrong. These findings suggest that knowing when to involve a person is just as vital as knowing what AI can handle.

For contact centres, the handoff from an AI agent to a human agent deserves as much attention as the technology itself. Customers shouldn’t have to repeat their concerns every time they’re transferred. Agents need access to previous conversations and the actions AI has already taken so they can pick up where the system left off. A smooth transition can make all the difference, especially when someone is already frustrated and simply wants their problem resolved.

Contact-centre leaders need to think carefully about how much control they give AI. Preparing a refund recommendation, for example, carries less risk than issuing a large credit without approval. Build these limits into the system from the start, with clear rules for when an agent needs to step in.

Contact centres can establish these boundaries by focusing on a few practical measures:.

Sources indicate that as AI takes on more responsibilities, these boundaries should be reviewed and adjusted based on how the technology performs in real customer interactions. This allows contact centres to expand automation while maintaining accountability for the decisions being made.

Recent findings suggest that A contact centre can celebrate a lower average handling time while customers lose confidence. If someone calls back the next morning because an AI agent promised a change that never happened, the first conversation was not a success. The reporting should make that visible.

In a recent development, alongside speed and containment, teams should examine repeat contacts, reopened cases, correction rates, customer complaints and how often a human must reverse an automated action. They should review escalations for missing context and track whether the AI’s recommendations were useful to the people receiving them. These measures are notable when automated actions affect a customer’s money or access to a service.

According to recent reports, leaders should also ask agents what the system gets wrong. Frontline agents hear the awkward pauses and recognize when a customer has lost patience. Their feedback is a source of operational intelligence. Give them a quick way to flag errors, and show them what changed as a result. If every correction disappears into a generic feedback form, the team will stop bothering.

Recent findings suggest that however, using AI to understand agent experiences also raises questions about how closely workers should be monitored. Some tools claim they can detect emotions through a person’s voice. For example, the EU AI Act generally prohibits using AI to identify agents’ emotions in the workplace, with limited exceptions. The European Commission has even used call centres as an example. Businesses should check the laws in their region before introducing these tools.

There is a tempting vision of a contact centre where almost every conversation ends without a person. It makes for a neat presentation slide. Actual customers tend to be less tidy. They change their minds, misunderstand instructions, ask for exceptions and bring personal circumstances that a system may not be able to judge fairly.

As AI takes on more responsibilities, contact-centre leaders need to make sure their teams can recognize mistakes and correct them quickly. Customers shouldn’t have to repeat their problems or deal with the consequences of an automated decision that went wrong.

AI’s success in customer service depends on how well it supports agents in delivering the service customers expect.

InfoQ Homepage Presentations Modernising Retail at Scale: Architecting a Cloud‑to‑Edge Platform for a Global Enterprise.

Jayesh Bhayani discusses Tesco’s decade-long enterprise transformation from fragmented legacy systems to a unified cloud-edge platform. He explains how aligning system, talent, and process modernizations allowed Tesco to scale mission-critical retail operations to millions of customers, while sharing practical lessons on build vs. buy, cloud cost management, and preparing for agentic commerce.

You have to find the right demand, where the business demand, the customer demand is there, and find the right opportunities to do transformation in small steps early on, and then it gets bigger and bigger. Now we get more demand from the business with more trust, less questions. You say, how can we do it right?

Recent findings suggest that we have been using AI for a very long time at Tesco. That's nothing latest for us. For example, start with all those business units I was saying, supply chain. One of the biggest challenges is forecasting how much customers would buy. If you go wrong in that one, it either leads to loss in millions or very poor customer experience. For example, if you forecast that you will sell 100kgs of tomatoes. It's in tons generally. I'm just taking an easy number. Except if you go wrong, either your shelves will be empty because customers are buying more and you need more than 100kg, or you will end up buying too much and it goes to waste. That's a tiny example, but that whole forecasting is dependent upon what's the lead time to getting the products.

According to recent reports, like tomatoes can be supplied four times in a day in our distribution center. Something like jeans might be six months in advance. Then the shelf life could be very different. Tomatoes will get rotten in few days, non-perishable items will stay on the shelf for longer time, so the combination of that. That's the supply chain side. Distribution, how are you going to lay out all that stock? What's the stock management? What's the truck routing algorithms? Because we are talking about hundreds and thousands of miles of trucks traveling every day. How are you going to optimize that? Good for environment, good for company, good for everyone. How do you fill the truck? This is just touching into the supply chain area. Likewise, when you talk about ranging, you talk about customer experience in personalization, you talk about pricing, everything is AI driven. How are we thinking about agentic commerce?

It has been revealed that because that changes the paradigm completely. What I noted is agentic commerce is a business decision. Because if you don't participate in agentic commerce, you can be marginalized. Because, let's say most customers are spending time on ChatGPTs and Geminis of the world, and they are going into agentic commerce to say, we can do grocery for you. Of course, they want that. Nothing wrong in it. That's where customers are. If you don't go there, you can be marginalized. If you go there, you can still be marginalized because you're losing the first touch, customer experience. Because now you outsource that experience to someone else. Hence, it's a business decision. It's not just a technology decision. Getting ready requires complete shift. How would you be ready for agentic commerce? Because what used to be the simple SEO and SEM, the metadata and data on your website where the search engines will come and crawl your website and then you appear in the searches, organic search or paid search.

Recent findings suggest that now the agentic crawlers will come and you need much more machine-readable format of that data so that agents can understand. That's just the AEO, agentic understanding. We'll look at the architecture as to how you will prepare for that kind of integration. You will need the same kind of identity consent and policy frameworks as to how much you can allow the agents to operate on your website or through your APIs. Then multiple protocol interfaces are emerging, UCPs, ACPs. The platform completely evolves from a system of record, that's how it used to be, to a system of delegation. Because now those agents are working with your data, with your services, making decisions for the customer. It's a complete delegation.

That's the harness, how we are thinking. We are still going to use the platform because the core capabilities are still within our retail platform. If you look at the bottom left, customers, the bottom part is the existing path, existing online channels or stores from that perspective, existing application gateway, existing experience APIs going into our platform, retail platform. When you're talking about the agents on the top, you'll need now the gateways for the agents. How would you allow them? How much would you allow them? Which one would you allow them? The commerce protocol, ACP and UCP, now there are severe regulations in the UK for making payments, not allowed for agents to make payments on behalf of customers. Again, there are differences between the countries and regions to say what is allowed, what is not allowed. Many of these technologies, and I'm talking about both UCP, ACP, we are in direct conversation, are not ready for production scale yet.

Industry observers note that as much as there is marketing, they are not ready. For Tesco scale, again you need very different readiness. We are not even talking about risk and compliance and anything here. I'm just talking pure technology risk here. Then you will have your own sub-agents that might be running, which might be talking to these agents and hence agent-to-agent protocol. You will need MCP for discovery of many of these services, discovery of data. Many of our application experience APIs were built for the applications that we built, like add item to basket, for example. What could have been better is, build central tech platform early. Sources indicate that location strategy. Most companies, they assume that engineering can be even in-sourced where they are your own teams. Try to create self-sufficient teams. I touched on three parts of those transformation, a little bit of each one of them to say what's important. There are many more in that one. Just system transformation is not enough. Change business processes when required, because they are just organically developed like your technology systems as well. Question that to say, is that really different? Why should four different countries have different operational processes? Simplify operation. Build core capabilities, we just talked about that. Breaking: The Agent Remarked It Was Done. The Database Disagreed.

📅 03 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2590 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row.
  • Figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind.
  • Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row. It is now available through Hugging Face.

Figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind. From our ThinkingBox paper.

A customer writes in. Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date.

Sources indicate that the AI agent does careful work. Nine tool calls: it pulls the order, checks tracking, looks up her customer profile, searches the refund policy twice, confirms no ticket exists, opens one, documents the timeline, and reads the policy correctly; her account segment genuinely does not qualify for late-delivery compensation.

Sources indicate that then it closes the ticket as resolved and replies “ Since your query is resolved, is there anything I may assist you with? ”.

Two things are wrong. The carrier exception is still open, so the required end state was on hold, pending resolution. And the customer never got a real answer to what she actually asked.

An AI grader checking tool calls would see nine well-formed ones. The grader checking whether the agent wrote to the database would see that too. The database is what disagrees.

It has been revealed that that gap is what ThinkingBox measures. Across 507 stateful business workflows, each run 20 times against various LLM models, it grades agents on terminal backend state and side effects. This post covers what we found, what consistency costs, and how to run the benchmark yourself through OpenEnv.

You can run this one yourself: the example above is adapted from a benchmark task sandbox_external_retail_group1.py:test_case_ST003_006, and the executable check that fails is a single field: the ticket's status is solved where the required end state is hold. The full trace is in Appendix D.4, Case 3 of our paper.

Want to try it before reading the results? Skip to section Run it yourself.

Final responses and valid tool calls are only proxies. An agent can sound correct while leaving the wrong value, changing the wrong record, or creating an extra side effect. Only the records it leaves behind settle the question.

The gap is substantial. In a common-set ablation covering 121,680 valid trials across 12 LLM models, 79,853 attempts failed the executable checks. Of those failures, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error. Executable checks nevertheless found wrong field values in 77.61% of them, unintended extra effects in 43.30%, and missing required effects in 25.36%. Those state-check findings overlap.

A trajectory is a claim. Database state is the evidence. Repetition is the trust test.

Industry observers note that an agent that processes a refund correctly once and mishandles it the next four times is not a working refund agent. So every task runs 20 independent times, each from an identical clean backend, and we report three different things:.

Table 1: The three numbers we report, and the question each one answers.

Recent findings suggest that we use observed 20/20 in this blog post as the literal count of how many of the 507 tasks passed 20 out of 20. No estimator, no smoothing.

Starting with the familiar view. The table below reports pass@1, the single-attempt score estimate, broken out by domain. This is the number most leaderboards publish, and on its own it reads like an ordinary capability ranking.

Table 2: ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain. Each model is evaluated on every task for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the group leader; underline marks the runner-up. The standard errors for the single attempt score estimates are provided in Table 4 in our ThinkingBox paper.

Claude Opus 5.5 leads overall at 67.16%, two-thirds of a point above Claude Opus 5. Kimi-K3 is the strongest open-weights model, within a point of GPT-6-Astra. Domain matters just as much: Claude Opus 4.6 scores 68.62% on retail but 8.30% on auto insurance.

In a recent development, one good run tells you a model can do the work. It does not tell you whether it will do it again. So run every task 20 times and ask how much of that score survives.

Figure 2: How much of each model's single-attempt score survives 20 repeats.

It has been revealed that only three hold on to most of their pass@1 scores: GPT-6 Astra retains 78% of its single-attempt rate, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Opus 5 each retain 71%. At the other end, GLM-5.1, Kimi-K2.6 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro each keep about 8%.

The gap between what a model can do once and what it does every time is the whole story.

Industry observers note that figure 3: Breadth and consistency pull apart. Twelve of the eighteen models are shown; six below 33% pass@1 are omitted for legibility.

In a recent development, kimi-K3 has the broadest coverage of any model we tested. It solves 93.89% of the benchmark at least once: 476 of 507 tasks. Only 31 tasks defeat it entirely, the lowest count in the field. On retail workflows it leads outright at 82.24% pass@1, ahead of every proprietary model.

In a recent development, kimi-K3 is also among the least consistent. Just 68 of 507 tasks, 13.41%, succeed in all 20 attempts.

Sources indicate that claude Opus 5 inverts this. It solves fewer tasks at least once (79.09%; 106 defeat it entirely) but completes 47.53% of the benchmark on every single attempt.

A newer model does not fix this. Claude Opus 5.5 scores higher than Claude Opus 5 on every-attempt average, 67.16% against 66.50%, and solves more tasks at least once. It passes exactly the same number of tasks on all 20 attempts: 241. Half a point of headline accuracy bought no additional dependability at all.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches real records, pass@20 is the wrong column to look at.

Sources indicate that capability comparisons usually stop at the score. For anyone deploying, the relevant question is what a successful unit of work costs. We measure that as cost per successful task attempt. We say task attempt because every benchmark task is run repeatedly and cost is incurred per attempt, so pass@1 is the matching quality denominator.

Sources indicate that we took each model's recorded token usage from its full 507 × 20 campaign and priced it at undiscounted list rates available on OpenRouter+, reversing promotional discounts and excluding endpoints that declare quantization. Input, output and cache rates all come from one provider endpoint per model.

Then we divided one run's cost by the number of attempts that succeeded:.

Cost per successful task attempt = estimated cost for 507 attempts, one per task ÷ (507 × pass@1).

This is a comparative efficiency index, not an invoice, and not the price of serving one production request. It also prices single successes, not consistency. We price consistency next.

Example: GPT-5.4 costs $43.49 for 507 attempts (one attempt per task) and has 65.36% pass@1, so $43.49 ÷ (507 × 0.6536) = $0.131 per successful task attempt.

A model is on the frontier if no other model is both no more expensive and at least as accurate. Three models qualify; every other model is dominated on at least one axis.

Figure 4: Cost per successful task attempt against pass@1. Ringed dots are pareto cost frontier models.

According to recent reports, the frontier has three steps. GPT-5.6 Sol has the lowest cost per success at $0.127; GPT-5.4 raises pass@1 by 3.45 percentage points for $0.004 more per success; Claude Opus 5.5 adds another 1.80 points at $0.276 per success. Each of the three remains on the cost frontier line because no cheaper model matches its pass@1.

Claude Opus 5 is the clearest case: at $0.475 per successful attempt and 66.50% pass@1, it is both more expensive and less accurate than Claude Opus 5.5 at $0.276 and 67.16%.

Industry observers note that cost per success rewards a model that is cheap and often right. It does not reward a model that is right every time. So we also compute cost per dependable task: the cost of the full 20-run campaign divided by the number of tasks the model passed on all 20 attempts.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of 20 runs of 507 attempts ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

Example: GPT-6-Astra costs 20 × $86.03 = $1,720.60 for the campaign and passes 231 tasks on every attempt, so $1,720.60 ÷ 231 = $7.45 per dependable task.

It has been revealed that table 3: The nine lowest costs per dependable task among models with at least one observed 20/20 task, sorted low to high. Estimated $, not actual cloud bills.

In a recent development, now rank by consistency. GPT-5.4 is the cheapest at $6.80, though only 128 tasks meet the bar. GPT-6 Astra reaches 231 at $7.45, and Claude Opus 5.5 the joint-highest 241 at $7.80.

According to recent reports, none of the three dominates the others: each additional dependable task costs more. Claude Opus 5 also passes 241, but at $13.30, so Opus 5.5 dominates it outright. GPT-5.6 Sol, the cheapest per single success at $0.127, costs $9.76 per dependable task. The cheapest way to get a right answer is not the cheapest way to get a dependable one.

We assign each failed trace one deterministic diagnostic signature, and the headline is actionable: roughly four in five failures are tool handling, not reasoning. Across an ablation study in Table 5 of our paper:.

These are unweighted averages of per-model shares and observable labels, not unique causal explanations.

The practical pattern is simple: agents usually get far enough to attempt the workflow, then fail to recover from tool errors, failed preconditions, or empty lookups. That is a retry and error-recovery problem before it is a model problem.

Difficulty also changes by domain: across the models listed in Table 2 above, retail averages 59.52% pass@1 while auto insurance averages 33.83%.

What to do about it. Treat the 20/20 rate as a design input, not a verdict. The same signal the benchmark grades on is available in production: check the terminal state before you commit, not the model's summary of it.

Recent findings suggest that classify tool and system errors so retries target the recoverable ones. Cut the tool surface to what the workflow needs. And require human approval on the changes you cannot cheaply reverse. We have not measured the lift from any of these on this benchmark, which is exactly the kind of thing the environment now makes testable.

ThinkingBox is the agent sandbox, while ThinkingBox-Bench is a dataset benchmark to evaluate agents. The diagram at the top of this post indicates the loop; here is what each part does.

Figure 5: The sandbox loop from panel A in Figure 1 above: isolated tool session, terminal database state, side effects, executable judges.

Each task defines a starting backend state, a user goal, the available MCP tools, the domain policy, and executable checks over the terminal state. A simulated user holds private context (a booking reference, a preference, or a date of birth) and releases it only when asked.

According to recent reports, every attempt gets an isolated MCP session with freshly initialized state. Two attempts of the same task never share a database row or cached tool state, which is what makes 20-trial comparison meaningful.

Sources indicate that at the end, a side-effect extractor derives what actually changed, and deterministic judges compare it against the required end state, accepting any trajectory that produces the right outcome while rejecting wrong, missing or extra effects. For requirements with no clean database value ("did the agent disclose this is not guaranteed?"), a narrow binary rubric question handles the semantics. 477 of the 507 tasks are graded on state alone; 30 add response rubrics.

The trust boundary: the model sees tasks, dialogue and tool schemas. Golden state, assertions, grading internals and credentials stay on the evaluator side.

ThinkingBox is now on Hugging Face, both the harness and the dataset. ThinkingBox-Bench now sits behind the OpenEnv interface, and each finished episode returns a binary pass/fail reward. The released adapter is designed for evaluation; separate, non-benchmark scenarios can use the same interface in training workflows.

Tested on Linux and WSL, with Python 3.11+, uv and Docker. You also need a thinkingbox-data checkout at the pinned release and model endpoints for the agent, simulated user and judge. One endpoint can serve all three roles, which is the simplest way to start. The OpenEnv image starts only the OpenEnv API; everything else you run yourself.

In a second terminal, start Typesense 30.1 and wait for its health check:.

In a third terminal, start the Session Proxy and MCP servers.

Back in the first terminal, start the OpenEnv server against a ThinkingBox YAML config naming your three models (config guide):.

Gate on readiness before running anything. It returns 503 until its observable data, configuration and Session Proxy checks pass. It cannot observe Typesense or live-probe every model endpoint, so confirm those separately:.

Now score a real episode. example_usage.py only resets and lists tools; for agent actions, effects and assertions use the packaged evaluator:.

The OpenEnv adapter writes operational failures to an errors sidecar so they can be rerun rather than silently mixed with model outcomes. A canonical result must resolve or explicitly account for those attempts; we counted system errors as unsuccessful trials.

Runs are gated on a pinned framework commit, a pinned data release and a bundle hash, so a canonical result is verifiable rather than asserted.

Recent findings suggest that the useful part of this work is not our pass@1 leaderboard. It is the environment.

If you are evaluating an agent that touches real records:.

Questions are welcome in the comments section below or on github or by email at firstnamelastname@microsoft.com.

+ OpenRouter cost snapshot taken on Sept 20th 2026; Opus 5.5 pricing as per the Anthropic site.

Recent findings suggest that ST003_006 delegates its pass check to validate_database. Unequal result and golden database hashes fail even when diff is empty. The diff explains a failure; it does not decide the pass.

In a recent development, this small replay exercises the released function with four authored effect inputs. Run python3 reproduce.py. It verifies the source pin and tests supplied hashes; it does not calculate a database hash, run an agent, or reproduce the full environment.

AI-assisted source reading and example by CyberNative AI LLC.

The useful cut is agent-reported "done" versus backend terminal state.

A green success from the same process that acted is a claim, not a grade. I'd want the eval to score durable side effects (ticket status, refund state, policy-cited fields) against a frozen oracle — and fail when the narrative is green while the database disagrees.

Practical check: can a run be marked done when the terminal-state fixture is red?

  • The platform is built on Microsoft Azure for secure, compliant cloud infrastructure and Microsoft Foundry for AI agents that interpret results and guide instrument control.
  • One initial application is MetaXpress Acquire AI Assistant, Molecular Devices’ software for its high-content cellular imaging systems, designed to provide product support.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Danaher declared a strategic partnership with Microsoft on November 20, 2026, to develop a shared agentic platform for scientific instrument control and insight generation, with initial commercial applications expected in 2026 and additional agent-enabled instruments planned for 2027.

The platform is built on Microsoft Azure for secure, compliant cloud infrastructure and Microsoft Foundry for AI agents that interpret results and guide instrument control. Danaher’s goal is to give specialized products a reusable foundation while keeping the system open to agents and digital solutions in multi-vendor laboratories. That architecture links reuse across Danaher’s technologies with interoperability in laboratories that combine multiple suppliers. For those laboratories, the stated openness extends the interoperability goal beyond any single Danaher product or business.

One initial application is MetaXpress Acquire AI Assistant, Molecular Devices’ software for its high-content cellular imaging systems, designed to provide product support. The companies are continuing to develop the wider platform. That first example sits at the product-support end of the roadmap; the planned instruments are intended to extend into experimental setup, execution and analysis.

Recent findings suggest that the instruments are being designed to translate scientific intent into experimental plans, instrument setup and methods. They would guide execution and troubleshooting while controlling hardware within defined safety boundaries and with user oversight. The design also includes interpreting results and identifying quality challenges in real time, then recommending corrective actions and next experiments for scientist review.

In a recent development, together, those functions would extend software assistance across the experimental cycle. The oversight model applies different constraints at different steps: instruments can operate hardware within set limits, while scientists assess the recommended corrections and subsequent experiments.

Sources indicate that in preliminary internal testing, Danaher reported, novice scientists conducting an AI-assisted experiment on a Leica microscope took up to 83% less time and up to 68% fewer steps to complete it than a novice working without the assistant. The assisted novices also produced high-quality data and completed the experiment in a time comparable to an expert. The reductions come from the novice-versus-novice comparison; the expert comparison concerns completion time.

Industry observers note that julie Sawyer Montgomery, Danaher’s president and CEO, remarked: “With Microsoft, we are building a common foundation, so our instruments and laboratories work together consistently, as one connected Danaher. Through context and learning, that foundation can continuously inform the next experiment and the best analysis.”.

The partnership sits within Danaher’s broader AI and autonomous-science strategy, connecting intelligence at the instrument with data, laboratory workflows and physical experiment execution. Intelligent instruments are the first step. As instruments and laboratory systems become more connected and interoperable, Danaher expects experimental results to help scientists determine what to do next, supporting increasingly connected and autonomous workflows under scientific oversight.

The planned instrument rollout will test whether one shared foundation can support reuse within Danaher and openness across multi-vendor laboratories while preserving the safety boundaries and scientist review built into the design.

  • In our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%.

In a recent development, we’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect. Developed at the Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in Abu Dhabi, it also supports English, French, Spanish and Portuguese.

In our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used. On our internal Emirati evaluation, it recorded the lowest word and character error rates among the systems we compared.

We also support word-level timestamps for transcriptions, linking each transcribed word to its position in the audio.

Sources indicate that arabic speech varies by region, speaker and setting. A model that handles a formal news broadcast may still struggle with a conversation in Emirati or with speech recorded over a phone line. Dialectal Arabic also has fewer transcribed resources than Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), which makes training and evaluation harder.

We trained Falcon-ASR on Emirati, MSA, other Gulf and Arabic dialects, and English. Our aim is to transcribe the words people use in everyday speech, including dialectal forms and changes between languages.

Recent findings suggest that the Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard, maintained by the ELM Research Center, ranks systems by the equal-weight average WER across six test sets. It also reports character error rate (CER). Lower values are better for both metrics. Our Falcon-ASR evaluation follows this protocol.

Recent findings suggest that WER = Word Error Rate; CER = Character Error Rate. A lower value indicates better performance.

Industry observers note that we evaluated Falcon-ASR on the same six benchmarks using the leaderboard’s pinned manifests. Competitor figures are the published leaderboard averages checked on 30 September 2026. Falcon-ASR’s average WER is 2.25 percentage points better than the best published result in that snapshot.

Recent findings suggest that public evaluation data already includes Emirati: Casablanca has a UAE subset. We complement that coverage with an internal evaluation of additional Emirati and Gulf speech, using held-out recordings and human-validated transcripts to assess transcription accuracy beyond the public UAE subset.

In our internal Emirati evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved 22.73% WER and 10.19% CER:.

Sources indicate that falcon-ASR has the lowest WER and CER among the systems compared here. Its WER is 4.07 percentage points below Qwen3-Omni, the next best result. The results show improved transcription accuracy at both the word and character level on this evaluation.

We included background noise, overlapping speech, music, room reverberation and telephony effects, as well as variations in speed and pitch. We applied the same treatment to Emirati recordings, exposing the model to a range of conditions it may encounter in meetings, calls and other everyday recordings.

It has been revealed that falcon-ASR also transcribes English with the same model weights. In our evaluation on the seven public English test sets used by the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard, it achieved a mean WER of 5.74%.

In a recent development, the model also supports French, Spanish and Portuguese. All five languages use the same weights, without requiring a language flag. The output is a transcript in the language spoken.

Falcon-ASR builds on our Falcon3-Audio work. The architecture and training approach for Falcon3-Audio are described in Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data.

Our Hugging Face Demo Space lets you try Falcon-ASR and explore its transcription capabilities. API access and native applications are planned. We invite you to try the Demo with your own recordings.

It has been revealed that we thank the team behind the Falcon-Emirati model for their support with Arabic foundation models. Read about their latest work in the Falcon-Emirati blog post.

We also extend our sincere thanks to Mikhail Lubinets for continued support with the compute infrastructure.

In a recent development, نقدّم Falcon-ASR، نموذجنا للتعرف على الكلام العربي بحجم 1.6 مليار معلمة، مع اهتمام خاص باللهجة الإماراتية. طوّرنا النموذج في معهد الابتكار التكنولوجي (TII) في أبوظبي، وهو يدعم أيضًا اللغات الإنجليزية والفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية.

في تقييمنا، حقق Falcon-ASR متوسط معدل خطأ في الكلمات بلغ 20.92% عبر ست مجموعات اختبار باللغة العربية، مقارنةً بأفضل نتيجة منشورة بلغت 23.17% في نسخة لوحة المتصدرين التي استخدمناها. وفي تقييمنا الداخلي للهجة الإماراتية، سجّل النموذج أدنى معدلات خطأ في الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة التي قارناها.

ندعم أيضاً الطوابع الزمنية على مستوى الكلمات في عمليات التفريغ النصي، بحيث ترتبط كل كلمة بموضعها في التسجيل الصوتي.

It has been revealed that يختلف الكلام العربي باختلاف المنطقة والمتحدث وظروف التسجيل. فقد ينجح نموذج في تفريغ نشرة إخبارية رسمية، ثم يجد صعوبة في تفريغ محادثة باللهجة الإماراتية أو تسجيل عبر الهاتف. كما أن الموارد الصوتية المفرّغة نصيًا للهجات العربية أقل من تلك المتاحة للعربية الفصحى، مما يزيد صعوبة التدريب والتقييم.

درّبنا Falcon-ASR على اللهجة الإماراتية والعربية الفصحى ولهجات خليجية وعربية أخرى، إلى جانب الإنجليزية. وهدفنا هو تفريغ الكلمات التي يستخدمها الناس في حديثهم اليومي، بما في ذلك الصيغ اللهجية والانتقال بين اللغات.

ترتّب لوحة المتصدرين المفتوحة الشاملة للتعرف على الكلام العربي، التي يديرها مركز ELM للأبحاث، الأنظمة وفق متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات عبر ست مجموعات اختبار، بوزن متساوٍ لكل مجموعة. وتعرض أيضًا معدل خطأ الأحرف (CER). وكلما انخفضت قيمة أي من المقياسين، كان الأداء أفضل. ويتبع تقييمنا للنموذج هذا البروتوكول.

Recent findings suggest that WER هو معدل خطأ الكلمات؛ وCER هو معدل خطأ الأحرف. تشير القيمة الأقل إلى أداء أفضل.

قيّمنا Falcon-ASR على مجموعات الاختبار الست نفسها، باستخدام قوائم العينات المثبّتة في لوحة المتصدرين. وأرقام النماذج المنافسة هي المتوسطات المنشورة في اللوحة، والتي جرى التحقق منها في 30 سبتمبر 2026. وكان متوسط خطأ الكلمات للنموذج أفضل بمقدار 2.25 نقطة مئوية من أفضل نتيجة منشورة في تلك النسخة.

تتوافر بالفعل بيانات عامة لتقييم اللهجة الإماراتية، إذ تضم مجموعة Casablanca قسمًا خاصًا بالإمارات. ونكمّل هذه التغطية بتقييم داخلي لتسجيلات إضافية من الكلام الإماراتي والخليجي، باستخدام تسجيلات مخصّصة للاختبار ونصوص مرجعية خضعت لمراجعة بشرية، لتقييم دقة التفريغ على مواد إضافية إلى جانب البيانات الإماراتية العامة.

حقق Falcon-ASR في تقييمنا الإماراتي الداخلي معدل خطأ كلمات قدره 22.73٪ ومعدل خطأ أحرف قدره 10.19٪:.

سجّل Falcon-ASR أقل معدل لخطأ الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة المقارَنة هنا. وكان معدل خطأ الكلمات أقل بمقدار 4.07 نقطة مئوية من Qwen3-Omni، صاحب النتيجة التالية. وتُظهر النتائج تحسنًا في دقة التفريغ على مستوى الكلمات والأحرف في هذا التقييم.

Sources indicate that ضمّنا بيانات التدريب ضوضاء خلفية وكلامًا متداخلًا وموسيقى وصدى الصوت وتأثيرات الاتصالات الهاتفية، إلى جانب تغيّرات في سرعة الكلام وحدّة الصوت. وطبّقنا المعالجة نفسها على التسجيلات الإماراتية، لتهيئة النموذج للتعامل مع ظروف مختلفة قد يواجهها في الاجتماعات والمكالمات والتسجيلات اليومية الأخرى.

According to recent reports, يفرّغ Falcon-ASR الكلام الإنجليزي باستخدام أوزان النموذج نفسها. وفي تقييمنا على مجموعات الاختبار الإنجليزية العامة السبع المستخدمة في لوحة Hugging Face المفتوحة للتعرف على الكلام، بلغ متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات 5.74٪.

According to recent reports, يدعم النموذج أيضًا الفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية. وتستخدم اللغات الخمس أوزانًا واحدة، دون الحاجة إلى تحديد اللغة مسبقًا. ويكون الناتج تفريغًا نصيًا باللغة المنطوقة.

Industry observers note that يستند Falcon-ASR إلى أعمالنا في Falcon3-Audio. وتعرض ورقة Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data بنية Falcon3-Audio ونهج تدريبه.

Sources indicate that يتيح عرضنا التجريبي على Hugging Face تجربة Falcon-ASR واستكشاف قدراته في تفريغ الكلام. أما الوصول عبر واجهة API والتطبيقات الأصلية فهو مخطّط له. ندعوكم إلى تجربة النموذج باستخدام تسجيلاتكم.

نتوجّه بجزيل الشكر إلى الفريق القائم على تطوير نموذج Falcon-Emirati على دعمهم في مجال النماذج التأسيسية للغة العربية. ويمكن الاطّلاع على أحدث أعمال الفريق من خلال المقال المنشور حول Falcon-Emirati.

كما نتقدّم بخالص الشكر والتقدير إلى Mikhail Lubinets على دعمه المستمر للبنية التحتية الحاسوبية.

Alphabet priced C$6 billion of Canadian-dollar senior unsecured notes on November 19, 2026, and filed the final pricing terms with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on November 20, 2026. Settlement is scheduled for November 24, 2026.

The pricing divides the debt into four fixed-rate tranches, with higher coupons and yields on the longer maturities:.

The pricing sheet lists Moody’s Aa2 and S&P AA+ ratings, both with stable outlooks. RBC Dominion Securities, Scotia Capital and TD Securities are joint book-running managers, with CIBC World Markets as co-manager.

Alphabet designated the proceeds for general corporate purposes, which may include repayment of outstanding debt; it did not earmark them for AI. The AI significance comes instead from the business growth and capital requirements surrounding the financing.

In a recent development, alphabet reported third-quarter 2026 Google Cloud revenue of $30.7 billion, up 103% year over year, led by enterprise AI infrastructure, enterprise AI solutions and core Google Cloud Platform services. Sales of Tensor Processing Unit systems were also a meaningful contributor to revenue growth.

Industry observers note that across Alphabet, capital spending is running ahead of operating cash generation. Third-quarter purchases of property and equipment were $51.4 billion, above $42.3 billion of operating cash flow, leaving negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion under Alphabet’s definition of operating cash flow minus capital expenditures.

For the first nine months of 2026, property-and-equipment purchases totaled $132.0 billion, compared with $63.6 billion in the same period of 2025. Those figures place the Canadian borrowing alongside a substantial increase in investment across the company.

It has been revealed that alphabet separately disclosed $28.7 billion of net proceeds from senior unsecured notes issued in the third quarter. For the first nine months of 2026, proceeds from debt issuance, net of costs, were $85.2 billion, showing that substantial borrowing preceded the Canadian offering.

In a recent development, long-term debt stood at $125.1 billion on September 30, 2026, up from $46.5 billion at December 31, 2025. Cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities totaled $265.1 billion, making the fresh notes an addition to funding capacity within a large investment program rather than an emergency liquidity raise.

The prospectus also points to substantial infrastructure commitments beyond those already recorded. Alphabet’s preliminary prospectus supplement disclosed $130.5 billion of future payments under leases primarily related to data centers that had not commenced as of September 30, 2026. Those leases were not yet recorded on the consolidated balance sheet, and a portion will represent finance lease obligations.

The Canadian notes add long-dated funding without creating a dedicated AI pool. The central issue for subsequent results is whether operating cash generation catches up with capital spending and the coming data-center commitments, or whether debt and other external financing take on a still larger role in Alphabet’s AI expansion.

The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself

📅 08 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1540 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1.
  • Sources indicate that over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way.
  • In a recent development, the first message is where I spend my effort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1. The official one is a 9B model that needs about 20 GB of memory and thinks for thousands of tokens before writing a single paragraph. On the Hub, I found only compressed copies of that same 9B model. So I described what I wanted to ML Intern, and the next day I had a 0.8B version that runs on a CPU. It returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens. The compute for the whole project, including having the 9B model label 8,797 example requests, came to USD 16.

Sources indicate that over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way. Each one started as a message in HuggingChat with ML-intern switched on, and each one ended as a public model on the Hub with its evaluation in the model card. ML-intern prepares the work, asks me for a budget before it spends anything, runs a small test before the real job, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware.

In a recent development, the first message is where I spend my effort. My first prompt, for the citrus model shared below, was about 450 words. By my 6th project it was closer to 2,000, because each project taught me something I wanted in the next one. All seven prompts are on GitHub at yvrjsharma/ml-intern-prompts, exactly as I wrote them.

Industry observers note that A prompt starts with the idea in one line and why I want it. Then it names the exact pieces: the dataset, the base model, the training script. Anything I have already checked goes under a heading that literally says "Verified facts, do not re-derive", so the agent spends its budget on the work instead of rediscovering what I know. For the camera-angle LoRA that section listed which trainer had just added transparent-image support, and which open GitHub concerns made the fallback trainer risky.

Sources indicate that two lines in the prompt are critical. The first asks for a baseline before any training. For example, the citrus prompt says: "Also report the base model's zero-shot score on the same metric before training so we can see the gain." Without it you get a trained model and no idea whether it is better than what you started with. The second is a smoke test with a check attached. For the image LoRAs I asked for 50 training steps, then a check that the saved weights had actually changed, before paying for the full run.

It has been revealed that at the end of the prompt, I lay out the expected deliverables and limit the cost. I define what belongs in the model card and include a instruction like: "Cap total spend at USD 12 and ask me before exceeding it." Because ML-intern begins every task with zero dollar budget and needs permission before executing paid jobs, this spending limit stays strictly enforced. When you leave out a budget, the agent suggests a couple of paths depending on project size and asks which one you prefer.

You don't necessarily need all of that on your first attempt. For example, I didn't have the verified-facts section in my citrus brief and ML Intern still produced a model that more than tripled the accuracy of the Qwen3.5-2B model. Let me walk you through 6 things I built with Ml-Intern in just a couple of days.

A general vision model can describe a yellowing citrus leaf. However, telling you whether it is a mite problem or a magnesium deficiency, and the bio and non-bio remedies to treat the plant is very hard. Using Claude, I put together a training dataset merged from three sources hosted by the Project-AgML organization on the Hub. The resulting citrus-disease-vlm-instruct is a dataset containing 3,017 annotated images across 21 distinct pests, illnesses, nutritional gaps, and treatment approaches. ML-intern handled the fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-2B using these examples, making sure to benchmark the foundation model beforehand.

On the 335 test photos, the base model named the right problem 14.9% of the time. After two epochs on one A10G, the fine-tuned model got 52.8%. Compute cost, about USD 1.90.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Citrus Doctor App.

According to recent reports, image models know plenty of characters. Huggy, drawn in the flat style of the Hugging Face brand assets, was not one of them. I asked ML-Intern for a LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B, trained on 84 captioned drawings from Chunte/huggy_for_training dataset.

The agent saved a checkpoint every 100 steps and drew the same set of prompts with each one, which made choosing easy. Step 200 was the first where Huggy was fully on-model. From step 500 on, Huggy's style started bleeding into prompts that had nothing to do with Huggy! The trained LoRA also works on the distilled klein model at 4 steps. Compute cost, about USD 7.60.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Huggy Generator App.

ML-intern rendered 1,030 scanned household objects from Google Scanned Objects at 24 angles each, 24,722 transparent images, on a CPU job that cost a few cents. It later finalised 461 objects for training and 40 held out for testing, and 1,844 before-and-after training pairs spread evenly over 23 camera instructions.

Training ran 2,000 steps in about 90 minutes on one A100 (~USD 3.75). The whole project took about half a day and 48 jobs, counting the ones that failed on missing packages or wrong paths and had to be resubmitted by ML-Intern. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Viewpoint Orbit App.

No dataset existed for this, so my prompt described how to make one. Start from a real photo in Open Images, remove one object with the LaMa inpainting model, and draw a scribble where the object used to be. The untouched photo is the target. ML-intern wrote and tested the pair-building scripts in a CPU sandbox, then ran them as GPU jobs, recording the author and license of every source photo along the way. It built 6,042 training pairs and a 160-pair test set, where 40 of the test pairs come from 23 object classes kept out of training entirely.

Industry observers note that before training, it measured the base model on its own and with the Viggle turbo LoRA, and checked that running edits in batches produced identical images, which made the evaluation cheaper. Training ran 2,000 steps in 1 hour 38 minutes on one A100 (~USD 4), and a comparison of the saved checkpoints on 48 test pairs picked step 500.

Paired with the Viggle turbo LoRA at 6 steps the LoRA performed really well. 67.5% of objects detected where they were drawn, at 4.7 seconds per edit. Objects from the 23 unseen classes landed as reliably as the rest (65.0% versus 64.2%). The project took a little over a day and 59 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 24.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Doodle-in App.

Training the 0.8B and 2B students took 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G (USD 0.75 for both). The 0.8B also ships as an 812 MB GGUF file for running on a CPU. The project took about 11 hours and 24 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Pocket rewriter 0.8B Student · 2B Student · Dataset · Pocket Studio App · Compare the teacher-student in Rewriter Arena.

It took two runs. The first cached 155,000 training images as latents, baked the guidance into the model, then cut the step count in stages from 16 to 8 to 4, all on A100s. The 4-step student beat the teacher run at the same 4 steps on GenEval and FID, after that ML-intern exported it to ONNX for the browser. This run took about 13 hours and USD 22.

I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. Total compute cost across both runs, about USD 37.

Check out: Agate 4-step model · Dataset · Run Agate in your browser · Agate 4-step LIVE.

With Japan facing a surge in cyberattacks and breaches, the Japanese government has passed a ¥10 billion ($63 million) emergency cybersecurity package aimed at establishing teams of industry and government experts to quickly respond to attacks and better secure its infrastructure.

The four pillars of the strategy include thoroughly implementing basic cybersecurity measures country-wide, including adopting AI for cyber-defense, strengthening the nation's cyber-investigations capabilities, better supporting the victims of cyberattacks, and partnering with private industry to jointly respond to cyberattacks.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called for the cybersecurity measures to be implemented "promptly and effectively" to enhance the nation's cyber resilience.

According to recent reports, "Even at this very moment, incidents of unauthorized access and information leaks continue to occur, significantly affecting people's daily lives and business activities," Takaichi said in a published statement announcing the emergency package on November 6. "Let us mobilize the full resources of the Government to strengthen Japan's overall capabilities to respond to cyberattacks.".

Related:AIを活用したサイバー攻撃の増加を受け、日本がサイバーセキュリティへの緊急資金拠出を推進.

A surge in cyberattacks has caused significant damage to Japanese companies and government agencies. In the first nine months of 2026, more than 600 cybersecurity incidents were publicly reported, surpassing the 594 incidents in all of 2025, according to data from TrendAI, a cybersecurity firm (formerly TrendMicro). The public reports are a conservative estimate: Japan's privacy regulator logged 2,094 breach incidents (original in Japanese) from April through mid-October, also above the total for all of fiscal 2025.

While AI has aided attackers elsewhere, TrendAI has not established a firm link between the increases and the use of AI by attackers, Ryan Flores, co-lead for threat research at TrendAI, a cybersecurity firm, noted in a statement on the threats.

"Cyberattacks are increasing globally, and so are the breaches and data leaks as a result," he said. "While AI might not be directly involved, its ability to help the attackers find targets and automate their operations makes cyberattacks scalable. Organizations need to shrink their cyber exposure and close the vulnerabilities in order to lower the odds of being victimized.".

Sources indicate that recent compromises include ransomware attacks on business, such as frozen food giant Nichirei and brewery and food giant Asahi, and data breaches targeting GMO Internet Group. While many of the attacks are criminal in nature, the worry is that the stolen information could be used by other criminal groups and nation-state actors against the Japanese public, says Mihoko Matsubara, chief cybersecurity strategist for Japanese telecom giant NTT.

Related:UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes.

Recent findings suggest that "If attackers can collect and aggregate enough personal information, they can build detailed profiles of Japanese citizens, from personal preferences to economic activities," she says. "That data could potentially be used for influence operations against Japan, such as targeted disinformation campaigns to manipulate public opinion or undermine trust in Japanese institutions.".

The Japanese government intends to use the emergency funding to pursue four broad initiatives to improve its overall cybersecurity posture. Pointing out that many recent breaches could have been prevented by good hygiene, the government's first initiative is to ensure organizations are implementing basic cybersecurity measures, according to the published Japanese notes of the ministerial meeting.

The second major initiative is to improve investigation and information collection capabilities, allowing better analysis that can then be delivered to the public to better prepare them for attacks. Third, the government will strengthen its response to cyberattacks, establishing international partnerships and implementing active cyber-defense measures. Finally, the government plans to create the capability and infrastructure to support victims so that citizens can recover damages and businesses can remain operational.

Related:UK Warns Its Critical Infrastructure Faces Grave Risk.

"Accessible consultation points and direct expert support will be expanded so that affected organizations and individuals can connect to support without confusion, and communication to prevent secondary harm will be strengthened," the Japanese notes stated. "Work will also begin on building a nationwide mechanism for flexibly dispatching public- and private-sector specialists.".

On October 1, Japan's Active Cyber Defense legislation came into effect, authorizing the police and the Self-Defense Forces (SDF) to take strong measures against any cyberattacks that pose a risk to Japan’s national security.

"Many countries would be keen to learn how swiftly Japan could respond to which kind of cyberattacks, and with what level of intensity," notes NTT's Matsubara, adding: "This emergency package is ... necessary to translate the law’s framework into practical capabilities across the broader economy, preparing organizations of all sizes to prevent, detect and respond to attacks as they become increasingly likely.".

However, the funds are only enough to get started, and more will be necessary to continue Japan's investment in cybersecurity, she says.

It has been revealed that "The vital aspect about this package is that it recognizes that cybersecurity cannot be left entirely to individual organizations," Matsubara states. "Government assistance, in the form of security assessments and incident response or recovery support, can make a difference.".

European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde used a November 20, 2026 keynote in Frankfurt to propose European public-private partnerships for chip plants and data centers in which public money, including EU budget funds, would absorb initial losses and attract private capital to an AI buildout estimated at €1.3 trillion.

Sources indicate that the recommendation, delivered at the 36th Frankfurt European Banking Congress, is a policy proposal, not an adopted EU funding program. It came in Lagarde’s eighth and final address to the congress as ECB president and illustrated her broader argument for stronger European institutions when a challenge requires a European solution.

The estimate came from A Transformative AI Strategy for Europe, an independent project written by experts in their personal capacities. It examines what would be required to raise Europe’s share of global AI computing capacity from around 5% to 15% by 2030.

Sources indicate that the strategy translates that goal into 45 gigawatts (GW) of AI compute on EU soil, measured as total facility power, up from less than 2 GW at its 2026 baseline and assuming global supply reaches 300 GW. Compute here means the specialized chips and data-center infrastructure used to train and deploy models. Its investment estimate assumes $34.4 billion of capital expenditure for each GW of that facility power.

According to recent reports, the strategy assigns governments a central role in attracting private capital rather than funding the entire buildout. Its recommended €100 billion public contribution would de-risk strategically important investment and increase European-only AI compute, defined as capacity owned and operated by European organizations. Of that amount, €25 billion would come at EU level through loan guarantees and advance purchase commitments, with €75 billion across member states through those instruments and potentially equity investment.

Lagarde argued that continued access to foreign computing providers and frontier AI models makes the upfront investment harder to justify politically. Yet lost industries are difficult to rebuild, and by the time a dependency is turned against Europe, its sovereignty has already been compromised. Ready availability lowers the immediate pressure to build European capacity without removing the vulnerability she described.

Lagarde framed AI infrastructure as a slow-moving risk: the investment is due immediately, the benefits are distant and the costs of inaction accumulate without a single moment forcing a decision, unlike crises such as the pandemic and Ukraine where the price of delay became plainly visible.

Industry observers note that lagarde attributed the ECB’s ability to commit early to its euro-area mandate, long horizon and Governing Council majority voting, and recommended stronger European institutions where challenges require European solutions. National governments must instead weigh concentrated domestic opposition against benefits spread across Europe while negotiating with partners facing similar constraints. Her parallel examples were an effective European capital-markets supervisor and European-level public-private partnerships for large technology projects.

It has been revealed that the cited strategy identifies lengthy data-center approval and grid-connection processes, rather than a lack of potential sites or investor interest, as the principal obstacle, and recommends reducing “time to power” through accelerated permitting and prioritized grid connections. The term describes how long a data center takes to connect to the grid.

The strategy also recommends guaranteeing host municipalities a share of local business-tax revenue based on installed facility power, facilitating developer investment in local infrastructure and requiring large operators to compensate for incremental electricity-system costs caused by their projects rather than spreading those costs across households and local businesses.

First-loss public capital could make large projects more attractive to private investors, but the cited strategy places grid access, permitting and local community benefits alongside financing as part of the same buildout challenge. Lagarde’s proposal therefore leaves governments weighing an explicit fiscal risk now against a technological dependency that becomes harder to reverse over time.
