📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

Industry observers note that LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

It has been revealed that pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:.

In a recent development, we evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

It has been revealed that for your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

It has been revealed that edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

AI in 2027: Memory Will Become the Next Test of Machine Intelligence

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2237 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An assistant remembers that Maya owns the project.
  • Sources indicate that memory is useful only when a system can decide what still applies, what deserves retrieval and what should be revised or forgotten.
  • It has been revealed that memory is already present in several forms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An assistant remembers that Maya owns the project. Then Maya hands it to someone else. The next day, the assistant confidently assigns her another task. It has retained a fact and lost track of the world. That small failure captures a much larger problem for machine intelligence.

Sources indicate that memory is useful only when a system can decide what still applies, what deserves retrieval and what should be revised or forgotten. In 2027, those decisions will become a sharper test of capability than the amount of history a model can hold.

It has been revealed that memory is already present in several forms. MemGPT explored hierarchical context management. Titans introduced a neural memory module updated at test time. Google’s Gemini personalization controls and Microsoft’s Copilot memory controls describe user-facing persistence and choices about it. These mechanisms should not be collapsed into one capability: retrieving a saved record, maintaining context, and updating learned parameters create different opportunities and failure modes.

In a recent development, the predictions below concern observable progress within those mechanisms. They do not attach an AGI arrival date to a memory score or infer consciousness from a system’s ability to retain information.

Industry observers note that remembering yesterday's answer is easy to celebrate until yesterday's answer becomes wrong. New memory evaluations in 2027 will put correction, appropriate abstention and the use of earlier experience into the same test. The system will need to do more than retrieve a sentence that resembles the question. It will need to recognize when the past is relevant—and when relying on it would make the present answer worse.

Temporal reasoning is more demanding than finding the right phrase. A customer may have received a refund, a policy may have expired or an exception may have applied to only one case. The assistant has to reconstruct which state matters now. That requires evaluations with contradictory updates, explicit time boundaries and questions the available record cannot answer.

In a recent development, longMemEval already evaluates abilities including temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, and abstention. It is therefore inaccurate to describe all earlier memory evaluation as simple recall. LongMemEval-V2, introduced in 2026, extends the discussion toward environment-specific experience: workflows, changing state, and recurring operational details. Its 451 curated questions illustrate the difference between remembering a conversation and becoming useful in a particular working environment.

LoCoMo offers another vital reference point, using long conversations with human verification and editing. Its construction also highlights a methodological matter: generated conversation histories can impose a cleaner structure than the contradictory, incomplete records of ordinary work. Passing a benchmark built from those histories does not establish dependable memory in every deployment.

It has been revealed that my forecast is for stronger combinations of these requirements. An agent should remember that a workflow failed, recognize why that experience matters to a later task, and avoid applying the lesson when its conditions no longer hold. That requires testing the relationship between retained information and a subsequent decision, rather than rewarding the reproduction of a phrase somewhere in the record.

Look for memory evaluations that test what an agent does after a fact changes, when the available record is incomplete, or when an earlier lesson becomes relevant to a newly introduced task. Public tasks and scoring methods will make progress easier to assess. Higher recall scores alone would provide limited evidence of dependable continuity across sessions.

Recent findings suggest that teams evaluating persistent assistants should build tests from the changes that occur in their own work: revised policies, reassigned owners, expired preferences, and incomplete records. Check whether the agent updates its behavior and acknowledges uncertainty. Those cases can reveal operational weaknesses that a demonstration of remembering names or preferences would leave hidden.

More history can create more opportunities for confusion. An obsolete instruction, a repeated anecdote and a useful observation can all compete for attention inside a long context. In controlled 2027 evaluations, I expect selected, structured memory to beat an undifferentiated full history by a meaningful margin. Holding the underlying model and available information constant will make the result especially interesting: the gain would come from organizing experience, rather than simply supplying a more powerful model.

Sources indicate that the intuition is that useful memory performs selection and organization. It can distinguish a current fact from a retired one, preserve the evidence for a decision, or retrieve a workflow lesson at the moment it matters. The complete transcript makes every detail available but also leaves the model to reconstruct the relevant state for each fresh question.

Sources indicate that that intuition is not a guarantee. A summarizer can delete the only detail needed later. A retrieval system can fail to fetch a relevant event. An indexing process can treat a model’s own conjecture as a confirmed fact. Full context may be the stronger baseline when the answer depends on a subtle detail that the memory writer discarded.

Sources indicate that the design space is already visible in the LongMemEval paper, which examines indexing, retrieval, and reading choices. MemGPT’s hierarchy offers an earlier systems-level approach to managing what fits in the active context. These are research contributions about evaluated designs. Their existence does not establish the 10-point advantage or the independent replication required by my forecast.

In a recent development, the most revealing cases will involve updates and temporal constraints. If a customer changed an address twice, a correct answer may need the latest authorized value and a record of when it became valid. A carefully maintained state representation can make that distinction explicit. A flat history can still contain every fact while giving the model more opportunities to select the wrong one.

Watch for comparisons that give structured memory and full-history context access to the same information through the same base model. The strongest results will use unseen questions and expose memory-writing costs as well as answer accuracy. Gains that depend on truncating the comparison history or selecting evidence with advance knowledge of the answer would be less persuasive.

Evaluate memory design as part of the application architecture. Compare retrieval, summaries, structured state, and longer context on representative tasks, including corrections and contradictory records. Account for the cost of maintaining memory and repairing errors. A larger context allowance may help, but the team still needs evidence that the system retrieves and applies the right information.

An assistant that remembers something about you should be able to show where it came from and let you correct it. That expectation sounds ordinary until a memory has been inferred from several conversations and reused in different settings. In 2027, major assistant products will make some of those relationships more inspectable. The practical advance will be a memory the user can question, edit or remove with a clear understanding of where it may be used.

Recent findings suggest that A memory entry is more useful when the user can ask where it came from and what depends on it. A preference stated in one conversation has a different status from a fact inferred from several documents. A mistaken inference should be correctable without requiring the user to discover every later answer it may have influenced.

Sources indicate that important controls already exist. Microsoft’s privacy documentation distinguishes memory settings from conversation history and other personalization choices. Google’s temporary-chat and personalization announcement describes choices about using previous conversations. Google’s 2026 chat and memory import announcement also shows how persistent context is becoming a portability feature. The forecast is for a stronger combined control surface, rather than the arrival of a delete button.

Provenance has to be specific enough to inspect. “Based on your history” identifies a data category, not the evidence for a particular claim. A source link or dated record can let the user distinguish an explicit instruction from an interpretation. A scope statement can explain whether the memory applies to future chats, a particular workspace, or actions taken through connected tools.

Deletion needs similarly careful language. Removing an entry from a product’s active memory store is not automatically equivalent to deleting the originating conversation, purging backups, or unlearning information from model weights. The product should explain the operation it actually performs. My forecast requires observable product controls and documentation, not a claim of perfect erasure from every storage layer.

Sources indicate that the reason for expecting progress is practical as much as ethical. An assistant cannot become a dependable long-term collaborator if its user cannot repair the state on which it acts. Corrections are part of operating the system. A polished interface that displays memories while leaving their origins and downstream use unexplained would meet only a portion of that need.

Watch for memory interfaces that connect a retained entry to an inspectable source, allow correction or deletion, and explain where the information may be reused. These capabilities should work together for an individual entry. A general memory summary or a whole-history delete control would leave vital questions about provenance and scope unresolved.

In a recent development, before deploying persistent assistants, establish how employees can inspect and correct what the system retains. Ask suppliers to distinguish active memory, source conversations, and other retained records, and explain the scope of each control. Those answers will help the business assign responsibility for maintaining accurate context as people, projects, and working relationships change.

Learning something new should not quietly erase something useful. That is the difficult bargain behind persistent parameter updates and neural memory. I expect bounded 2027 progress on substantial models: a clear gain on new knowledge while performance on established evaluations remains largely intact. Such a result would be interesting precisely because it preserves the constraint. Removing the old tests would make improvement easier to claim and much less meaningful.

Sources indicate that this is a narrower claim than a system learning every task indefinitely. Updating a model with new experience can interfere with capabilities it already has. A convincing result has to measure both acquisition and retention across repeated updates, with the compute required to perform those updates made visible.

Industry observers note that the Titans paper studies neural long-term memory and test-time memorization. MIRAS frames a family of sequence models through choices about associative memory, learning objectives, retention, and optimization. Google’s research explanation makes clear that this work concerns particular architectures and memory mechanisms. It should not be presented as evidence that every deployed language model continuously changes its core knowledge.

The more recent sleep-framework announcement, published October 27, 2026, describes alternating active processing with offline consolidation into pre-allocated memory components. It reports a research approach to acquiring information while mitigating forgetting. The name is a computational analogy; the framework operates through a fixed architecture and specified revision rules.

It has been revealed that these directions make the forecast plausible, but the evidence remains early and strongly dependent on experimental design. A system can appear to learn because its evaluation questions resemble its enhancement examples. It can preserve an average score while losing a small but crucial capability. It can also spend so much additional compute consolidating experience that the gain is unattractive for a real deployment. Independent reproduction and separate reporting of old and upcoming performance are essential.

It has been revealed that follow independently reproducible experiments that report upcoming learning and retained capabilities separately across repeated updates. Compute costs, contamination checks, and performance on older tasks will be essential context. Improvements on newly taught material accompanied by losses elsewhere would show that the acquisition-and-retention trade-off remains substantial, even if the headline learning score rises.

R&D teams and model vendors should distinguish a promising learning mechanism from a deployment-ready update process. Any pilot needs regression tests, controlled update data, version tracking, and a way to recover an earlier state. Product prepares should depend on demonstrated acquisition, retention, and operating costs rather than an assumption that continuous adaptation will work reliably across all customer tasks.

A useful memory system has to be selective enough to avoid drowning in experience and revisable enough to survive a changing world. Its mistakes will often look mundane: an old preference, the wrong owner, a remembered exception applied too broadly. Those are revealing failures. They show whether an assistant can turn a history of interactions into sound judgment about the next one.

Inside an AI Attack Against a US Retailer

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (866 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Darkreading

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When hand-typed commands failed to breach a US retailer, the attacker turned to AI-generated scripts, achieving lateral movement in minutes.
  • A threat actor deployed an AI model during a stalled cyberattack and rescued the campaign, achieving lateral movement in the process.
  • Sources indicate that the attack, detailed today by Symantec, targeted an unnamed US retail organization in September.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When hand-typed commands failed to breach a US retailer, the attacker turned to AI-generated scripts, achieving lateral movement in minutes.

A threat actor deployed an AI model during a stalled cyberattack and rescued the campaign, achieving lateral movement in the process.

Sources indicate that the attack, detailed today by Symantec, targeted an unnamed US retail organization in September. The threat actor's hand-typed commands were repeatedly blocked, so the attacker switched to what appeared to be AI-generated commands and rapidly broke through the retailer's defenses. The attacker ultimately harvested credentials and achieved lateral movement within minutes.

Symantec believes AI was used because the timing between commands was more indicative of automation than direct hands-on keyboard. That said, the timing was such that investigators believe this activity was "more consistent with an operator relaying output to an AI tool than with an autonomous agent.".

The security firm remarked this incident is one of dozens of AI-assisted attacks Symantec has investigated since May, though it added that activity was heavily concentrated around September.

Related:Second Norwegian Energy Company Breached in 2 Days.

Threat actors have utilized large language models (LLMs) in their attacks as long as the technology has been widely available. Early applications involved generating convincing phishing lures or conducting basic data reconnaissance, but recent evidence shows attackers deploying AI to execute end-to-end attacks, assist with malware development, and more. More recently, attackers have abused — and continue to abuse — agentic penetration testing tools to break into target environments at machine speed.

In this attack specifically, Symantec remarked it did not identify the initial access vector, focusing more on the timeline it was able to glean from its post-incident investigation. According to the blog post, the attacker worked at first by hand, which investigators determined due to artifacts like typing errors.

When every staged payload was terminated by security software, indicators suggest attacker tactics changed when they tried again the next day. "For almost two hours," Symantec remarked, "the attackers submitted long, error-free PowerShell scripts with labelled output sections and, in places, comments that read as a model's reasoning." Approximately 10 minutes after querying the victim's SolarWinds Orion monitoring software, attackers managed to laterally move to a second server.

The blog post hypothesizes that the attackers behind the attack were likely financially motivated, as they searched point-of-sale scripts for passwords, and one address they contacted was linked to an operation that stole card data from online retailers.

Related:Russia's Cold Relic APT Turns One Cloud Breach Into Another.

It has been revealed that during the second-stage activity, the threat actor gained initial access to a Web server and stole credentials from configuration files tied to the SolarWinds Orion monitoring software. And while the idea of AI speeding up or improving attacker tradecraft is nothing new, the attack is its deployment of AI to a hands-on keyboard attack in progress and possibly seizing victory out of an apparent defeat. It presents LLMs as a difference-maker for a less skilled threat actor.

Dick O'Brien, principal intelligence analyst on the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, tells Dark Reading this incident is one of several the team has seen in recent weeks where AI revived an attack. While he calls this a game-changer for attackers, "defenders can potentially leverage that pattern" as AI behaves in a particular kind of way, such as testing variants of a technique in quick succession.

"The retry pattern is a signal itself," he indicates. "Blocking on behavior rather than file names or exact commands matters much more. Treating a blocked attempt followed by a variant as a high-priority alert is worth considering.".

It has been revealed that although no vulnerability was exploited and no patching was required, O'Brien believes this trend of AI accelerating attacks is and will continue to affect the patching race. "Our view is that defenders need to start looking at mean time to mitigate rather than mean time to patch. Patching is still notable, but it can’t be the only countermeasure.".

Related:China-Nexus Actors Breach 10 Organizations in AI-Driven Attacks.

Industry observers note that black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something latest, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:.

You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):.

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:.

FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

Industry observers note that pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

Recent findings suggest that with several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:.

Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

Boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

Sources indicate that for edits, each region says where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:.

Recent findings suggest that everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

It has been revealed that black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

According to recent reports, FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:.

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:.

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

In a recent development, A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as .

See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:.

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call.

According to recent reports, let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:.

FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

According to recent reports, so one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

The text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

Sources indicate that this gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:.

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

Industry observers note that in stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

Recent findings suggest that at the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

In a recent development, every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

Each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

In a recent development, in FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

According to recent reports, the noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

In a recent development, the distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Recent findings suggest that attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:.

Sources indicate that text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

According to recent reports, FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

Recent findings suggest that at every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps reveals how the image takes shape:.

The fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are latest to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Nov 20, 2026 2 min read.
  • It has been revealed that google has confirmed it is donating Agent Substrate and gVisor to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), placing two notable components of its AI agent infrastructure under vendor-neutral open-source governance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Google Donates Agent Substrate and gVisor to the CNCF to Secure AI Agents at Scale.

Nov 20, 2026 2 min read.

It has been revealed that google has confirmed it is donating Agent Substrate and gVisor to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), placing two notable components of its AI agent infrastructure under vendor-neutral open-source governance. The move is intended to address two emerging challenges in running autonomous agents at scale: securely executing untrusted, AI-generated code and managing the substantial compute overhead created by agents that frequently pause and resume.

The announcement also includes OpenRL, Google's open-source reinforcement learning orchestration project. Together, the projects target different layers of agent infrastructure, from isolated code execution to managing agent lifecycles and coordinating large-scale training workloads. The goal is to establish an open foundation for agentic applications, much as Kubernetes helped standardise container orchestration.

Google argues that conventional Kubernetes workloads and AI agents have fundamentally different execution patterns.

Industry observers note that A traditional application typically starts, serves requests, and continues running. An AI agent, however, may execute a tool or code for a few seconds before waiting for model inference, an external API, or human approval. Google estimates that agents can spend 90-95% of their time idle while still holding notable state, including memory, files, repositories, and active sessions.

Industry observers note that keeping every agent in a dedicated Pod wastes resources, while scaling to zero introduces delays when environments must be reconstructed. At the other extreme, large-scale agent evaluations can overwhelm Kubernetes control planes when thousands of short-lived execution environments are repeatedly created and destroyed.

Google developed Agent Substrate to address these limitations by separating agent state (actors) from the compute resources (workers) used to execute it.

According to recent reports, actors represent individual agent sessions and retain their state, including filesystem contents, memory, and execution context. Workers provide reusable, pre-warmed execution environments drawn from shared Kubernetes pools.

Industry observers note that when an agent needs to resume, Substrate assigns it to an available Worker and restores its previous state. When the agent becomes idle, its state can be saved and the underlying compute resource released.

According to Google, this approach lets agents resume in under 500 milliseconds without creating a fresh Kubernetes Pod for every execution. It also reduces pressure on the Kubernetes control plane by managing agent lifecycles independently of individual Pod objects.

The second major challenge is security. AI agents routinely execute generated shell commands, install packages, and interact with external tools. Treating this code as trusted creates significant risks, particularly when multiple agents share infrastructure.

It has been revealed that google's gVisor provides an additional isolation boundary through a user-space application kernel. Instead of letting containerised applications interact directly with the host Linux kernel, gVisor intercepts system calls and handles them within its own isolated environment.

This reduces the exposure of the underlying host while retaining much of the efficiency associated with container-based execution.

Agent Substrate also supports Cloud Hypervisor microVMs for workloads requiring hardware-level virtualisation. This gives platform teams flexibility to select an appropriate isolation boundary without changing the overall agent lifecycle model.

According to recent reports, the announcement reflects a broader shift in cloud-native infrastructure. Kubernetes was designed around long-running applications and relatively stable workloads. Agentic systems introduce more dynamic execution patterns, where environments must be created, suspended, restored, and isolated at much greater frequency.

According to recent reports, other providers are addressing similar challenges through technologies such as Kata Containers, Firecracker, and dedicated sandboxing platforms. Google's contribution is to combine secure execution with an agent-aware orchestration model and place the resulting technologies within an open ecosystem.

According to recent reports, the wider implication is that AI agents need more than an orchestration framework and access to tools; they need their own secure, stateful, and efficiently managed execution infrastructure. By donating these projects to the CNCF, Google is helping establish the foundations for that next layer of cloud-native computing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Unite.AI may receive compensation when you use links to products we review. This does not influence our editorial evaluations. Read our affiliate disclosure.

A team can leave a workshop with a wall full of ideas and still have no usable record of what it decided. Miro and Notion help at different points in that journey. Miro is our choice for visual thinking and facilitated collaboration. Notion is our recommendation for keeping decisions, documents, and ongoing plans useful after the meeting.

It has been revealed that both feature in our best AI collaboration tools guide. The notable choice is whether your team needs a shared canvas to develop its thinking or a structured workspace to preserve and use it.

Miro gives a group a shared surface on which to make a problem visible. A customer journey can sit beside research notes, a process map, and competing proposals. The arrangement matters: colleagues can see relationships that would be harder to follow across separate documents. That makes Miro especially useful before the answer is settled.

Recent findings suggest that its diagramming tools support flowcharts and technical diagrams, while presentation and facilitation features help a group work through material together. Miro also includes Docs, Tables, timelines, and Kanban formats on the canvas. It can carry a workshop into a plan without requiring every result to be exported immediately.

Official Miro guide to using its AI canvas.

Industry observers note that we recommend Miro for product discovery, design workshops, process improvement, and technical discussions where seeing the system helps people understand it. The tradeoff is the freedom of the canvas. A sprawling board needs clear frames, ownership, and a useful conclusion; otherwise colleagues return to a large collection of objects without knowing where to start.

Recent findings suggest that notion starts with a page rather than a canvas. That page can hold a proposal, a decision, an onboarding guide, or a database view showing the tasks connected to it. The result suits work that people need to read, update, and find again. A well-maintained product brief stays useful long after the discussion that created it.

In a recent development, the strength is the connection between explanation and structure. A research database can link to a roadmap; a roadmap item can link to its specification and meeting notes. Notion’s wiki tools add a stronger home for shared knowledge, including page ownership and verification. Its project features also include subtasks, dependencies, and timelines.

Official Notion introduction to projects and tasks.

We prefer Notion for a company handbook, an editorial operation, or a product team that wants its reasoning beside its blueprint. Someone still needs to maintain the organization. Its flexible pages work best when there is an agreed home for crucial information and a clear owner for keeping it reliable.

Sources indicate that consider a product team trying to improve its first-week customer experience. It has interview notes, a rough journey map, several proposed changes, and a deadline for choosing what to build. Here is how we would use each tool for the same project.

According to recent reports, our choice: Miro. Arrange the customer journey, interview observations, and friction points on one board. Keep the original notes beside the proposed themes so colleagues can inspect the evidence behind a suggestion. This is a stronger working surface when the group needs to move ideas around, spot relationships, and compare alternatives together.

In Notion, we would organize the interview notes in a research database and write a synthesis page. That is a good fit for an asynchronous review, especially when colleagues primarily need to read the findings rather than rearrange them in a workshop.

Recent findings suggest that our choice: Notion. Give the agreed change a brief containing the customer problem, selected approach, evidence, and owner. Link it to tasks with a status and deadline. A upcoming collaborator should be able to understand both what the team chose and why it chose it.

Industry observers note that miro can also keep the strategy on its canvas using Docs, Tables, and timelines. We would stay there when the map remains the team’s main working surface. We would prefer Notion when the result becomes an ongoing specification, operating guide, or searchable record that colleagues maintain between meetings.

It has been revealed that if the team uses both products, put the exploration in Miro and the approved brief in Notion. Link the board from the brief, name the decision owner, and agree which task list is authoritative. The benefit comes from preserving the thinking without maintaining two competing versions of the delivery initiative.

Sources indicate that for a service-design workshop, a visual map lets participants place observations beside the stage of the customer experience they describe. They can group related problems, trace dependencies, and vote on priorities. Miro’s Starter blueprint includes a timer, voting, and private mode, which are useful tools for running that session rather than merely recording its notes.

According to recent reports, notion is better suited to the brief before the session and the agreed decisions afterward. It can host collaborative notes and embed supporting material, but we would choose Miro when the exercise depends on arranging, connecting, and discussing objects across an open surface.

A workshop output becomes more valuable when it has an owner, a next action, and a dependable home. Notion makes that transition natural: a decision can become a page with context, linked tasks, and a place for later revisions. Database views help people see the part of the blueprint relevant to them.

Miro’s Tables and Docs make it a more capable ongoing workspace than a simple whiteboard. We would keep a visually complex roadmap there when the surrounding maps remain essential. For policies, research libraries, and specifications that colleagues primarily read and search, Notion is our clearer recommendation.

Extortion Group Luna Moth Flits Into Law Firms a Second Time

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (907 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Darkreading

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The cybercriminals are retargeting law firms that refused to pay its first ransom, with a social engineering con aimed at stealing Microsoft access tokens.
  • A data extortion outfit has returned to previously targeted law firms for a second go, via a "vishing"-based social engineering campaign where they purport to be IT staff.
  • That's according to the ReliaQuest Threat Research team, which today published a blog post disclosing that Luna Moth, a threat extortion group that has targeted law firms since at least mid-2023, has for now abandoned remote-management tools and manual exfiltration to steal data, instead looking to swindle victims out of access tokens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The cybercriminals are retargeting law firms that refused to pay its first ransom, with a social engineering con aimed at stealing Microsoft access tokens.

A data extortion outfit has returned to previously targeted law firms for a second go, via a "vishing"-based social engineering campaign where they purport to be IT staff.

That's according to the ReliaQuest Threat Research team, which today published a blog post disclosing that Luna Moth, a threat extortion group that has targeted law firms since at least mid-2023, has for now abandoned remote-management tools and manual exfiltration to steal data, instead looking to swindle victims out of access tokens. Then, they're using these tokens to access and steal information.

Joseph Keyes, author of the blog post and cyber threat intelligence analyst at ReliaQuest, wrote that this latest wave of targets are "likely" those that didn't pay Luna Moth's first extortion demand, with this second hit coming weeks-to-months later.

A ReliaQuest spokesperson tells Dark Reading that these firms were targeted a second time because the group knows these organizations can be socially engineered (so it tries again with different tactics), for a second set of data. Moreover, as fewer organizations are paying, law firms make a good fit to target, because "their client data is highly sensitive and the reputational hit from exposure is severe, so repeated leverage is worth the effort.".

Related:3AM Affiliate Embraces AI-Like Loops in European School Attack.

In a recent development, in the initial variants of the attack, Luna Moth would reach out as IT support and trick victims into connecting to Windows' built-in remote assistance tool. It would then download data directly. This time, the group sent blank-subject emails from a free email address with a broken PDF masquerading as a business report; the "report" would then fail to open. The attacker would use this pretext to reach out soon after, posing as IT support responding to a malicious alert, while at the same time offering to fix the PDF.

Once on a video call, the "IT support" directs the target to turn on screen-share functionality so they can direct the target through a "fix." The attacker then tells the target to open Microsoft Copilot from the Web browser on their work laptop, open the browser's developer tools, find the request Copilot sends to Microsoft Graph, and copy the application's access token.

The attacker instructs the target to paste the token into a public text-sharing site the attacker can access. Finally, the attacker gives the token to its own folder and downloads files through the Microsoft Graph API.

This social engineering tactic requires no malware and no vulnerability. It relies solely on tricking a target into giving an access token, effectively a master key into the front door of an organization. The use of IT support to "fix" a technical problem evokes ClickFix, as both techniques rely on human problem-solving tendencies to trick an end user.

Related:'AdFection' Turns Ad Impressions Into Zero-Click Spyware Delivery.

It has been revealed that the ReliaQuest spokesperson says the firm considers this attack representative of a gap in how controls are scoped within an organization. Because the token is issued to the victim's compliant device and handed over "willingly," security red flags do not go off.

"A token is a bearer credential, so it works from anywhere until it expires, unless CAE [Continuous Access Evaluation] with strict location enforcement (or token binding) applies," the spokesperson states. "Similar to device code phishing, the user completes a legitimate flow, so MFA is satisfied. The weakness is the assumption that authentication equals ongoing trust. Microsoft's defaults, such as the 60- to 90-minute lifetime and CAE not being enforced by default, make it easier.".

Recent findings suggest that reliaQuest recommends that organizations turn CAE on by default, block browser developer tools and token-inspection pages on managed browsers, and restrict remote-support and screen-sharing tools where there's no business need. Additionally, it may be wise to inform employees of the ways threat actors attempt to steal credentials from employees.

Related:Biomemory Rolls out DNA Shield, First Commercial Product Built on Its Molecular IT Platform.

As the blog post put it, "Tell people that IT will never ask for developer tools or tokens and that they should verify IT requests by callback.".

Latest Update: Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta

📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3039 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta.
  • Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.
  • Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input.

Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.

Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post demonstrates you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here.

According to recent reports, meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that plans, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images.

The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4.

Muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the new modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each.

The language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum.

Muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang recipes below.

A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention.

According to recent reports, muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images.

Industry observers note that muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm.

The context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text.

Grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context.

The Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template.

Recent findings suggest that use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed.

You can initialize the model and processor as follows.

It has been revealed that prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template, enabling add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=True, return_dict=True, and return_tensors="pt". Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt.

The Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt.

According to recent reports, video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor:.

In a recent development, as a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template.

Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate.

The Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference.

If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood:.

The processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings.

According to recent reports, once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. Industry observers note that you can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer. This section highlights how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples.

According to recent reports, first, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP and split the experts across GPUs, using DistributedConfig, which tells transformers how to split the model when it loads:.

It has been revealed that in the snippet above, fsdp_size=64 shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and ep_size=8 splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch.

Now, we can configure the SFTConfig for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case.

Industry observers note that the core parts here are packing=True which joins examples into 2048-token sequences without padding. A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. save_only_model=True saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. LoraConfig targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen.

Then we can run this command across each node:.

According to recent reports, we trained for 500 steps, which took about 2 hours on 64 H100s, at about 8,000 tokens per second. Mean token accuracy rose from 72% to 84% and the loss fell from 1.26 to 0.57, which signals a good fine-tuning run.

Sources indicate that muse Spark Open is a coding and agentic model. We wanted to see that for ourselves, so we tried a mixture of multi-modal and agentic tasks that use the model's image and audio inputs. Everything below is something you can run or fork.

In a recent development, we combined 2-bit quantized Muse Spark open (served on llama.cpp) with the Pi coding agent to generate and iteratively improve 3D assets in Three.js. It then sends those images back to the same model on llama server for visual feedback. Pi uses that feedback to edit the code and repeats the process.

Recent findings suggest that we tested Spark on computer use tasks and were amazed by the performance, so we have built a lean demo that also serves to teach you how a computer use agent works. #23390. Why Sovereign AI Is Worth Building, and Where It Breaks

Why Sovereign AI Is Worth Building, and Where It Breaks

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1198 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, that meant chats users had already asked to delete.
  • It has been revealed that enterprise customers were carved out.
  • It has been revealed that I’m not picking on OpenAI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, that meant chats users had already asked to delete. It covered ChatGPT Free, Plus, Pro and Team accounts, plus API customers without a zero-data-retention agreement. OpenAI fought it. Its COO, Brad Lightcap, called it “an overreach.” The broad order ended in late September, but data from accounts the Times flagged stays on legal hold.

It has been revealed that enterprise customers were carved out. Plenty of business teams on Team intends and standard API keys were not. None of them were parties to the case. They hit delete. A judge in someone else’s lawsuit decided delete didn’t mean delete.

It has been revealed that I’m not picking on OpenAI. They pushed back hard. That’s the point. When your data sits on someone else’s platform, someone else’s legal fights, contracts and policies decide what happens to it.

According to recent reports, now swap in your own tech giant. Your contracts, your claims files, your source code, your customers’ health records. More and more of it is flowing through AI models running on infrastructure you don’t own, governed by terms you didn’t write.

That’s what sovereign AI is really about. Not flags and borders. Control.

McKinsey surveyed 300 executives, investors and government officials late last year. Seventy-one percent called sovereign AI an “existential concern” or a “strategic imperative.” McKinsey sizes it as a $600 billion market by 2030, with up to 40% of AI workloads potentially moving into sovereign environments.

Industry observers note that notice the thread. Sovereignty and open source keep showing up together. That’s not an accident.

I’ve stated it before: the models are good enough. For most of the day-to-day work enterprises actually need, summarization, research, instruction following, document processing, the frontier gains don’t move the needle. A model that wins an Olympiad math contest doesn’t make your claims process any faster.

I’ve run open models like Qwen on my own hardware and watched them handle real application tasks well. I can fine-tune on my own data, on my own machine, without sending a single record out the door. Two years ago that wasn’t a serious enterprise option. Today it is.

That changes the sovereignty math. You don’t have to build a frontier model to own your AI. You can take a strong open-weight model, run it inside your own walls or a sovereign cloud, tune it on your data and keep the weights.

The supply side is moving too. In August, Nvidia agreed to pay Poolside $6 billion to license its model-building platform and offered jobs to more than 100 of its engineers, all aimed at its Nemotron family of open-weight models. When the organization that sells the picks and shovels pours that kind of money into open models, the open models are going to keep getting better.

Sources indicate that and the security tooling is catching up. Confidential inference uses a trusted execution environment inside the CPU or GPU so data stays encrypted until it reaches a walled-off section of the chip. Even the cloud provider can’t see it. That moves you from hoping your data is safe to knowing it is.

So yes. Sovereign AI can be really, really good. Lower cost per workload, no surprise price hikes, no model deprecated out from under you, and a straight answer when your board asks where the data goes.

But I’d be doing you a disservice if I stopped there.

Sources indicate that compute is concentrated, and it isn’t cheap. The Center for a Newly introduced American Security’s Sovereign AI Index finds about 90% of frontier AI compute sits in the United States and China. McKinsey notes only about 30 countries host compute capable of advanced AI workloads. Owning your stack means GPUs, power, cooling and people who know how to run them. Budget for all of it, not just the chips.

Sovereign doesn’t mean self-sufficient. CNAS tracks 184 government-backed sovereign AI projects. More than three-fifths disclose at least one foreign partner, and most of those partners are U.S. companies. Even nations can’t do this alone. The World Economic Forum and Bain argue sovereignty is really “strategic interdependence.” I agree. Decide which layers you must control and which you can safely rent.

Sources indicate that open models still trail on the hardest tasks. McKinsey flags that localized models can fall short of frontier performance. For some workloads that gap matters. The answer isn’t all or nothing. Route sensitive, high-volume work to models you own, and keep a governed path to frontier APIs for the problems that truly need them.

Sources indicate that operations is where most programs break. Infrastructure, data and model control get the attention. Operational sovereignty, who can access the system, who can change its configuration, who can audit what it did, is the pillar most enterprises miss. That gets serious fast once AI agents start taking actions on your behalf. If an outside vendor holds the keys to your agents, you don’t have sovereign AI. You have a hosted service with a nicer name.

Don’t lock yourself in a upcoming box. The point of sovereignty is choice. Build so you can swap models without rebuilding everything around them. If your “sovereign” stack only runs one model from one vendor, you’ve just moved the dependency.

Sources indicate that the organizations getting this right treat each piece as an engineering requirement with an owner and a metric. Where does inference physically happen? Where are prompts and outputs logged, and for how long? Which model sees which data? Who can turn it off?

The ones struggling treat sovereign AI as a checkbox on a vendor questionnaire.

This is consistent with everything I see in our work at Marlabs. The model is rarely the problem anymore. The implementation is. The humans, the architecture, the governance. Sovereign AI doesn’t change that. It raises the stakes on getting it right.

Sources indicate that those Team-plan customers didn’t do anything wrong. They trusted their vendor agreement. The decision about their data got made in a courtroom they never entered.

You get to make that decision yourself. When your board, your regulator or your biggest customer asks who controls their data and who else can see it, sovereign AI done well gives you a straight answer. Point to exactly where it lives. Show them who has the keys.

It has been revealed that that’s worth building. Just build it with your eyes open.

Recent findings suggest that what’s driving the sovereign AI conversation in your organization? Let me know.

Sources indicate that brian Rowe is the Senior Vice President of AI & Machine Learning at Marlabs. With 30 years of experience and 2,200 employees, NYC-based Marlabs is an AI transformation partner that helps Fortune 500 organizations operationalize AI and deliver sustained, measurable value across industries.

Apertus 1.5 Release Notes

📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1291 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use.
  • According to recent reports, apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively.
  • We introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

According to recent reports, apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

The full Apertus 1.5 training pipeline.

We introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:.

According to recent reports, overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All fresh data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

Alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

Recent findings suggest that the multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

According to recent reports, while still trailing frontier open-weight models, the upcoming release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

It has been revealed that we also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 demonstrates strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

Apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

The results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

All recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

The report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

In a recent development, proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

Access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been revealed by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

Thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team announced the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

Sources indicate that in summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

If you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

Project Apertus, et al. “Apertus 1.5: From Open Text Models to Open Multimodal Reasoners.” arXiv:2610.15542. Preprint, arXiv, October 11, 2026. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2610.15542.
