Breaking: Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale

📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3334 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face!
  • Recent findings suggest that beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases.
  • According to recent reports, beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the latest US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Recent findings suggest that beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

According to recent reports, beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post highlights you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

According to recent reports, reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:.

Industry observers note that if you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.

Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

The decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

Inside the attention block (both layer types).

The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

According to recent reports, attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

Industry observers note that the first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

The router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

In a recent development, the residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

It has been revealed that beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

Every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

According to recent reports, the most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

According to recent reports, A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Plan for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

Install the latest version of transformers.

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:.

The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.

In a recent development, beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

Pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

Beam's config defines an expert-parallel plan. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:.

According to recent reports, launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

According to recent reports, beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

Recent findings suggest that for faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:.

Both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.

Sources indicate that beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:.

Sources indicate that on Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):.

Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.

Recent findings suggest that we are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

Industry observers note that below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

According to recent reports, * Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

† Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

Don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

Recent findings suggest that you can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

The quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

According to recent reports, after one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

Training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.

It has been revealed that reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can update the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the latest weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

It has been revealed that the recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:.

Sources indicate that sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

Update: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

Optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

It has been revealed that evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

According to recent reports, the next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one update behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

Sources indicate that you can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

It has been revealed that if you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.

Sources indicate that at Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.

Sources indicate that we asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.

Recent findings suggest that we used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.

You can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.

Sources indicate that we wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

For the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

According to recent reports, our score-versus-latency plot highlights the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.

Decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

Sources indicate that we wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

Recent findings suggest that first, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

For a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.

It has been revealed that beam is a 501B open model that you can run on your own hardware and change. Start with the BF16 checkpoint, or try one of the quants FP8, NVFP4. If you build something with Beam, share it in the discussions tab.

Well why don't you build something that can run on cunsumer GPU like Qwen 3.8 Flash Next for example using strata ?

That’s a good question. Apart from large corporations, no one would be able to set up this model in a way that allows it to function properly—it requires 8 RTX 6000 graphics cards, which would cost around 150,000 euros in total.

It has been revealed that thanks for sharing this! Small nit, but would you be able to add higher resolution diagrams for the model architecture figures? They come out pixelated for me (and possibly others) so I can't read the smaller annotations in the figures.

According to recent reports, this is a genuinely exciting release — 501B Apache 2.0 with 1M context is the kind of thing that makes "open" in open-source mean something again. The residual stream design with the 1/sqrt(k) weighting is a nice touch; it's the sort of architectural detail that makes a real difference at scale without being a headline feature.

One question from the NLP side: the post focuses heavily on coding and agentic use cases, which makes sense for the target audience. But how does Beam handle multilingual text? I'm asking specifically because the 1M context window is exactly what you need for cross-lingual document understanding, and if the training data is skewed toward English + code, that's a gap that matters for non-English research communities.

According to recent reports, also — is the training data or at least the data mixture documented? For a model this size under Apache 2.0, reproducibility of the training setup is part of the open-source promise, and I'd love to see it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Levent Alpöge said on November 20, 2026, that he believes he and Claude discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis and a method resolving the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. The Anthropic mathematician released a personal statement linking to Lean code, but identified no independent validation of the completed argument.

Alpöge is also a junior fellow at Harvard’s Society of Fellows. The Riemann hypothesis dates to 1859 and concerns the zeros of the Riemann zeta function, which describe the distribution of prime numbers. It places the zeros that determine the primes on a particular vertical line; many mathematical results assume it to obtain a form of randomness in the primes.

Alpöge says he expects, with more time, to address the Extended Riemann Hypothesis as well. That is an expectation rather than another completed result.

Industry observers note that alpöge indicates the arguments were formalized without assumptions and released as code for Lean, a formal proof system, in 14 compressed archive parts. He chose not to add a conventional write-up, describing the argument as incredibly long and the prospect of a massive generated document as unreadable; a footnote puts the generated version at more than 250,000 pages.

The release therefore pairs a formalization presented as complete with limited human-readable explanation. Alpöge says he is presenting the argument before mastering a large body of surrounding mathematics. His next steps are to understand and explain it, pursue simplifications, speak about it and write it properly. His cautions include possibly strange or suboptimal choices and timeline descriptions paraphrased from Claude that may need editing.

Alpöge describes a division of labor in which he guided the conceptual move from a toy setting to its suitable analogue, while Claude supplied expertise he lacked, particularly on automorphic forms for higher-rank groups. The argument builds on Stepanov’s function-field method, which uses a divisor to obtain multiplicity; reproducing that effect over the integers was a central obstacle. Fourier-analytic ideas led the pair to repeated theta lifts in an automorphic framework, with Claude proposing a chain of length X for an underlying sum of length X.

The rough timeline in the statement, supplied by Claude after a search, lists a Stepanov determinant on October 6, 2026, iterated theta lifts and related computations on November 15, 2026, and the generalized result on November 16, 2026. Alpöge cautions that some descriptions paraphrase Claude and may need revision. The dates therefore document his retrospective account of the research, not independent verification of the argument.

In a recent development, anthropic reported on August 10, 2026 that an unreleased research version of Claude increased a longstanding lower bound for the proportion of zeta zeros satisfying the Riemann hypothesis from 41.6% to 67.2%, while explicitly stating that Claude had not proved the hypothesis and that the techniques were not expected to yield a proof. The earlier work was a partial bound; the new statement presents a complete proof through a different approach.

That earlier effort used two Claude Code sessions and 31 million output tokens. Claude initially generated 650 ideas that did not work, then coordinated about 60 subagents in a second attempt. Alpöge and Ralph Furman examined the result; Brian Conrey and Dan Goldston reviewed the paper; and the Lean formalization passed the comparator validation tool.

The new statement names no equivalent review of the full proof it describes. Independent mathematical scrutiny and successful checking of the released Lean code are therefore the decisive tests before Alpöge’s announcement can be treated as a solution to the Riemann hypothesis.

China-Nexus Actors Breach 10 Organizations in AI-Driven Attacks

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1098 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Darkreading

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Attackers used Cairn once again in autonomous attacks that targeted advanced manufacturing and defense sectors, as well as civil and human rights organizations.
  • China-nexus threat actors unleashed another wave of attacks using autonomous AI tools to compromise microprocessor manufacturers, US defense contractors, and other organizations.
  • The malicious activity, tracked as CL-STA-1238 by researchers at Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42, is the second documented attack in which China-linked actors used the open source AI penetration-testing framework called Cairn for automation, they revealed in a blog post.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Attackers used Cairn once again in autonomous attacks that targeted advanced manufacturing and defense sectors, as well as civil and human rights organizations.

China-nexus threat actors unleashed another wave of attacks using autonomous AI tools to compromise microprocessor manufacturers, US defense contractors, and other organizations.

The malicious activity, tracked as CL-STA-1238 by researchers at Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42, is the second documented attack in which China-linked actors used the open source AI penetration-testing framework called Cairn for automation, they revealed in a blog post. In this latest campaign, attackers conducted 25 operations between August and September against at least 19 organizations, achieving "unauthorized access or data retrieval at 10 of the targeted organizations," according to the post.

In the successful attacks, the threat actors obtained dozens of valid credentials; achieved mass exposure of personal data, exceeding 1 million records at one organization; retrieved military and government identities; created persistent administrator accounts in a production system; and modified a live industry standards-ballot document.

Related:Second Norwegian Energy Tech giant Breached in 2 Days.

According to recent reports, of the total organizations targeted, seven were in the semiconductor and advanced-manufacturing supply chain, and three organizations were in US defense and defense policy. The attackers also targeted various human rights and civil society organizations.

According to Unit 42 researchers, the victims included an industry standards body, which suffered a password-spraying attack; a semiconductor manufacturer, where attackers brute-forced a production credential on a partner-integration application; a US teacher's union, which suffered an unauthenticated account-creation bypass on a content management system; and a defense policy think tank, where attackers targeted an open back-end registration endpoint on its identity platform.

The China-nexus actors also targeted content management systems through identity and configuration weaknesses at other organizations, including a semiconductor-lithography manufacturer, an industrial-automation manufacturer, and an education nonprofit.

Cairn played a significant hand in the campaign, and the use of it "represents a shift in how attackers are applying AI to targeted offensive operations," according to the post.

"The attackers supplied a target and a goal, then Cairn planned, executed, and recorded results on its own," Unit 42 researchers wrote.

Cairn is AI model agnostic, and in this case, attackers weaponized it using Chinese large language models (LLMs) Zhipu GLM 5.2 and DeepSeek V4 Flash and Pro. However, initial exposure to the organizations' networks came through many of the traditional security gaps found across industries, the researchers noted.

Related:Russia's Cold Relic APT Turns One Cloud Breach Into Another.

"It doesn't matter much to a victim whether a human or an AI agent is behind the keyboard," Tyler Oliver, CEO and founder of threat-hunting platform Huntbase, tells Dark Reading. "A human might hand the tool a mission and walk away, or direct it step by step. Either way, the password spraying looks like password spraying.".

Indeed, the vulnerabilities the attackers exploited were known, according to Unit 42, including "authentication bypasses; insecure direct object references; mass-assignment privilege escalation; weak and default credentials; exposed cloud APIs; and dated public CVEs.".

As in the previous Cairn-driven attacks, the findings once again provide a look under the hood at how threat actors can weaponize the tool against organizations, a blueprint that may be used in future attacks.

According to recent reports, rather than manually directing every stage of an attack, operators supplied Cairn with a target and a high-level objective. The framework then developed its own strategy, conducted reconnaissance, identified potential vulnerabilities, attempted exploitation, and recorded its findings.

Related:Inside an AI Attack Against a US Retailer.

Industry observers note that "An AI model drives each Cairn 'agent worker,'" according to the post. "Cairn coordinates its activities through a shared 'blackboard.' Agents read the blackboard and write their findings back as a fact-intent graph, while human operators can inject 'hints' at any time to help guide the operations if needed.".

"Cairn has a shared record of what it's already learned, so it can build on earlier findings without a person reviewing every result and deciding what happens next," Rickard Carlsson, CEO of AI security firm Detectify, tells Dark Reading. Meanwhile, this ability to work with limited supervision is already showing up across multiple tools, including another AI penetration-testing framework, Artex, which is also being weaponized by attackers, he says.

Sources indicate that individual CL-STA-1238 operations lasted anywhere from 20 minutes to more than 50 hours, according to Unit 42. Moreover, attackers could achieve simultaneous operations against multiple organizations, which reduced the dependence on human operators to manage each intrusion.

Though AI is changing the game in terms of speed, volume, and expanse of attacks, it does not change the "complexity" of attacks, which, as mentioned, often rely on known security gaps, according to Unit 42.

That's a spot of good news for defenders, because "identity hygiene, attack-surface reduction, and software patching remain effective" against attacks that use Cairn or other AI tools, according to the post.

However, there are other safeguards that organizations can put in place to defend against AI-driven attacks, too, claims John Strand, owner of security consulting firm Black Hills Information Security.

"There are two things I think every organization should be doing right now," he tells Dark Reading. "First, continuous attack surface management. Organizations need to identify all the different services and systems they have exposed to the internet and start restricting access wherever possible.".

The second key defense move is to start using cyber deception as much as possible by setting up "tripwires" that can detect attackers during reconnaissance and lateral movement "before they accomplish their objectives," Strand adds.

Uber Cuts Translation Cache Memory by up to 90% While Keeping P99 Latency Below 1 MS

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (602 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Uber Cuts Translation Cache Memory by up to 90% While Keeping P99 Latency Below 1 MS.
  • Nov 20, 2026 2 min read.
  • Uber has redesigned its Go-based translation cache to reduce its initial memory footprint by more than 90% while keeping p99 cache miss latency below one millisecond.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Uber Cuts Translation Cache Memory by up to 90% While Keeping P99 Latency Below 1 MS.

Nov 20, 2026 2 min read.

Uber has redesigned its Go-based translation cache to reduce its initial memory footprint by more than 90% while keeping p99 cache miss latency below one millisecond. The hybrid architecture retains translation keys and frequently accessed values in memory while storing the remaining values on disk. The system serves millions of translations per second and maintains a cache hit rate above 99.9%.

The optimization addresses two problems identified through memory profiling across Uber's Go services. Garbage collection (GC) consumed more than 20% of CPU utilization in some services, with translations accounting for approximately 70% of allocated objects.

At Uber's scale, even small inefficiencies in memory management can add up.

In a recent development, the first optimization replaced Go's sync.Map with a conventional map[string]string protected by an RWMutex. The workload was predominantly read-heavy, with infrequent updates and no individual deletions. The previous implementation created multiple objects and pointers for each translation entry, increasing GC overhead. Moving to a value-based map reduced object allocations and improved CPU utilization by more than 30% in the affected service.

According to recent reports, however, reducing object allocations did not solve the overall memory consumption problem. Translation datasets could contain two to three million keys, although individual services typically accessed only a small subset. Cache refreshes introduced another issue: the service built a replacement cache in the background before atomically swapping it with the existing one. Both copies therefore occupied memory simultaneously, causing some services to run out of memory during refreshes.

Sources indicate that uber considered external caching and generating service-specific translation subsets, but both introduced additional operational or maintenance costs. The team instead adopted a hybrid storage design that preserves the existing Get() and Put() API. All keys remain available in memory for fast lookups, while translation values are stored in disk-backed files.

Uber's hybrid translation cache (Source: Uber Blog Post).

The implementation uses 256 shards, each with its own read-write mutex, in-memory entries, and disk file. Six-byte hash-based keys reduce metadata overhead, with a fallback to the original key format to handle collisions. A time-based global least recently used (LRU) policy manages in-memory entries. During cache refreshes, the system uses access history to preload translations accessed within the previous 15 minutes, avoiding a cold cache after the swap.

In one example, a translation dataset that previously consumed approximately 800 MB in memory required around 40 MB for metadata after the redesign. With a configured limit of 50,000 in-memory entries, actual memory consumption typically ranged between 80 MB and 120 MB. In another reported workload, approximately 30,000 of more than four million entries were loaded in memory, while the cache hit rate remained above 99.9%. The p99 latency for disk-backed cache misses stayed below 100 microseconds.

Memory usage decreased from approximately 2.7 GB to 750 MB (Source: Uber Blog Post).

Sources indicate that uber's experience highlights the cost implications of in-memory caching at scale. The team recommends minimizing object references to reduce GC overhead and measuring how frequently cached values are accessed. When only a small proportion of cached data is actively used, a hybrid approach can retain frequently accessed values in memory while moving the rest to disk.

TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, torchNeuron provides a newly introduced native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium.
  • Industry observers note that torchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a upcoming backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP.
  • 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, torchNeuron provides a newly introduced native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

Industry observers note that torchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a upcoming backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

It has been revealed that torchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

Sources indicate that for the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron customers use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

Industry observers note that text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

Industry observers note that the following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

Now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

Recent findings suggest that here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

Sources indicate that parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

It has been revealed that nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:.

The command below launches training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

Sources indicate that many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:.

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

In a recent development, more and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

Make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, people can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

Brad Wardell, Founder and CEO of Clairvoyance AI – Interview Series

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1864 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that brad Wardell is Founder and CEO of Clairvoyance AI and the founder and CEO of Stardock.
  • Clairvoyance AI develops a workspace for named AI staff with ongoing assignments and memory, connecting local files and development tools with cloud services and models running on a user’s own hardware.
  • Industry observers note that you’ve spent more than three decades building desktop software and strategy games at Stardock, including products such as Fences and Galactic Civilizations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that brad Wardell is Founder and CEO of Clairvoyance AI and the founder and CEO of Stardock. He has spent more than three decades building desktop software and strategy games, including products such as Fences and Galactic Civilizations. His work on game development pipelines, creative assets, and everyday business reporting shaped his interest in persistent AI agents that can work directly with local files and applications.

Clairvoyance AI develops a workspace for named AI staff with ongoing assignments and memory, connecting local files and development tools with cloud services and models running on a user’s own hardware. Incubated at Stardock, it supports workflows that produce reusable notes, reports, and other artifacts. In this interview, Wardell discusses how game development informed the product, where local models fit into daily work, and the routing, memory, and permission controls needed to make agents useful.

Industry observers note that you’ve spent more than three decades building desktop software and strategy games at Stardock, including products such as Fences and Galactic Civilizations. What problem inside your own business prompted you to build Clairvoyance AI, and when did you realize it could become a company of its own?

It has been revealed that the real pressure point was Ara: History Untold, which Stardock helped Microsoft and Oxide Games finish. A huge amount of time was going into just moving creative assets into the game. Writing came in as .DOCX files that had to be painstakingly hand-converted into XML or CSV. 3D assets had to be carefully brought into our engine. A single balance change meant touching a dozen different files. Localization meant matching translated strings back to the right keys in the right files by hand. Clairvoyance AI made all of that painless and let us ship on time.

By late 2025, we had an internal debate about whether to make it public at all. It was a real competitive advantage, like having a superset of something like OpenClaw a year early. What pushed us toward going public was watching friends and colleagues lose jobs to AI automation that they could have kept if they’d had better tools. At that point, we knew we wanted to open Clairvoyance AI to the public.

You’ve argued that many AI agent tools reveal a lack of experience shipping consumer software. What mistakes do you see most often, and what lessons from your own career should AI developers be applying?

The biggest tell is terminology. If you don’t already know the words, like “glyph” for the little graphic on a button, you’re at a real disadvantage talking to an AI, because it’s trained on people who already know the lingo. Most of the teams building these tools are very smart but very young, and it shows in the usability choices. A good example is when Anthropic added the ability to drag text from one terminal session to another, that got millions of views. We’ve had agents that you can just @ by name to hand off work automatically, no dragging anything. Theirs requires the user to do the work the AI should be doing.

The lesson from 30 years of shipping desktop software is that you have to actually use the thing you’re building, every day, with real deadlines, before anyone outside the company sees it. A lot of AI products feel like they were built by people who haven’t had to live inside their own software.

You describe the next phase of AI as a routing problem: deciding what runs on a device, across a local network, or in the cloud. Could you walk us through a real workflow and explain how those decisions should be made?

Sources indicate that routing isn’t really an individual decision anymore, it’s becoming a company-level one. We’re about to release a feature called Hivemind that makes this concrete. Most enterprises already own plenty of capable machines that sit idle every night. Hivemind lets a company pool those idle GPUs across its own machines so anyone on the team can run AI work on them instead of sending it to the cloud. If you’re tracking tens of thousands of shipments across a supply chain, or auditing where a company’s money went, you don’t need a frontier cloud model for that. You need enough compute, and most companies already have it sitting unused after hours.

Recent findings suggest that at the individual level, the same logic applies, just on a smaller scale. I run dashboards, crash reports, sentiment reports, and sales data every night on a local model instead of a cloud one. I used to run that same workload through Claude and it cost about $100 a month in tokens. Now it runs for free overnight on hardware I already own, and I read the results in the morning.

So the actual decision isn’t “local versus cloud,” it’s “does this need to happen while someone is staring at the screen, and does the company already have the hardware to do it without paying per-token.”.

In a recent development, you believe a substantial share of everyday agentic work can already run on local hardware. Which tasks have you demonstrated this with, on what hardware, and how do you measure success beyond whether a model produces a plausible answer?

We have had a lot of success with using local AI for adding metadata to our files. Like many companies, we have terabytes of data on our network. Stardock develops both software and games and on the game side, there’s decades of 3D and 2D art assets, videos, work products, etc.

Around the company we have a lot of pretty decent video cards from AMD and NVIDIA. We have found that 8B to 12B parameter models are more than enough to do everything we need and those will run on even relatively older hardware. Right now, we have a Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 laptop doing some of this work in the background during the evening.

Local AI is really good at just slowly chewing through and reviewing these files and adding metadata to it so that when we need to find something, you can search for it and find it rapidly. Hence, we discovered that we have 16 different 3D models of wolves. Sigh.

According to recent reports, what should trigger escalation from a smaller local model to a more capable cloud model? How do you detect when the local model is struggling before it makes a consequential mistake?

Right now, anything that requires open-ended judgement should probably go up to the cloud. The frontier models have largely solved hallucinations. When you go to smaller (local) models, hallucinations return. So on local models we tend to need to keep a lot of guardrails on them.

Industry observers note that clairvoyance organizes agents as AI staff with persistent memory and ongoing assignments. What have you learned about preserving useful context over time without allowing outdated instructions, incorrect assumptions, or conflicting memories to accumulate?

Under the covers, Clairvoyance stores its memories in a graph structure so when one thing updates, it tends to recursively trigger updates to other nodes. This helps ensure that the memories stay organized and up to date.

The challenge has been to prevent infinite recursion and that has required a lot of trial and error over the last couple of years.

It has been revealed that giving agents access to files, applications, and development tools makes them more useful, but also increases the consequences of errors. How do you structure permissions, human approvals, and recovery when an agent takes the wrong action?

The one concrete point we have is File Protection: Clairvoyance can block agents from wiping out directories, enforced at the app level rather than through hooks that an agent could work around.

Industry observers note that when a workflow combines local execution with cloud inference, “local-first” can mean different things. What information leaves the user’s machine, and how can customers understand and control that boundary?

Sources indicate that cloud security is about keeping other people out. It doesn’t answer whether the model provider should have your organization’s secrets in the first place. Clairvoyance is local-first by design: your notes, projects, and staff memory live on your own machine. What goes to a cloud model is your call, made per staff member, not a blanket setting. Run a local model and nothing has to leave your hardware at all. We’re hearing this directly from enterprise customers who are frustrated about uploading entire confidential workflows to Anthropic or OpenAI just to get work done.

Clairvoyance has over 40,000 people. What have you learned from how people actually use Clairvoyance, and can you share a measurable example of a recurring workflow where it has delivered sustained value?

The retention rate is highly dependent on the amount of data the user is generating through their sessions.

Recent findings suggest that most owners of AI haven’t really crossed the threshold where they are taking the data the AI generates to build back onto it. Most users still think in terms of prompts. The users who stay with Clairvoyance are the ones generating a lot of Exhibits and Reports which in turn act as the foundation for further work.

It has been revealed that looking ahead a year, what developments would most expand the work agents can reliably handle locally? What would need to happen for you to reconsider your view that routing matters more than model size?

I think within 18 months, 90 to 95% of AI work will be local, with maybe 5% needing the cloud for frontier work. That’s mostly because almost nothing is being delegated to AI yet, even trivial tasks like screening resumes for location or checking shipment timing are still done by hand, and a 4B model can already do that on a laptop. What expands this is Hivemind-style pooled compute (letting a company’s underused GPUs serve everyone on the domain) and routing getting good enough that nobody has to know what a 4B model or an Opus even is.

Thank you for the great interview, readers who wish to try a desktop app for managing persistent AI agents across their computers should visit Clairvoyance AI.

Industry observers note that antoine is a visionary leader and founding partner of Unite.AI, driven by an unwavering passion for shaping and promoting the future of AI and robotics. A serial entrepreneur, he believes that AI will be as disruptive to society as electricity, and is often caught raving about the potential of disruptive technologies and AGI.

It has been revealed that as a futurist, he is dedicated to exploring how these innovations will shape our world. In addition, he is the founder of Securities.io, a platform focused on investing in cutting-edge technologies that are redefining the future and reshaping entire sectors.

Industry News: AI Can Scale Security. But Scale What?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (979 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that enterprise security teams today face more activity, telemetry and alerts than they can realistically investigate manually.
  • Sources indicate that for defenders, AI agents can change that equation by taking on investigations and other repetitive tasks across the environment.
  • Sources indicate that an agent investigating millions of endpoints must understand what it is looking for, what constitutes unusual behavior in that particular environment and which findings warrant further investigation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that enterprise security teams today face more activity, telemetry and alerts than they can realistically investigate manually. Estimates vary, with some research suggesting the average security operations team receives more than 4,400 alerts a day. As organizations expand and add more tools, and AI enables more attacks, that number is bound to grow. We’re already seeing examples of enterprises that have two million endpoints in their environment, and security teams that are investigating these alerts manually are not fighting a fair fight against attackers that are increasingly agentic.

Sources indicate that for defenders, AI agents can change that equation by taking on investigations and other repetitive tasks across the environment. However, the ability to process more data does not automatically translate into better threat detection or response. What’s needed is not just scale but context.

Sources indicate that an agent investigating millions of endpoints must understand what it is looking for, what constitutes unusual behavior in that particular environment and which findings warrant further investigation. Without this context, automation risks scaling noise and generating irrelevant or misleading conclusions.

And it’s important to keep in mind that not every organization will be able to rely on frontier model investigations for each alert; that will get far too costly.

Security environments differ in their infrastructure, applications, operational requirements, regulatory obligations and risk tolerance. Defenders must keep applications running while managing compliance requirements and avoiding operational disruption.

To be effective, agents must incorporate organizational knowledge, including historical investigations, established procedures and the judgment of experienced analysts. Much of this knowledge isn’t something that can just be fed to an agent in a spreadsheet or other format; it’s something that needs to be observed in action, by learning from experienced defenders at work.

For enterprises, the big question here is how to take that institutional knowledge and translate it into systems capable of making consistent, contextually appropriate decisions at machine speed.

Sources indicate that organizations need mechanisms to capture and apply the knowledge that informs investigations, including previous case decisions, established procedures and how analysts interpret evidence. Enterprises may have “custom” types of processes, tools and tribal knowledge that need to be captured, as well.

Model specialization is one potential approach. Fine-tuning models for individual enterprise customers can support large-scale investigations at a more predictable cost while maintaining strong performance. Fine-tuned open-source models may be particularly useful for tasks involving very large endpoint populations.

According to recent reports, organizations must also evaluate agent performance as models, workflows and enterprise environments change. Synthetic environments, or digital twins, can provide representative settings for testing different agent versions when production data is no longer available or has become outdated.

Industry observers note that fine-tuning is not the only way to provide context. Retrieval, memory, workflow orchestration and explicit policy controls are alternative approaches. The central requirement is that the chosen method improves an agent’s performance in the environment where it will operate.

Industry observers note that correctly identifying a threat is only part of the challenge. Agents must understand which actions they are authorized to take, when human approval is necessary and how to avoid disrupting legitimate business operations. Determining where agents can act autonomously and where human decision-making is required is essential to trusted deployment.

According to recent reports, autonomy at scale also requires economy of scale. Companies that use frontier models for millions of investigations are going to bankrupt themselves. That makes finding the most efficient method of investigating with an AI model, whether a Small Language Model (SLM) or a proprietary one, paramount.

Autonomy should be proportionate to risk. Routine, well-understood tasks may be suitable for autonomous execution, while consequential or disruptive actions may require human approval or additional authorization. Enterprise security also depends on coordination across teams. An investigation that identifies a threat requiring a firewall configuration change must transition seamlessly to the team responsible for that system, with appropriate authorization and accountability for remediation.

Governance and workflow design are therefore essential components of agent deployment, not controls that can be added after the technology has been scaled.

Organizations should assess agents using outcome-based measures, including investigation accuracy, false-positive and false-negative rates, time to investigate and remediate, cost per investigation, escalation quality and adherence to authorization policies.

It has been revealed that continuous evaluation is essential as models and workflows change. Testing different agent versions against representative cases and using synthetic environments can help organizations identify regressions before deploying updates into production.

Recent findings suggest that security leaders must balance the benefits of automation against the operational risks of deployment. Application availability, compliance obligations, organizational risk tolerance and implementation timelines all influence how promptly new capabilities can be adopted.

AI offers security teams an opportunity to address a longstanding capacity problem, but raw scale is not the end goal. The real opportunity lies in combining machine speed with organizational context, appropriate authority and human judgment so agents can distinguish what matters, take the right actions and involve the right people when necessary.

Eyal Fisher is Co-Founder and CTO of Legion Security, where he leads the technical vision behind the tech giant’s agentic security operations platform. An AI thought leader and entrepreneur, Eyal previously co-founded generative AI company ART AI and a cloud security startup, and brings research experience from the University of Cambridge. A recognized pioneer in generative AI, he has spent his career pushing the boundaries of how machine learning can be applied to real-world security operations.

MPS in PyTorch 2.15

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1356 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15!
  • Recent findings suggest that A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face.
  • If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and newly introduced Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

Recent findings suggest that A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:.

It has been revealed that FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

According to recent reports, you can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:.

Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each newly introduced token goes through the model as a single row, so the substantial matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

Sources indicate that A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The upcoming Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:.

According to recent reports, the decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:.

In a recent development, working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:.

Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

Audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:.

Token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:.

Industry observers note that one of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:.

In a recent development, you can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:.

Several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

It has been revealed that work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

Once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:.

Scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

According to recent reports, bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

Sources indicate that pyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A big thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Sources indicate that local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this newly introduced generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

Here's what changed, and what's next:.

The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:.

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:.

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Industry observers note that support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:.

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too substantial to run on the device with the same session code:.

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the upcoming provider can't replay them.

Industry observers note that API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

Recent findings suggest that while we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:.

Industry observers note that the first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:.

And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

In a recent development, language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

Breaking: Brizy AI 1.9.5 Generates Website Images and Lets Customers Rework Individual Sections

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that brizy has released version 1.9.5 of its AI website builder, replacing the use of Unsplash stock photos in the AI generation workflow with generated imagery.
  • In a recent development, the changes give users a way to revise part of a site without discarding a draft that already works.
  • In its version 1.9.5 announcement, Brizy notes it uses components to construct a layout and can take design or content references as input.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that brizy has released version 1.9.5 of its AI website builder, replacing the use of Unsplash stock photos in the AI generation workflow with generated imagery. The update also changes how the builder assembles pages. Brizy says it can now generate an individual section from a prompt instead of relying on ready-made blocks for the page design.

In a recent development, the changes give users a way to revise part of a site without discarding a draft that already works. They also make a distinction that matters for businesses: a stock image is an existing photograph chosen for a page, whereas a generated image can be tailored to the prompt without depicting a real product, location or member of staff. That makes some designs easier to prototype, but creates more for the site owner to verify before going live.

In its version 1.9.5 announcement, Brizy notes it uses components to construct a layout and can take design or content references as input. Those references can include images or HTML for layout direction and documents for source material. An owner could start with a brand reference and then regenerate a services section when the first version misses the point, rather than regenerate every page just to change one area.

Industry observers note that the company also states the release improves support for Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Russian and Arabic, including right-to-left layouts for Arabic. On multilingual sites, that affects more than text. Menus, buttons and page sections must remain usable when a language runs in the other direction or when the translation takes up more space than the original. An initial generation still needs review in each language, especially on mobile.

Brizy’s separate Cloud changelog shows that the editor and the generation flow have their own updates. For example, Cloud has added AI-assisted creation of newly introduced pages in an existing project. That is different from the new release’s ability to regenerate a single section during website creation. It is worth checking which editing surface a feature belongs to before adopting it as part of a workflow.

According to recent reports, brizy’s support guidance for WordPress import describes a generation and refinement stage before the user imports a design. It advises completing AI-based customization before the import, because the same generation controls are not available afterward in that workflow. For teams preparing a WordPress launch, that makes the handoff a good point to check copy, images and layout rather than expecting every generation option to remain available after import.

Generated imagery is useful for abstract backgrounds or illustrations when no suitable photograph exists. It is a less suitable substitute when customers need to see the actual item they are buying. Uploaded documents present a similar issue for copy: the text may look polished even if it misstates a price, service area or refund condition. Giving the builder reliable source material helps, but a person still needs to compare the published wording against it.

There is also a cost to repeated experimentation. Brizy’s Cloud terms say designated AI features use credits and that consumption varies with the action. A team evaluating the upgrade can try one representative page, revise just the section that needs work, and check how much editing remains before publication. The useful measure is not how rapidly the first design appears, but whether the site is faster to finish without losing control of what visitors see.
