💡 Key Takeaways
  • Andrew Nassar is CTO of IC Realtime, where he has helped guide the company through shifts from analog cameras to digital recording, remote monitoring, and AI-assisted video analysis.
  • Recent findings suggest that IC Realtime designs video surveillance systems and software for residential and commercial environments.
  • It has been revealed that you’ve helped lead IC Realtime through the transitions from analog cameras to digital recording, remote monitoring, and now AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Andrew Nassar is CTO of IC Realtime, where he has helped guide the company through shifts from analog cameras to digital recording, remote monitoring, and AI-assisted video analysis. With more than 20 years in the surveillance industry, he focuses on turning advances in computer vision and edge computing into practical tools for understanding events, finding footage, and improving security operations.

Recent findings suggest that IC Realtime designs video surveillance systems and software for residential and commercial environments. Its Bunker platform adds AI analysis to compatible camera systems through a dedicated NVIDIA Jetson-powered gateway, supporting contextual alerts and natural-language video search. The platform combines local analysis with cloud-connected services for remote access and video history.

It has been revealed that you’ve helped lead IC Realtime through the transitions from analog cameras to digital recording, remote monitoring, and now AI. What convinced you that AI could fundamentally change surveillance, and what advances have made sophisticated video analysis practical at the edge?

In a recent development, we have worked with machine learning and computer vision on our cameras for years. The opportunity became much more useful when the system could help someone understand an event and find the relevant footage, rather than simply produce more video to review. A homeowner wants to know what deserves attention. A business wants to find an incident without spending hours searching.

Industry observers note that bunker brings that approach to a dedicated NVIDIA Jetson gateway at the property. Moving core analysis closer to the cameras can reduce the dependence on sending every analytical task to the cloud and improve responsiveness. The practical advance is the combination of local computing and software that turns video into contextual alerts and searchable events.

Recent findings suggest that my standard is still proven value. The technology has to solve a real problem in the environment where the customer will use it. A good demonstration is the beginning of that process.

It has been revealed that using Bunker as an example, could you walk us through what happens between a camera capturing an event and a user receiving an alert? Which AI functions run locally, what still requires the cloud, and what data leaves the property?

It has been revealed that at a high level, a compatible camera sends video to the Bunker Gateway, and core AI analysis happens on that gateway at the property. The platform links detected activity to video events and can send a contextual alert with a snapshot and a plain-language description. The user can then review the video in the app.

Sources indicate that bunker uses a hybrid architecture. Cloud connectivity supports remote access, subscription services and video history, so it would be misleading to call the platform cloud-free or to say no video leaves the property. What matters is how that data is protected when it does leave. Everything is encrypted in transit, including live video, which stays encrypted from the gateway all the way to the viewer’s screen. The infrastructure in between relays it but can’t watch it. Each gateway authenticates with its own certificate, never shared credentials, and footage stored in the cloud is encrypted.

Customers should get a clear explanation of that flow, including which features depend on the internet and what happens when the connection is down.

It has been revealed that security cameras operate in rain, darkness, glare, and constantly changing environments. What is the hardest real-world failure you’ve encountered, and how do you measure whether improvements reduce false alarms without increasing missed incidents?

I’ve been in this industry for more than 20 years, and camera technology has improved dramatically, especially in low light and difficult conditions. Nighttime and noisy images are now nearly as clear as daytime. Even so, rain, glare, fog and snow can still reduce an AI model’s accuracy. Better sensors don’t remove those variables.

In a recent development, so we chose a dynamic approach that adjusts to changing environments and times of day, rather than relying on one fixed configuration. Over the past two years of development, we’ve put thousands of hours into testing in real-world installations, not just cameras on a bench, and we’ve built the system around what those deployments taught us.

In a recent development, I wouldn’t judge an improvement by a lower notification count alone. The question is whether it removes irrelevant alerts while still catching the incidents that matter. Reducing noise is only valuable if the system stays useful when something key happens.

Sources indicate that detecting a person or vehicle is different from deciding that behavior is concerning. How do you define an anomaly, adapt that definition to each location, and prevent the system from treating harmless activity as a threat?

Sources indicate that A detected object does not, by itself, tell you whether there is a problem. A delivery at the front entrance and activity in a restricted area can involve the same type of object but require very different responses. The starting point should be the customer’s use case and the context of that particular property.

I would distinguish an event worth reviewing from a conclusion that someone is a threat. The system should help a person understand what was observed and why it was surfaced, with access to the underlying footage. It should not encourage the user to treat every unfamiliar activity as evidence of wrongdoing.

As these systems become more capable, the challenge is to make that context useful without overstating what the AI knows. Human judgment remains notable, particularly when an alert could lead to a consequential action.

Natural-language search promises to replace hours of manually reviewing footage. How does your system connect a user’s description to the right video, and how do you test for missed events, incorrect matches, or AI-generated descriptions that the footage doesn’t support?

In a recent development, the concept is to make video searchable in the language a person would naturally use. As activity is detected, Bunker creates time-stamped descriptions associated with video events. A user’s question is used to search that indexed record and surface relevant footage. That gives the user a starting point without manually scrubbing through the entire recording.

The footage should remain the basis for checking the result. A generated description is useful for navigation, but it should not be treated as more authoritative than what the camera actually captured.

For testing, I would separate three questions: Did the system miss a relevant event? Did it retrieve something that does not match the request? Did the description include something the footage does not support? Those are different failure modes. Evaluating only whether the search returns a plausible-looking answer would not be enough.

Recent findings suggest that what trade-offs does NVIDIA Jetson hardware impose on model size, accuracy, power consumption, and the number of camera feeds you can analyze? How do you maintain reliable performance when using older third-party cameras, reaching processing capacity, or losing internet connectivity?

The design question is how to deliver useful analysis within the resources available at the property. Model complexity, the amount of video being processed and the required response time all have to fit the gateway’s operating limits. That is why the number of supported streams alone does not tell the whole performance story.

Bunker’s launch intends support up to 10 camera streams. Compatible ONVIF cameras let customers keep their existing hardware, but compatibility still needs to be verified for each installation. Profiles, firmware, image quality and the features being used all matter.

We also need to be precise about resilience. Local processing and cloud-connected services are different parts of the system, and having an edge gateway doesn’t mean every feature works normally during an internet outage. Updates are part of reliability too. Every patch is signed and verified on the gateway before it installs, older vulnerable versions are rejected, and a failed update rolls back automatically. A bad update shouldn’t be what takes a property’s security system offline.

Local inference alone doesn’t answer every privacy question. Where does Bunker store footage, search queries, and AI-generated metadata, how long are they retained, and who can access them? How do you improve your models without assuming access to customers’ private footage?

Industry observers note that footage and the databases behind the service are encrypted at rest. Passwords are hashed and sessions expire, so even a database breach wouldn’t give anyone working logins. The gateway itself is encrypted too, so a stolen device yields no footage and no credentials. Bunker’s launch offering included 60 days of cloud video history on Standard and 365 days on Premium, plus Video Vault for clips a customer chooses to save.

We don’t use customer footage to train our models, and we don’t create biometric templates of anyone the cameras capture. A customer using the product is not permission for us to reuse their private video.

Industry observers note that the controversy surrounding Flock Safety has highlighted questions about who can search surveillance data and whether access is properly revoked. Although your deployment model differs, what lessons apply to your systems, and which safeguards should be mandatory rather than optional?

In a recent development, the backlash against Flock isn’t really about the AI. It’s about who can get in and search the data. Much of the scrutiny came down to account security, including lawmakers asking why multi-factor authentication wasn’t mandatory. When a stolen password is enough to search a surveillance system, it doesn’t matter where the model runs.

Industry observers note that with Bunker, the only people with access to a system’s data are the consumers that system’s owner has granted access. We don’t share it with third parties, we don’t use customer data to train our models, and we don’t create biometric templates.

Industry observers note that security has to start at the device and carry through to the account. Every Bunker gateway ships with its own cryptographic identity, so there are no default passwords to change or for an attacker to look up. Firmware is verified at every boot, updates are signed and checked before they install, and logins are protected with multi-factor authentication. Beyond that, access should be removed promptly when it’s no longer needed, and sensitive activity should leave an auditable record. Trust depends on being able to explain who did what.

People captured by a camera often aren’t the people who bought it. How should AI surveillance account for the privacy of neighbors, employees, visitors, and passersby, and are there capabilities you would deliberately refuse to build?

The installation needs a defined purpose, and that purpose should guide what is captured, what is analyzed and who can see the results. Wanting to secure an entrance doesn’t mean every activity on a neighboring property should become part of a searchable record.

Sources indicate that one line we’ve drawn is identity. Bunker doesn’t create biometric templates, and it doesn’t attach an identity to anyone it detects. It describes what happened, not who someone is. That keeps the system focused on events rather than on tracking or profiling people.

More capability doesn’t automatically mean more value. If a feature creates a serious trust problem without solving a clear customer problem, that’s a reason not to build it.

Looking ahead three to five years, what meaningful capability do you expect edge AI to unlock beyond today’s detection and search—and what technical or trust problem must be solved before it deserves widespread adoption?

According to recent reports, honestly, the future of AI is uncharted right now, and it’s moving faster than anything I’ve seen in my career. We’re following those changes almost daily and looking at where they can genuinely benefit the people using our platform.

Industry observers note that the areas that matter most to us are context, understanding, and systems that keep learning and improving. The value is in helping someone understand a developing situation and decide what needs attention, instead of piecing together a string of separate notifications.

Sources indicate that the technical challenge is to do that reliably in changing environments and within the limits of the local hardware. The trust challenge is to make the system’s limits and data practices easy to understand. People need to know what it observed, what it inferred and when a human needs to make the call.

Thank you for the great interview, readers who wish to explore professional security cameras, recorders, and AI-powered video surveillance systems should visit IC Realtime.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:.

LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:.

In a recent development, the payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

The vision and audio models also get two upcoming in-house encoders:.

It has been revealed that each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

According to recent reports, reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:.

For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:.

See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a upcoming in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:.

Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:.

Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:.

See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

Industry observers note that reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:.

Then ask a question about a photo by voice:.

See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

In a recent development, reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies:.

Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:.

In a recent development, LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

Industry observers note that we adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

Stavros Gadinis, Berkeley Law Professor and Author of Corporate Ordering – Interview Series

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2485 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Johnson Professor of Law at UC Berkeley School of Law.
  • Sources indicate that his fresh book, Corporate Ordering: How Corporations Navigate Social Conflict, published by Cambridge University Press, examines how businesses develop governance systems when public rules are unsettled.
  • It has been revealed that your career spans corporate legal practice in Europe and research on corporate governance and financial regulation at Berkeley Law.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stavros Gadinis is the George R. Johnson Professor of Law at UC Berkeley School of Law. His research examines corporate governance, financial regulation, and the internal systems companies use to make and monitor decisions. Before entering academia, he practiced corporate law in Europe.

Sources indicate that his fresh book, Corporate Ordering: How Corporations Navigate Social Conflict, published by Cambridge University Press, examines how businesses develop governance systems when public rules are unsettled. Through cases involving ridesharing, climate sustainability, and artificial intelligence, it considers how companies make rules, exercise authority, and oversee their own conduct.

It has been revealed that your career spans corporate legal practice in Europe and research on corporate governance and financial regulation at Berkeley Law. How did that background shape your thinking, and what inspired you to write Corporate Ordering?

According to recent reports, I began my career practicing corporate law in Europe, and then spent many years at Berkeley studying corporate governance and financial regulation, including how rules spread across borders when no single government is in charge. We tend to think of the business world and the regulatory world as opposites, one eager for quick decisions and large profits, the other committed to bureaucratic process and the public good. Practice and research both taught me that the line is much blurrier than that.

It has been revealed that the book grew out of conversations with general counsel and senior executives about how they handle controversial decisions, the ones where employees, customers, communities and governments all want different things. What struck me is how closely their methods resemble those of a good regulator. They gather information by reaching out to the people affected, they explain their choices publicly, and they build mechanisms to check whether those choices hold up. These are not regulatory habits or corporate habits. They are the principles of sound decisionmaking in any institution that wields power over others. Corporate Ordering is my attempt to describe that machinery, show where it works, and show where it fails.

What is “corporate ordering,” and how does it help explain the way AI companies set rules for technologies that regulation has yet to catch up with?

Corporate ordering is the internal governance infrastructure companies build to make contested decisions before the law tells them what to do. It has three functions, which mirror the branches of a state. Rulemaking is how a company writes its own principles. Executive action is how it applies them to concrete decisions. Monitoring is how it checks whether it followed through, and how it finds out when it did not.

AI companies show all three at work. The frontier labs write constitutions, model specifications and safety frameworks, which is rulemaking. They decide whether a model is ready to launch, what it will refuse and who gets access, which is executive action. And they commission red-teaming, outside evaluations and incident reporting, which is monitoring. In the book I chart these functions across the major labs. The differences are real, but so is a striking convergence, as each firm discovers why it needs every piece.

I want to be clear about one thing, because it is often misread. Corporate ordering is not an argument against regulation. It describes the material regulation will be built from. When legislators act, they borrow concepts the companies developed first. The real question is whether that first draft was written carefully enough to deserve borrowing.

Your book examines ridesharing, climate sustainability, and AI governance. Which lessons from the first two areas are most useful for AI, and where does AI present fundamentally different challenges?

The lesson from ridesharing and climate is that corporations very often write the first draft of the law. Uber and Lyft developed insurance and safety reporting practices before states had rules for them, and much of corporate carbon accounting runs on the GHG Protocol, a standard business helped build. Regulators then condoned those practices, supplemented them or wrote them into law. Regulation rarely starts from a blank slate. And the more thoughtful companies are about their choices, the more they take affected parties into account, the more likely those choices are to survive into regulation.

AI differs in two ways. The first is speed. Regulators are often a step behind industry, but in AI the gap is far wider. Regulators will have to look to companies to develop standards and internal processes, and concentrate their own efforts on oversight, verification and enforcement. That makes their role different, not smaller. Verification is where public power matters most, because it is where the conflict of interest with management is strongest. The second difference is reach. AI touches nearly every part of daily life, and it has become a major investment for the nation as a whole. The systemic risk implications are as hard to miss as they are to fathom.

When an AI company selects and pays its own outside safety evaluators, what safeguards make that oversight meaningfully independent?

This conflict of interest is familiar from financial auditing, and corporate law already has tools to manage it. The first is who hires and fires. The relationship with the evaluator should sit with independent directors who have no other financial ties to the company, much as the audit committee, not the CEO or CFO, oversees the external auditor. Management should not be able to dismiss a reviewer whose findings are inconvenient.

The second is access and publication. The evaluator needs to see what it asks to see, and it needs the right to publish its findings, or at least a meaningful summary, without a tech giant veto. Reputational risk is what gives a review its teeth. The third is common review standards, so that an evaluation means the same thing across firms and evaluators cannot compete by being lenient. The fourth is protection for whistleblowers, and even rewards when they bring actionable information, because people inside the company are often the first to know when an evaluation was steered.

It has been revealed that suppose an outside evaluator identifies a serious safety concern just before a major model launch. Who should receive that finding, and who should have the authority to delay or stop deployment?

Industry observers note that the finding should go to the board directly, ideally to a committee of independent directors responsible for safety, and not only through the management team that is pushing for the launch. Management can and should respond, but it should not be the filter. The authority to delay or stop deployment should rest with the board, because this is exactly the kind of decision boards exist to make, one with large stakes, conflicting interests and no obvious right answer.

Industry observers note that but the more key point is that the decision must be explicit and documented, and traceable to the people who made it. If the board goes ahead despite the concern, the record should show what it knew, what it weighed and why it judged the risk acceptable. That paper trail creates the conditions for liability, or at least reputational damage, and it makes people think twice. Courts are increasingly willing to recognize that design choices in software have consequences for owners, and a company that can show a serious, documented effort stands in a very different position from one that cannot.

When safety concerns conflict with revenue targets or competitive pressure, what should a credible board decision-making process look like?

It has been revealed that A credible process is an informed one, and it leaves a record. The board should see concrete information about the costs of delay, the nature and likelihood of the safety concern, and the options for mitigating it. It should ask whether the testing was adequate and, where it was not, commission more or invite outside review. Where real uncertainty remains, there are options between launching and shelving, such as a limited release, a staged rollout or a sandbox, that let the company learn more before it commits. And whatever the board decides, what the company then indicates publicly about the model’s safety must be accurate, which is where much of the current litigation risk lies.

Then the board should write down what it decided and why. Over time those records become a body of precedent, so the next hard call is measured against the last one, and anyone reviewing the firm can see whether its stated principles actually bind. Microsoft has started to build this kind of decision record, and I think it is one of the most underrated tools in AI governance. Competitive pressure is real, and a board may reasonably decide to move ahead. What it cannot do is decide by default.

Sources indicate that your work proposes a “social business judgment” standard for evaluating board decisions. How would that apply to an AI tech giant that postpones a profitable product launch because of potential public harm?

Under existing corporate law, a board that postpones a profitable launch is already well protected. Courts defer to directors’ business judgment, and accepting lower profits today to avoid harm tomorrow fits comfortably within it. The harder question runs the other way, whether the board took public harm seriously at all.

Social business judgment asks the board to evaluate potential public harm the way it evaluates any other business risk, through tangible, measurable and specific metrics wherever possible. The emphasis is on process and due diligence, not on the outcome. A board that sources the right information, hears from those affected and records its reasoning has earned deference, whether it postpones the launch or proceeds with it. A board that does none of this has not. So in the case you describe, the postponement itself is not the glitch. The issue is whether the board can show how it reached that decision, and whether it would reach the same one again on the same facts.

Industry observers note that AI companies publish safety frameworks and voluntary commitments, but readers rarely see how those policies affect individual decisions. What evidence would distinguish effective governance from a public relations exercise?

It has been revealed that very often, when companies publish frameworks, the public is left wondering whether the framework ever applies to specific decisions or remains rhetoric the company never follows through on. The answer is disclosure of a particular kind. Rather than more statements of principle, companies should report the specific choices they made and how the framework shaped them, which releases were delayed, which capabilities were held back, which risk thresholds were triggered and what followed.

According to recent reports, the most telling evidence is a decision that cost the tech giant something. A framework that has never changed an outcome, never delayed a launch and never been invoked against revenue is hard to distinguish from public relations. These disclosures also need to be specific enough to verify, and for the most consequential questions they should be verified by a third party with the standing to say so publicly.

Sources indicate that where does corporate self-governance reach its limits? Which decisions about acceptable AI risk require public rules or democratic oversight?

In a recent development, the most important limit has to do with failures to monitor. Even a well-intentioned, responsible company can face a major crisis, and at that moment conflicts of interest multiply. Employees may withhold information that would hurt their jobs or their bonuses. Executives may suppress bad news to avoid public criticism. Fear of lawsuits may keep the company from being open. In past corporate crises, the crucial information usually came from people leadership could not control, external auditors and reviewers, affected parties, or internal whistleblowers using independent reporting channels.

This is where public rules matter most. The law can add relatively little at the rulemaking stage, because statutes tend to borrow their key concepts from the companies. It can add more on disclosure, by reaching firms that will not disclose voluntarily. And it adds the most on verification, by requiring independent review, protecting whistleblowers and giving outside checks real authority.

According to recent reports, the other limit is collective. The most a single company can do is stop itself. It cannot stop its competitors. Decisions about catastrophic risk, including whether to slow the frontier, require coordination across firms and governments, at home and internationally. One model I find promising is an international standard-setter along the lines of the ISSB in sustainability reporting, independent of governments but overseen by trustees that include them. Corporate ordering is necessary for this work, because the taming of these models happens inside the companies that build them, but it cannot carry the work alone.

If you were advising the board of a fast-growing AI company today, what three governance changes would you prioritize, and what evidence would you look for a year later to determine whether they worked?

In a recent development, first, outreach in rulemaking. Before adopting or revising its safety framework or usage policies, the manufacturer should consult the people affected (people, civil society, domain experts) and publish what it heard and how it responded. Second, regular responsibility reporting, an annual account of the hard decisions the board and management made under the framework, with enough detail to be checked. Third, an external monitor, hired by and reporting to independent directors, with full access and the right to publish.

A year later I would look for evidence that each one actually bit. For outreach, at least one rule that changed because of what the company heard. For reporting, disclosed decisions the company would rather not have discussed, including ones that cost it revenue or time. For the monitor, findings the company did not want, and a record of what the board did about them. If after a year everything reported is good news, the changes have not worked.

Industry News: Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2053 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • They write, summarize, translate, and call tools.
  • Recent findings suggest that say a customer calls your support line.
  • In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

Recent findings suggest that say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they stated (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Today we're announcing two packages:.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's fresh speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

It's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:.

In a recent development, the package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:.

Industry observers note that the steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

Industry observers note that qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:.

Sources indicate that qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

Recent findings suggest that to add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:.

According to recent reports, each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

Industry observers note that downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

According to recent reports, when you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who stated what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:.

The diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

Industry observers note that the diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

Sources indicate that we measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:.

According to recent reports, parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

Sources indicate that these numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

Industry observers note that anyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't newly introduced, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

Sources indicate that what's latest is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

Industry observers note that apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:.

urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

Recent findings suggest that the app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:.

The session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:.

You use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

Raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

According to recent reports, language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

Each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

AnyDecisionModel has six backends:.

The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

Like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

Both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

Add the packages to your Package.swift:.

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

According to recent reports, each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

It has been revealed that try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Issues and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

OpenAI Introduces MedChemBench for Medicinal-Chemistry Reasoning

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (995 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that openAI introduced MedChemBench, a 99-problem medicinal-chemistry benchmark, on November 20, 2026, and reported that GPT-6.2 Astra earned 84.5% of available credit at the xhigh reasoning-effort setting.
  • It has been revealed that the other reported xhigh scores were 83.3% for GPT-6 Astra, 82.0% for GPT-6.1 Sol and 58.2% for GPT-5.6 Sol.
  • The technical paper describes a retrospective set of tasks drawn from 117 papers and patents, encompassing 761 distinct graded molecular structures.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that openAI introduced MedChemBench, a 99-problem medicinal-chemistry benchmark, on November 20, 2026, and reported that GPT-6.2 Astra earned 84.5% of available credit at the xhigh reasoning-effort setting. It tests whether models can connect molecular structures with experimental evidence to explain results, compare compounds and predict properties.

It has been revealed that the other reported xhigh scores were 83.3% for GPT-6 Astra, 82.0% for GPT-6.1 Sol and 58.2% for GPT-5.6 Sol. The benchmark addresses a central difficulty in medicinal chemistry: a compound can be potent against a disease-related protein while being poorly absorbed or metabolized too quickly. Selecting what to test next therefore requires weighing competing properties rather than optimizing one measurement.

The technical paper describes a retrospective set of tasks drawn from 117 papers and patents, encompassing 761 distinct graded molecular structures. Prompts generally stop at a selected decision point in a research program, providing the biological context, earlier compounds and selected experimental findings. Later results are withheld to inform reference answers and grading criteria.

The tasks cover preclinical drug discovery, not clinical development, across seven categories. These include integrated lead selection with 48 tasks, structure–activity relationship forecasting with 26, and smaller groups covering ADME (absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion) and delivery, molecular design and enumeration, safety and liabilities, retrosynthesis, and assay biology and mechanism. Eighty-five tasks span more than one scientific-content domain, reflecting how a lead choice can depend simultaneously on potency, selectivity, cell assays, metabolism, exposure and safety.

Sources indicate that one problem concerning PRMT5, a protein studied in cancer drug discovery, asks models to reconstruct three related compounds and predict cellular potency, permeability, efflux and human microsomal clearance. The withheld results illustrate the tradeoff: compound 23 was more potent in cells, while compound 24 crossed a cell barrier more readily and broke down more slowly in a liver-enzyme assay.

Grading combines deterministic checks with model-judged rubrics. Molecular structure and scientific rationale account for 37.49% and 35.78% of available credit, respectively; ranking and candidate selection account for 17.51%, and numerical or categorical prediction for 8.92%. For structures, RDKit converts submitted SMILES, a text representation of molecular graphs, into canonical isomeric form while preserving stereochemistry and isotopes. Numerical predictions generally receive partial credit based on fold error, while a separate GPT-6 Astra judge at medium reasoning effort scores scientific-rationale criteria as zero, half or full credit.

Across 11 GPT models and 61 model–effort conditions, the paper reports 60,390 graded responses, with ten retained responses for each task in every condition. GPT-6.2 Astra is not among those 11 models; its result comes from the announcement.

It has been revealed that at xhigh, the paper reports that GPT-6 Astra earned 95.37% of available molecular-structure credit and 91.05% of scientific-rationale credit, compared with 50.42% for ranking and candidate selection and 47.02% for numerical prediction. The components cover different applicable tasks and scoring rules, but the results distinguish strong reconstruction and explanation from weaker compound selection and quantitative forecasting.

A reconstruction task described in the paper makes the structural differences concrete. Models had to assemble a molecule from a central structure and two attached groups while preserving an 18-atom ring. GPT-6 Astra produced the correct compound in all ten xhigh responses, whereas GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-5.6 Luna failed in all ten of theirs. The illustrated Sol answer contained a 15-atom ring, while Luna returned two disconnected fragments. Such errors change the molecule’s identity before any property reasoning begins.

It has been revealed that openAI states that the scores do not establish whether models can discover fresh drugs or improve laboratory decisions. Every answer was a single attempt without tools, feedback or new experiments, and the tasks use historical evidence rather than prospective discovery. Prior exposure to the published sources also cannot be ruled out.

For a heuristic check, the authors added source DOI or patent identifiers to all 99 prompts for nine models at xhigh. Mean overall-score changes ranged from a 0.23-percentage-point decrease to a 0.80-point increase, and every model-specific 95% confidence interval included zero. The check cannot establish whether source material appeared in training data.

In a recent development, the paper describes MedChemBench as close to saturation in its current form and states open-ended design and synthesis grading remains partly tied to reference answers, which may penalize plausible alternatives. Proposed extensions include prospective cases, expert adjudication of alternative answers, explicit treatment of assay uncertainty, and an agent-based track allowing retrieval, calculation, structure verification and multistep revision.

MedChemBench therefore separates chemical comprehension from demonstrated drug-discovery impact. Its strongest results concern reconstructing and explaining fixed historical problems, while compound selection and numerical forecasting lag. The proposed prospective and agent-based evaluations address the resulting open question: whether models can make better research decisions when they must gather evidence, calculate properties and revise their answers over multiple steps.

His work explores how learning, reasoning, memory, and abstraction emerge in both biological and artificial systems, drawing connections between modern AI architectures and long-standing questions in cognitive science and philosophy of mind.

Industry observers note that with a conceptual and reflective approach, Jonas examines frameworks such as reasoning models, agentic systems, emergent cognition, and alignment theory, aiming to clarify what progress toward AGI actually means—and what it does not. Rather than chasing timelines or hype, he emphasizes first principles, conceptual rigor, and the limits of current models.

Breaking: Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1589 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral.
  • There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team.
  • Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:.

There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

In a recent development, mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

Industry observers note that mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

It has been revealed that mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That mentioned, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

Recent findings suggest that mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

For each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

Mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

It has been revealed that on coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

In a recent development, cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:.

Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing demonstrated promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

Mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

Industry observers note that the Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

FBI Arrests Executive at Ransomware Negotiation Firm

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Agents with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) on Thursday arrested an executive at a Canadian cybersecurity firm in connection with an investigation into the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently relieved the FBI of sensitive data on thousands of agents, multiple sources tell KrebsOnSecurity.
  • The Upcoming York Times reported today that the FBI has arrested a Canadian man in Pennsylvania on suspicion of assisting ShinyHunters.
  • One source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity the Canadian person arrested this week was visiting Pennsylvania for a cyber insurance conference, and that the suspect’s organization specialized in handling ransomware negotiations with cybercrime groups.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Agents with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) on Thursday arrested an executive at a Canadian cybersecurity firm in connection with an investigation into the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently relieved the FBI of sensitive data on thousands of agents, multiple sources tell KrebsOnSecurity.

The Upcoming York Times reported today that the FBI has arrested a Canadian man in Pennsylvania on suspicion of assisting ShinyHunters. The Times story did not identify the man, nor did a statement on Twitter/X about the arrest from FBI Director Kash Patel.

One source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity the Canadian person arrested this week was visiting Pennsylvania for a cyber insurance conference, and that the suspect’s organization specialized in handling ransomware negotiations with cybercrime groups. Another shared that control over the ShinyHunters investigation has been centralized at an FBI field office in Texas.

Sources indicate that an online search reveals the Cyber Risk Summit was held at the Loews Philadelphia Hotel between Oct. 5 and Oct. 7. The conference had several sponsors, but according to the summit’s website its biggest sponsor was a Canadian security firm called Cypfer.

According to LinkedIn, one of Cypfer’s “ex-founders” was Edward Dubrovsky, who is now associated with another Canadian security firm and sponsor called CyberSteward. In a post to LinkedIn approximately one month ago, Dubrovsky mentioned he had prepares to attend the Cyber Risk Summit with the rest of the CyberSteward team.

Sources indicate that [Revision: Oct. 10, 9:58 a.m. ET: A spokesperson for Cypfer noted Dubrovsky was not a founder or co-founder as his LinkedIn profile claims, but instead served as a managing director before resigning in December 2025].

Edward Dubrovsky’s LinkedIn profile.

“Looking forward to continuing conversations around strategy & compliant driven coercive (ransomware, extortion) advisory, negotiations and settlement services that are global and truly agnostic,” Dubrovsky wrote.

Recent findings suggest that federal court records show that on October 8, an Edward Dobrovsky (note the slight misspelling of the last name) was arrested in Pennsylvania on cyber extortion and conspiracy charges. Several of those documents — including the core complaint — are now sealed. But a handful of them were indexed at Courtlistener.com, including a summary of the complaint, which charges the defendant with “conspiracy to threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with the intent to extort money,” and “interference with commerce by threats.”.

According to recent reports, the inmate locator at the U.S. Bureau of Prisons website reports that a 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky is currently being held at a federal facility in Philadelphia. But the court records indexed by CourtListener include a notice filed on October 9 that moved the case to the Eastern District of Texas, which sources say is now the epicenter of the FBI’s ShinyHunters investigation. The FBI declined to comment for this story.

Dubrovsky’s LinkedIn profile states he is the author of Cyber Extortion Strategic Response, a 252-page book that promises to “take readers beyond the ransom note and into the decisions that determine how an organization responds, recovers, and protects what matters.”.

Edward Dubrovsky’s book, which centers on the intricacies of ransomware negotiations.

Sources indicate that “At the heart of the book is a critical distinction: communicating with a criminal is not the same as negotiating a payment, and negotiating is not a commitment to pay,” reads an excerpt from the book’s listing on Amazon. “Engagement can serve other objectives, including testing claims, gathering information, creating time, and preserving options while the organization evaluates its next move.”.

Mr. Dubrovsky could not be immediately reached for comment. KrebsOnSecurity also sought comment from other executives at CyberSteward, and will update this post in the event they respond. The available court records in Dubrovsky’s case show that he does not at the moment have an attorney and has yet to be appointed a public defender by the courts.

ShinyHunters typically uses phishing and stolen credentials to siphon data from corporate accounts at software-as-a-service companies, and then threatens to publish the stolen data online unless a ransom demand is paid. According to the FBI, the group has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

Sources tell KrebsOnSecurity the FBI has been poring over devices that were seized last month when the Dutch police arrested the convicted cybercriminal Pepijn van der Stap in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation, and that charges against principals at other companies that specialize in ransomware negotiation may be forthcoming.

Immediately after Van der Stap’s arrest, another member of ShinyHunters named “Rey” assumed control over the group and began taunting the FBI over data the group stole from the agency’s online recruitment portal, which included each’s person’s unit and specialization, as well as medical and psychiatric records.

Sources indicate that last week, Reuters reported that Rey — identified as a teenager named Saif Al-din Khader — had been detained and was cooperating with FBI investigators. On October 7, we detailed how Rey was apprehended as the cybercrime group allegedly sought to extort a navigation and digital aviation unit that was divested by Boeing in late 2025.

This is likely to be a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted along with timestamps.

#23343. Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready
