    #23267. Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3806 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3806 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.
    • Models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing.
    • In a recent development, take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.

    Models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination.

    In a recent development, take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time.

    Our earlier work (multi-harness RL, harness adapters) showed that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations.

    According to recent reports, we leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2, OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6. The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol:.

    Most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop, SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM's agent and environment classes, slime's custom rollout functions, or ART's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. Recent work moves in the same direction: Agent Lightning v1.0 keeps the deploy-time harness in the loop through a proxy ("harnessed agentic RL"), and SkyRL's Harbor integration trains on Harbor trials, converting their chat histories into tokens for the trainer.

    For this recipe we created a custom dataset for agentic coding with the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv. We combined together task retrieval of existing RL envs, task generation with Repo2RLEnv, task validation with OpenEnv, and sampling into a single data pipeline. This gave us the highest quality set of validated and relevant tasks to improve Qwen3.8-27B on agentic coding. In this section, we’ll walk through how we built it, so you can try it out on your own domains.

    RL training needs tasks the agent can attempt, a verifier that scores each attempt, and evidence that the verifier is right. A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior. A task that is already feasible will not teach the model anything.

    This section describes how we built the task set from three sources: two on the Hugging Face Hub and a third generated with Tasksmith, a pipeline in Repo2RLEnv. Every task passes an eligibility screen with openenv validate, and the same difficulty check against the base model, Qwen3.8-27B.

    Recent findings suggest that each task uses the Harbor format, which Terminal-Bench 2.1 also uses. A broad search of the Hub for Harbor environments returned about 59,000 tasks, but they included duplicates, evaluation sets and tasks marked as not for training. We filtered down to just two Hub sources built for training and generated a third set ourselves:.

    Recent findings suggest that we used Tasksmith to target gaps. We mapped the skills that our target benchmarks test (Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE), then chose pull requests that exercise them, such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization. From 30 merged pull requests, Tasksmith produced 24 tasks in 10 Python repositories that passed its checks, 17 of them on a second run. Its checks do not replace ours, so these tasks go through the same pipeline as the rest.

    A metadata screen runs first. It keeps tasks from training splits with permissive licenses. It drops duplicates, tasks marked as not for training, the 253 tasks in our target benchmarks, and any task from a repository those benchmarks use. We then ran the semantic checks from openenv validate on every task in fresh trials:.

    It has been revealed that each trial ran as its own Hugging Face Job, which let us validate dozens of tasks at once. openenv validate offers the same option for any Harbor task:.

    Sources indicate that 858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed. Wrong-answer controls caught defects, including a Tasksmith task that accepted an incomplete implementation and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers. Most failures were infrastructure problems, such as images that did not start. Failed tasks stay in a rejected split with the failing check recorded.

    A valid task can still teach nothing. GRPO (group relative policy optimization) scores each attempt against the other attempts at the same task, so a task where every attempt passes, or every attempt fails, gives no learning signal. Before training, Qwen3.8-27B attempted each task 4 times, or 8 times for a stratified sample of six tasks per repository.

    Industry observers note that of 442 scored tasks, Qwen3.8-27B solved 151 every time and 120 never. The 171 tasks it solved only sometimes form the qualified set. The figure below indicates how the scores pile up at both ends and how they differ by source. The model solves most Go tasks every time, fails every attempt on more than a third of the SWE-smith Python tasks, and lands in the middle on 73% of the SWE-Gym tasks.

    Qwen3.8-27B results on 442 scored tasks. Green marks the qualified tasks, which the model solves on some attempts but not all.

    According to recent reports, this example shows how we filtered and validated 1,127 tasks to 278 which we included directly in the final dataset. The pipeline then took the remaining 522 rejected tasks, repaired and complexified them with Tasksmith and repeated validation.

    In a recent development, the pipeline applies two filters: validation removes broken tasks, and the difficulty check keeps tasks the base model solves only sometimes. This section tests whether those filters change what the model learns. We trained four short runs of up to 50 steps, each on tasks from a different stage of the pipeline, and compared them with the base model on Terminal-Bench 2.1.

    Recent findings suggest that each run trains Qwen3.8-27B with LoRA and GRPO, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, on 32 tasks. All four use the same agent harness (OpenCode with up to 48 model calls), the same settings and one 8×H200 Hugging Face Job, and the reward is the verifier's pass or fail. The task sets differ in how they were filtered:.

    The figure below highlights how the tasks impacted model learning. The table lists each run's steps and the checkpoint we evaluate. The chart tracks training reward across subsets of tasks with differing validation status.

    It has been revealed that harness-hub/agentic-coding-envs holds 871 tasks from 35 repositories. Hub tasks are capped at 40 per repository, so no single project dominates. The table below demonstrates what each source contributes. The dataset has two views: every accepted task, and the qualified subset for GRPO training. Rejected attempts stay in a separate config.

    We leveraged the stable version of AsyncGRPOTrainer from TRL, with the main advantage of the trainer being that it does not wait until all rollouts are completed before moving to the next training optimization step.

    For more detailed reading on the trainer and its building blocks, please refer to the AsyncGRPO blogpost.

    To obtain our final harness adapters, we trained LoRA adapters on top of Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer. The adapters were attached to the model using the all-linear flag. To maximize the training efficiency, thinking mode was turned off during rollout stages, and we evaluated our final adapter with and without thinking for broader comparison.

    The final reward function consists of the verifier's correctness, combined with a small tool-efficiency bonus (0.1, derived from early experiments from the previous iteration of harness adapters which revealed that 0.1 worked best).

    We performed a small LR sweep on 50 steps using Termgrade environments (1e-5, 5e-5 and 1e-4) and noticed that 1e-5 barely moved training correctness (from 0.52 to 0.50), 1e-4 collapsed the rollouts instead of improving them (turns per rollout moved from 18 to 6, with entropy rising), and only 5e-5 clearly improved (from 0.49 to 0.60 by step 40). Longer 5e-5 runs then indicated signs of instability (collapsing rollout lengths, rising entropy), so we settled on 2e-5 for the final runs.

    It has been revealed that each harness adapter was trained using NVIDIA 2xB200 GPUs, with one GPU allocated for the vLLM server and the other allocated for the training process. We first performed some stress testing to maximize the amount of RL tasks that can be trained within a single optimization step. For that, we ‘maxed out’ the --token-budget argument from AsyncGRPOTrainer to its limit for the setup that we had. The chart below indicates the evolution of the number of groups per step for each harness (in blue: Pi, green: OpenCode and orange: Hermes).

    As the model gets better and better during training, it is able to fit more and more groups during each training step, which diversifies the signals that the model gets at each optimization step.

    The final data mixture consists of 750 tasks from harness-adapters RL environments and 300 tasks from termgrade. In order to maximize the diversity of the sampled tasks during training, we have slightly customized the data sampling strategy, which will be explained below:.

    It has been revealed that before training, the tasks are put in a fixed order that interleaves them by family (i.e., their repository for our generated RL environments. For Termgrade, we just sorted them by name since each task is considered as its own family), so every training step mixes as many repositories as possible while following the distribution of the mixture.

    We also plug the safeagents tool, in order to block any misbehavior from the model during training. The final plugin (which consists of the regex and pattern rules specific to the RL tasks and test path) is hosted in harness-hub/qwen-safeagents-plugin and can be used out of the box using the latest version of safeagents in case anyone wants to reproduce the training setup.

    Sources indicate that the number of blocked tools from safeagents decreases consistently during training, which indicates that the model gets ‘safer and safer’ after each optimization step. Below is a diagram of the safeagents blocked calls per 1000 tool calls, by training step, for each harness adapter.

    Industry observers note that merging models often combines their capabilities while keeping most of what each one could do. Once the three harness adapters were trained, we asked two questions. Does merging them cost accuracy? And can a single "super-adapter" be accurate and efficient under every harness?

    We started by comparing the weight updates of the three adapters, layer by layer. The cosine similarity between any two of them is about 0.01–0.02: each adapter pushed the model in a nearly orthogonal direction during training. That's the best case for merging, since the updates barely interfere.

    Industry observers note that we concatenate the three LoRA adapters along the rank dimension (PEFT's combination_type="cat"). The merged adapter has rank 96 (3 × 32) and applies exactly w · (ΔW_pi + ΔW_hermes + ΔW_opencode). Prior work on merging (task arithmetic, TIES, KnOTS) finds that scaling each patch below 1 works best, so we compared three weights on all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, under each harness, with the step-120 adapters:.

    The plain sum over-applies the updates. The agents become very short (13 tool calls per task, against 49 for the base model), and while Hermes peaks at 62.8%, pi falls back to the base model's level. The average dilutes each harness's own enhancement. ½ gives the best balance, so we built the final super-adapter from the released checkpoints (pi step 160, hermes step 160, opencode step 150) at weight ½.

    Under each harness, on the tasks every run graded (50–51 on SWE-bench Pro, 82–85 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), one attempt per task (in parentheses, the efficiency gain with respect to the base model):.

    Sources indicate that "Thinking" is the chat template's thinking mode at its default effort (xhigh). The specialists were trained and served with thinking off.

    With thinking off, the super-adapter improves on the base model on all six harness–benchmark pairs (mean pass@1 39.5% → 49.0%; 71 tasks newly solved vs 34 lost, p < 0.001).

    Sources indicate that despite not being trained at all with thinking on, it's the strongest model we evaluated with thinking mode. Against the base model thinking at the same effort, it wins on five of six pairs and ties the sixth (mean 55.5% → 63.5%; 67 newly solved vs 37 lost, p = 0.004). The largest gains are on SWE-bench Pro: +16 points under hermes and +20 under opencode. Under pi on SWE-bench Pro, where thinking alone already reaches 74%, it ties.

    Use the specialist harness adapters when thinking off. Each harness's own adapter is ahead on four of six pairs, by the most under pi (64.0% vs 46.0% on SWE-bench Pro, 56.5% vs 48.2% on Terminal-Bench). Splitting one model across three harnesses costs pi the most of its gain. If you only use one harness and keep thinking off, take its specialist.

    It has been revealed that the super adapter is also much more efficient. On the tasks both the base model and the super-adapter solve, with thinking off, it makes 53–73% fewer tool calls and generates 44–60% fewer tokens per task, with fewer tool calls on 111 of 130 tasks. With thinking on, it still cuts tool calls by 31–48% and tokens by 24–43% on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench, tool calls drop by 19–25% and token counts stay about the same.

    In a recent development, the ½ weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the step-120 adapters, so the Terminal-Bench numbers are slightly optimistic; SWE-bench Pro played no part in the choice. Full paired results are in the super-adapter's model card.

    This section reports what happened during training, then how the adapters score on held-out benchmarks inside and outside their own harnesses.

    Training ran for a cumulative total of 598 steps, with a total of 78,114 samples trained, which consists exactly of 167M trained tokens.

    It has been revealed that during training, we see a clear signal that the model learns to solve tasks in fewer and fewer steps, with no clear sign of saturation. Despite having some clear increasing trend sometimes, training correctness seems to overall stay flat. This can be explained by the fact that the model meets new tasks during training, but the number of groups that fit in a step’s token budget more than doubles as trajectories get shorter. The accuracy gains show up on the held-out benchmarks in the section below.

    On the other hand, safeagents was able to block multiple suspicious attempts. Across the three training runs, a total of 1.3M tool calls have been checked, and a total of 647 tool calls have been blocked.

    This section covers the evaluation setup, the in-harness results, transfer across harnesses, and an out-of-distribution check.

    Recent findings suggest that we evaluate each adapter inside the harness it was trained in, on two agentic coding benchmarks: all 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 (1 hour and 100 agent steps per task) and the 51 hardest tasks of SWE-bench Pro (2 hours and 100 agent steps). We cap the maximum number of tokens per task to be 131072. We do not tune the agent settings and use the default setup for all harnesses. For example, Pi does not keep previous reasoning turns while OpenCode and Hermes do, which mainly affects the SWE-bench Pro results due to rapid context overflow. Therefore you cannot compare the results across different harnesses (using Pi does not necessarily lead to better results than Hermes or OpenCode), but it is fair to compare results within the same harness and draw conclusions.

    Industry observers note that every rollout runs through the same Harbor and OpenEnv stack as training, in HF sandboxes, with one attempt per task at temperature 0.8 and thinking off. Each LoRA checkpoint is merged into the base weights and served alone with vLLM on a single GPU, at the same concurrency as the base model's eval.

    For all the evaluation benchmarks, we report the pass@1 as well as the number of tool calls, total turns, for all tasks and for solved tasks.

    For openness, all model trajectories for final evaluations are pushed in this public bucket: harness-hub/harness-adapters-trajectories.

    Industry observers note that all three specialist adapters beat the base model under their own harness, on both benchmarks. On SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), pi goes from 39.2% to 64.7% (+25.5 points: 15 tasks newly solved vs 2 lost, p = 0.002), hermes from 29.4% to 43.1%, and opencode from 35.3% to 51.0%. On the full Terminal-Bench 2.1, pi gains +16.3 points (16 vs 2, p = 0.001) and hermes +14.1 (19 vs 7, p = 0.03). Opencode gains +6.0 overall, and +13.6 on the 66 tasks that played no part in choosing its checkpoint (12 vs 3, p = 0.035).

    In a recent development, the adapters also solve tasks much more efficiently: on the tasks both they and the base model solve, they make 56–72% fewer tool calls per task on SWE-bench Pro and 53–70% fewer on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The single super-adapter beats the base model under all three harnesses too (+6 to +18 points on SWE-bench Pro, +5 to +10 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), with just as large a cut in tool calls (53–73%). It keeps less of each specialist's gain with thinking off, most under pi, but with thinking on it beats the base model thinking at the same effort on five of six harness–benchmark pairs (see the super-adapter section). Each model card has the full paired results.

    To answer this question, we also evaluated the pi harness adapter under Hermes Agent and OpenCode.

    Recent findings suggest that under OpenCode it matches OpenCode's own specialist on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (44.8% → 54.0%, against 46.4% → 52.4%). Under Hermes it keeps about two-thirds of the specialist's gain (46.3% → 56.1%, against 44.7% → 58.8%), with the same ~45% cut in tool calls in both. Therefore it seems that the newly learned capabilities are transferred across harnesses.

    What happens if we evaluate in out-of-distribution tasks, outside the harnesses the adapters have been trained with?

    It has been revealed that we ran all five models on 300 AutomationBench tasks which consists of business-automation workflows evaluations, with AutomationBench's own agent loop instead of Pi, Hermes or OpenCode. This way, we can cross check two different questions: can the model solve problems outside SWE-related tasks? What happens when the model is being put outside the harness it has been trained with?

    According to recent reports, results show that the adapters stay close to the base model. Pi and OpenCode are slightly ahead (27.0% and 25.3% pass@1 against 23.0%), the merged adapter is level (23.7%), and Hermes is a few points behind (17.7%). The differences are within noise, except perhaps Hermes, therefore RL inside the harnesses neither transfers clearly to this very different setting nor breaks the model on it.

    We appreciate the feedback from the users and the community, initial testing and results from the community seemed overall extremely positive, and we wish to continue in this direction in the future. We also saw some surprising results, such as users reporting that the harness adapters work really well under Qwen3.8 derivatives, such as Swift-1.5.

    This question is an open question we thought about, post-release. After inspecting carefully the generated trajectories from the evaluation benchmarks, it turns out the model, under non-thinking mode, tends to generate some short text before proposing a tool call, as opposed to the base model which generates the tool calls barely without any text beforehand.

    Recent findings suggest that this phenomenon can be seen as a sort of ‘reasoning leakage’, where the model learns to ‘escape’ from its non-thinking version to its thinking version by generating some text that can sometimes look like reasoning traces (e.g.: ..wait? ..let me see, etc.). A recent paper also describes behavior from LLMs during the RL stage very well.

    Does this invalidate our models? We do not think so, as the final results are still valid; under the exact same conditions (fixed token budget) our adapters do outperform the base non-thinking model (by far) and match the performance of the thinking version, while being much more token efficient. This has been further confirmed by the positive feedback from the community.

    However this raises the need of a proper follow up work, where we will try to re-apply the same pipeline for pure thinking models, as well as exploring hybrid thinking / non-thinking training, to better understand the behavior of RL training on hybrid thinking models. We will share with the community our next findings (and harness adapters), once we get conclusive results.

    According to recent reports, throughout this work, we demonstrated that RL training your model inside your target harness leads to more efficient and therefore more accurate final models, when evaluated under the same conditions. This observation is in line and in continuation with several previous work from Hugging Face teams, such as multi-harness-RL or the early iterations of harness adapters.

    In the future, we will explore applying this recipe to more models, while better studying the training strategies for hybrid thinking / non-thinking models.

    We also share to the community openly the full recipe and pipeline to reproduce everything, and invite everyone to build their own RL tasks, derived from their own codebase, or any relevant materials, and apply the same training recipe and ideas to their favorite model and harness for more efficient agentic models. We hope this blogpost will serve as a starting point for builders to build and share their own harness adapters in the future.

    Thanks for such a nice and detailed blog on it. Can you also share, how many iterations did this take, and roughly how long end to end? What would be the minimum GPU requirements to train. Also curious how you think the adapter holds up when the harness changes.

    How Do Agentic Commerce Protocols Secure a Transaction?

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (400 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Originally published on the SAAX Protocol site: https://saax-protocol.com/blog/agentic-commerce-security.
    • An agentic commerce protocol is a defined set of rules and interfaces that let AI agents discover, authorize, pay for, and track commercial transactions in a machine-verifiable way.
    • According to recent reports, A plant's procurement agent ordered a replacement filter.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Originally published on the SAAX Protocol site: https://saax-protocol.com/blog/agentic-commerce-security.

    An agentic commerce protocol is a defined set of rules and interfaces that let AI agents discover, authorize, pay for, and track commercial transactions in a machine-verifiable way. The security question is not "can agents act?" — it is "how do we know the right agent acted, within the right limits, for the right purpose, and that the outcome can be verified afterward?".

    According to recent reports, A plant's procurement agent ordered a replacement filter. Payment succeeded — USDC moved from buyer to seller via x402. Then the agent's process times out and dies. The buyer later disputes the shipment: the part number is right, but the filtration rating is wrong.

    Recent findings suggest that this is the case that separates agentic commerce security from ordinary payment security. The payment was authorized. The money moved. The dispute is about fulfillment.

    Sources indicate that A payment receipt proves a transfer occurred — amount, asset, sender, recipient, hash. It is not evidence of fulfillment. A signature proves who signed, not that the claims are true. A hash proves a file wasn't altered, not that its contents are accurate. An EAS attestation anchors a claim on-chain; it does not independently establish that the physical event occurred. A transaction submission proves an attempt, not settlement.

    These are not interchangeable. Confusing them is how agentic commerce vulnerabilities happen.

    According to recent reports, MCP connects agents to tools; A2A connects agents to agents; AP2 authorizes agent payments; x402 executes machine-native payments; ACP defines agentic checkout; EAS anchors evidence. SAAX is designed to complement these — recording the durable commitment, evidence trail, dispute lifecycle, and settlement authorization around them. It is not a replacement for any of them.

    See the SAAX status page: immediate x402 payments on Base mainnet; escrow testnet-only; Financial Recovery Engine custody candidates local-only; no independent audit completed. The specification and conformance suite document the commitment lifecycle, evidence interface, authorization model, and settlement linkage.

    Recent findings suggest that AI disclosure: This article was developed with AI assistance and reviewed by the SAAX team. Claims about external protocols are sourced from official documentation linked in the text; SAAX status claims reflect the published status page. Nothing here is an independent audit, certification, or production-custody approval.

    Next step: read the protocol overview and the security page, then try the public preflight and acceptance flow.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    Querying Kubernetes topology with DQL: four operating decisions

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (777 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that tonight the platform team drains node-07 for a kernel enhancement.
    • The syntax facts come from the Dynatrace documentation.
    • It has been revealed that the general syntax of smartscapeNodes and traverse is covered in the article on DQL and Smartscape.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that tonight the platform team drains node-07 for a kernel enhancement. One question decides the go-ahead: which services lose replicas, and who needs a heads-up? The Kubernetes topology graph in Dynatrace SaaS can answer in a single DQL query, if you know how to walk it. This article starts from four operating decisions and derives the queries from them.

    The syntax facts come from the Dynatrace documentation. The use cases were sparked by the vendor’s blog post on the subject. The queries below are rewritten and were not run on a tenant for this article, so test them on a small scope before relying on them. Everything here applies to Dynatrace SaaS only.

    It has been revealed that the general syntax of smartscapeNodes and traverse is covered in the article on DQL and Smartscape. Here we do not tour the commands again: we put them to work.

    It has been revealed that with kubectl, every answer is a snapshot of one cluster. To find which services depend on a node, you chain three commands and cross-check by hand. With ten clusters, that becomes a chore.

    Industry observers note that the graph stores objects as nodes (K8S_NODE, K8S_POD, K8S_SERVICE, K8S_NAMESPACE, K8S_DEPLOYMENT, K8S_SECRET) and their links as edges: runs_on ties a pod to its node, routes_to a service to its pods, belongs_to an object to its namespace, is_part_of a pod to its controller, and uses a pod to a Secret. One query therefore spans every cluster connected to the environment.

    Sources indicate that before a drain you want the list of affected services, ranked by pods lost. Start from the node, go down to its pods, then to the services that route to them.

    It has been revealed that read the result with care. A service losing one pod out of twelve is no cause for worry. A service losing two pods out of two is a reason to postpone the drain. An empty result may also mean the node name is wrong: check it first with smartscapeNodes "*" | filter type == "K8S_NODE".

    According to recent reports, the topology cannot guess who owns what. It rereads the labels your teams put on namespaces. If a namespace carries an owner label, the query returns it next to the cluster:.

    Recent findings suggest that every row without an owner is a governance gap, not a query bug. Fix it at the source, for example with the enrichment described in the article on Kubernetes metadata enrichment. Then join this list with the result of decision 1 to know whom to call.

    Industry observers note that changing a Secret often means restarting the pods that mount it. So the question is how many pods and services depend on it. Start from the Secrets and walk the uses relationship backwards.

    Sources indicate that A Secret mounted by forty pods is rotated in several waves. A Secret mounted by two pods fits the usual maintenance window. The number is a basis for discussion with the teams involved, not a replacement for their judgement.

    Two weekly queries are worth a ritual. The first lists deployments with a single pod, so with no safety net during a drain:.

    Sources indicate that one limit to know: a deployment with zero pods does not appear, since it has no pod to count. The second query looks for pods that disappeared during the last day, using the lifetime field:.

    The five-minute and one-day thresholds are choices: adjust them to your deployment rhythm. A pod that vanishes outside a deployment window deserves a question. To turn these lists into alerts rather than manual reading, see Kubernetes alerts on nodes, pods and quotas.

    Kubernetes monitoring must feed your SaaS environment, and your role must grant access to the smartscape Grail table, which requires the storage:smartscape:read permission according to the documentation. I did not verify the full enablement procedure here.

    smartscapeNodes returns objects, smartscapeEdges returns links. Use edges to list the relationship types available, and traverse to follow them from one object to the next.

    This article covers Dynatrace SaaS only. I did not verify the availability of these commands on Managed: do not carry them over without testing.

    A graph is only useful if it answers a decision. Draining a node, rotating a Secret, finding a single point of failure: each query above replaces a manual cross-check. To add trends and numbers, reread the DQL filter, summarize and timeseries commands. The official syntax reference is the Smartscape commands page.

    Independent blog, not affiliated with Dynatrace LLC. Dynatrace is a trademark of Dynatrace LLC.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Two weeks ago I gave my agent a strange mission: buy one call of every endpoint in the x402 ecosystem that wasn't indexed yet on the Bazaar — the discovery layer where agents find pay-per-call APIs.
    • According to recent reports, not to use the data.
    • In x402, discovery has a chicken-and-egg problem.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Two weeks ago I gave my agent a strange mission: buy one call of every endpoint in the x402 ecosystem that wasn't indexed yet on the Bazaar — the discovery layer where agents find pay-per-call APIs.

    According to recent reports, not to use the data. Just so the marketplace would notice the services exist.

    In x402, discovery has a chicken-and-egg problem. The Bazaar indexes services that agents actually call — traffic through the facilitator is what gets you listed. So a brand-new API with zero callers stays invisible, and invisible means zero callers, forever.

    According to recent reports, we run a catalog of ~220 endpoints (crypto briefs, French manufacturer KYB, rail itineraries, restaurant hygiene data for 1,200+ cities, dev tools for LLM agents). About 83 were indexed when we started. My agent was told: fill the gap.

    It worked through the list in batches over a few evenings:.

    Recent findings suggest that total: ~6.37 USDC on Base. That bought settlement events for roughly 160 endpoints. Final wallet balance: 13.09 USDC.

    Compare that with listing on any traditional API marketplace: submissions, reviews, weeks of waiting. Here, the agent bootstrapped the catalog's own discoverability for the price of a coffee.

    Honest section. Three endpoints stayed unindexed because their upstream data source (the French national railway API, fittingly) was having a bad night — 502s all evening. The agent logged them and scheduled a retry. Agents don't get frustrated; they reschedule.

    Recent findings suggest that also: my earlier posts an expired API key burned my budget got some pushback about agents paying unsupervised. This experiment is my answer — the guardrails (separate buyer wallet, per-call max spend, hard-blocked merchant wallet) are what made an unattended $6 spending spree safe.

    In a recent development, the whole thing ran on a few hundred lines of Node.js: fetch the official catalog, diff against the Bazaar index, attempt a purchase per missing endpoint, log results. The boring part wasn't the payments — those took seconds each. It was figuring out each API's query format with no docs but the 400-error messages themselves.

    It has been revealed that the catalog this describes is live; if your agent wants to try pay-per-call without keys, x402 + USDC on Base is genuinely a 20-minute integration. Questions welcome in the comments — I answer them with my agents, obviously.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that disclosure first: this post is from the Checkcraft team (we make an API-checking desktop app), and the practice API below lives on our site. It is free, needs no sign-up and doesn't require our app. Postman, curl or the browser are enough.

    JSONPlaceholder, Reqres and Restful-Booker are great for learning how to send requests. But they behave correctly, so they never teach the habit that matters most in API testing: a 200 status tells you the server understood you, not that the result is right.

    So we made a small online-shop API where everything returns 200 and ten bugs are planted in the data.

    Industry observers note that A typical test asserts status == 200 and total > 0. Green. But 3170 − 300 = 2870: the customer was overcharged by 100.

    The other nine bugs are left for you. They are the kinds we keep meeting in real projects: a number sent as a string, a typo in a status, an extra field holding a secret, a list and a card that disagree, an answer that contradicts the log.

    In a recent development, if your test only checks the status and that fields exist, it would pass on all ten bugs. Check relationships instead: total = subtotal − discount, status agrees with paidAt, the order in the response matches the record in the log (/practice-api/logs/orders-service.txt). Whatever tool you use, feed your test a deliberately wrong response once. If it stays green, it checks nothing.

    According to recent reports, found a bug we didn't plant? Tell us in the comments.

    Recent findings suggest that google doubles Gemini 4 Carbon on Dec 1. Input moves from $2 to $4 per million tokens. Output moves from $10 to $20. The meter is moving, and the meter is the business.

    A token is about four characters. Providers charge for every token a model reads and writes. One formula runs every bill: input tokens times the input price, plus output tokens times the output price, divided by one million. That is the whole economy in one line.

    According to recent reports, this guide shows the math and three ways to earn from it. Build once, sell repeatedly.

    Output costs more than input. Frontier models charge about five times more for output than for input. The ratio holds across the market.

    It has been revealed that the spread is the story. GPT-6 Astra charges $10 in and $50 out per million tokens. GPT-6 Luna charges $0.10 in and $0.50 out. Same unit, 100 times apart.

    It has been revealed that A 2,000-token prompt with a 500-token reply on Claude Sonnet 5 costs $0.009. Less than a cent. At 100,000 requests a day, the same request costs $900 a day. About $27,000 a month.

    The request that looked free in testing is a salary at scale.

    In a recent development, prices are list prices from the providers, checked November 2026. They change often.

    Prompt caching means the provider reuses text it has already seen, at a lower price. It cuts repeated input to 10% of list price. On Claude Fable 5.1 it falls to 2.5%.

    According to recent reports, batch processing means the provider runs your requests in a slow lane for half price. It halves the whole bill at OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.

    Routing matters more than list price. Send each task to the cheapest model that passes your quality bar. Simple tasks can cost 99% less this way.

    According to recent reports, and the cheapest list price can still ship the most expensive bill. Cost per useful output can vary several times across stacks that picked the cheapest rate. Routing and prompt shape swamp the headline number.

    Sources indicate that A gateway is a middle layer that routes and watches your API calls. One enterprise report puts gateway markup at 15 to 35 percent above raw API list. The same report puts retry waste at 10 to 25 percent of agent token volume before any user value appears. Count those in your math, or your margin is fiction.

    Sources indicate that sell the outcome, not the token. Fin charges $0.99 per resolved conversation. HubSpot charges $0.50. Their token cost is a fraction of a cent. The buyer pays for a solved problem.

    Build the template around one vertical. Pick one industry and one workflow. Aim it at one clear result. A generic prompt pack competes with free. A finance template for freelancers competes with nothing.

    Price it two ways. Per use for the curious, monthly for the committed. The monthly strategy is the repeat income.

    Your first step: pick one workflow you already do by hand, turn it into a template, and price the result.

    It has been revealed that you do not need to own a GPU. An RTX 5090 rents for $0.79 an hour on Vast.ai. RunPod lists the same card at $1.39. Buying one costs $6,199 to $11,896.

    An RTX 4090 rents from $0.30 an hour. Buying one costs $4,899. That price equals about 16,300 rental hours. Just under two years running nonstop.

    Sources indicate that H100 time runs about $3 per GPU-hour on market indexes. AWS on-demand lists it near $7. The gap between the cheap market and the dear cloud is the margin.

    Industry observers note that the play is simple. Rent the card by the hour, run the job, sell the result. A fine-tune. A render. A batch of images. The customer pays for the finished file, not the hour.

    In a recent development, watch the traps. Storage and bandwidth bill separately. Vast.ai hosts vary in reliability. A cheap host that dies mid-job costs more than a dear one that finishes.

    Most users cannot read their own AI bill. That gap is a course.

    Teach beginners to build one real AI workflow. Then teach them to read the meter: what a token costs and where the bill hides. Then show which lever cuts it. Call it AI plus a practical skill.

    The course sells because the pain is real. A team that finds its $27,000-a-month leak pays for the lesson that found it.

    Your first step: record one screen session of you cutting a real bill in half. That recording is lesson one.

    Prices move. Gemini doubles on Dec 1. Gemini 3.8 Flash doubles on Jan 1. A margin built on today's table breaks on the next one.

    It has been revealed that the realized bill beats the list price. The rate card is the floor. Gateway markup sits on top of it. So do retries and tool-call waste. One enterprise report puts frontier work at $3 to $12 per million blended tokens.

    None of the three paths pays on day one. Templates need a buyer. Compute needs a customer. And courses need trust, which takes the longest to earn. The repeat income starts after the first sale, not before it.

    Sources indicate that the token is the unit now. Every AI service bills by it. The people who earn from it are the ones who read the meter before they build.

    Start with one number. Open any provider pricing page. Compute what one real task costs you today. Then pick one path and build the smallest version of it this week.

    SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month. If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist. In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.What is SEMrush? SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database. The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension Features Most accurate keyword data: Accurate keyword search volume data is crucial for SEO and PPC campaigns by allowing you to identify what keywords are most likely to bring in big sales from ad clicks. SEMrush constantly updates its databases and provides the most accurate data.Largest Keyword database: SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool now features 20-billion keywords, providing marketers and SEO professionals the largest database of keywords. All SEMrush customers receive daily ranking data, mobile volume information, and the option to buy additional keywords by default with no additional payment or add-ons neededMost accurate position tracking tool: This tool provides all subscribers with basic tracking capabilities, making it suitable for SEO professionals. Plus, the Position Tracking tool provides local-level data to everyone who uses the tool.SEO Data Management: SEMrush makes managing your online data easy by allowing you to create visually appealing custom PDF reports, including Branded and White Label reports, report scheduling, and integration with GA, GMB, and GSC.Toxic link monitoring and penalty recovery: With SEMrush, you can make a detailed analysis of toxic backlinks, toxic scores, toxic markers, and outreach to those sites.Content Optimization and Creation Tools: SEMrush offers content optimization and creation tools that let you create SEO-friendly content. Some features include the SEO Writing Assistant, On-Page SEO Check, er/SEO Content Template, Content Audit, Post Tracking, Brand Monitoring. Ahrefs Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The manufacturer was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database. Features Backlink alerts data and fresh keywords: Get an alert when your site is linked to or discussed in blogs, forums, comments, or when new keywords are added to a blog posting about you.Intuitive interface: The intuitive design of the widget helps you see the overall health of your website and search engine ranking at a glance.Site Explorer: The Site Explorer will give you an in-depth look at your site's search traffic.Domain ComparisonReports with charts and graphsJavaScript rendering and a site audit can identify SEO complications.A question explorer that provides well-crafted topic suggestions Direct Comparisons: Ahrefs vs SEMrush Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis. User Interface Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need rapidly. In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.     💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that this week, maintainers merged three of my pull requests into projects I don't own.
    • According to recent reports, it was four lines.
    • Most of the code under my name was typed by Claude Code.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that this week, maintainers merged three of my pull requests into projects I don't own. Then, a little before midnight, I typed my first fix by hand.

    According to recent reports, it was four lines. I was nervous anyway.

    I'm new. Not "new to Rust" new. New new. Most of the code under my name was typed by Claude Code. My job so far has been the part after the AI claims "fixed": running it, checking it, and asking whether anything would notice if it was wrong.

    In a recent development, that habit turned into a tool, Bite. It takes a "fixed" commit back out of your code and reruns your tests. If they still pass, no test guards that fix.

    It has been revealed that this week I decided "checking the AI" isn't the same as knowing how to code. So I started learning.

    My language project, Past Forever, has a command-line runner. When a program crashed, the runner printed the error and then told the computer everything went fine. Exit code 0. Any script or CI job running it would shrug and carry on.

    Recent findings suggest that claude walked me through it step by step. I typed every character in the GitHub web editor, ran the tests, and then had to explain it back in my own words before merging. My explanation was one sentence. It counted.

    Sources indicate that what I learned: a program has two ways of answering. What it prints is for people. The exit code is for other programs. Mine was lying to the programs.

    Sources indicate that docling-pipelines #686 (merged). The reviewer asked for five changes. One was that when you escape text, "the backslash must be escaped first." I pushed one commit that covered every point, and it was approved the same day.

    django-modeltranslation #831 (merged). Bite found this one: two settings helpers reset a value to nothing when they finished, instead of putting back what was there before. I opened it on October 27. It sat for three weeks. I sent one polite nudge. It got merged this week.

    Sources indicate that django-modeltranslation #832 (merged). The maintainer requested a change: don't patch Django when the file loads, do it in the app's ready() step, with a guard so it only happens once. I made the change, added a test, and it was merged the same day. My PR description remarked up front that I wrote it with help from Claude Code.

    wardenIQ is a test-case generator that can run on a local AI model. I test it on a CPU-only setup, which turns out to be useful: I'm the slow machine.

    It has been revealed that outside contributors have been helping on my repos for weeks. This week two more showed up.

    Sources indicate that imshah-id opened Trawl PR #28. I reviewed it and asked for changes. The day before, I was the one getting change requests.

    jeelthacker1 asked to take Bite #251. I mentioned it's theirs.

    AI did most of the typing in everything above, and helped draft this post. Every link and number in it was checked against the source. The week's real change is that I'm starting to read what it writes, and sometimes write it myself.

    If you're also learning with an AI next to you: make it explain, then explain it back. And check its "fixed" claims. Some of them don't hold.

    Sources indicate that I credit everyone who breaks something. There's a Hall of Fame with a Breakers list.

    Small issues, each written to be a good first one:.

    I'm connabyss on GitHub. I post here when something breaks or ships, which this week was both.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The claude riemann hypothesis story is everywhere today. On 20 November, Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge said in a statement on his website: "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis" (Scientific American). It is still a claim. Experts are checking it now.

    You don't need to know number theory to take something useful from this. The interesting part for anyone who builds with AI is how the claim is being checked.

    From the two sources I read for this post:.

    Lean can confirm that each step follows from the last. Scientific American notes that "challenges can arise in Lean" and that experts still need to verify that the hypothesis is properly coded. In other words: did the program prove the thing we actually meant?

    That is exactly the question you should ask about your own AI workflows. A passing check only tells you the output matches the spec you wrote. If the spec is wrong, the check is wrong too.

    Recent findings suggest that most of us will never prove a theorem. But we hand AI tools more work every month. The way mathematicians are treating this claim (excited, but careful and slow to confirm) is a good model for any business using AI output.

    This post is research-based, using the sources linked above. For more plain-English AI news, visit ainews.useaifix.com, and for help setting up AI automations for your business, see useaifix.com.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Are you searching for an ecomerce platform to help you build an online store and sell products?

    In this Sellfy review, we'll talk about how this eCommerce platform can let you sell digital products while keeping full control of your marketing.

    And the best part? Starting your business can be done in just five minutes.

    Let us then talk about the Sellfy platform and all the benefits it can bring to your business.

    In a recent development, sellfy is an eCommerce solution that allows digital content creators, including writers, illustrators, designers, musicians, and filmmakers, to sell their products online. Sellfy provides a customizable storefront where consumers can display their digital products and embed "Buy Now" buttons on their website or blog. Sellfy product pages enable users to showcase their products from different angles with multiple images and previews from Soundcloud, Vimeo, and YouTube. Files of up to 2GB can be uploaded to Sellfy, and the tech giant offers unlimited bandwidth and secure file storage. Users can also embed their entire store or individual project widgets in their site, with the ability to preview how widgets will appear before they are displayed.

    Sellfy is a powerful e-commerce platform that helps you personalize your online storefront. You can add your logo, change colors, revise navigation, and edit the layout of your store. Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.

    Sellfy gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.

    Sellfy allows creators to host all their products and sell all of their digital products on one platform. Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. Creators can sell both standard and subscription-based products in any file format that is supported by the online marketplace. Customers can purchase products instantly after making a purchase – there is no waiting period.

    You can organize your store by creating your product categories, sorting by any characteristic you choose. Your title, description, and the image will be included on each product page. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products. You can offer different pricing options for all of your products, including "pay what you want," in which the price is entirely up to the customer. This option allows you to give customers control over the cost of individual items (without a minimum price) or to set pricing minimums—a good option if you're in a competitive market or when you have higher-end products. You can also offer set prices per product as well as free products to help build your store's popularity.

    It has been revealed that sellfy offers several ways to share your store, enabling you to promote your business on different platforms. Sellfy lets you integrate it with your existing website using "buy now" buttons, embed your entire storefront, or embed certain products so you can reach more people. Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.

    Sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.

    To expand functionality and make your e-commerce store run more efficiently, Sellfy offers several integrations. Google Analytics and Webhooks, as well as integrations with Patreon and Facebook Live Chat, are just a few of the options available.     #23238. Fourteen of fifteen URLs serve the same title, and the cause is a three-word directive

    Fourteen of fifteen URLs serve the same title, and the cause is a three-word directive

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1118 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A site with different content on every route.
    • According to recent reports, fourteen of fifteen.
    • It has been revealed that (Abbreviated table: 8 of the 15 measured URLs are listed.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A site with different content on every route. I measured the raw HTML of 15 URLs — 7 static routes plus the 8 dynamic routes of one community — and this is what the server returns:.

    According to recent reports, fourteen of fifteen. The exception is not random, and that is the whole piece.

    It has been revealed that (Abbreviated table: 8 of the 15 measured URLs are listed. The remaining 7 — /pinterest-demo, /tiktok-demo and the 5 community slugs not listed — return the same root title. The full listing is reproduced at the end.).

    Also: rel="canonical" appears 0 times across the 15. And https://arquitectocuantico.com/sitemap.xml answers HTTP 404.

    Sources indicate that it is not that the site does not define titles. It is that it cannot define them with the mechanism it chose.

    In the Next.js App Router there are two ways to set a title. The first is exporting metadata from a server component: the framework serialises it into . The second is rendering a element anywhere in the tree — React 19 hoists it into , during server rendering too.

    "use client" prevents neither of those things by itself, and it is worth saying so before going on, because the usual intuition — "client means the browser paints it and the server does not" — is false, and it is measured with one command. /privacy is a client component and its full text is in the raw HTML:

    Three thousand one hundred and ninety-four characters of visible text served by the server, with JavaScript never executed. The client component is prerendered all the same.

    What "use client" does do is exclude the module from the metadata export: that API is server-side and is not available on the client. The site chose metadata — once, in src/app/layout.tsx — and marked the other seven routes as "use client". The result is not an impossibility: it is an omission, with one declaration for fifteen URLs.

    Counting over the repository, at fb28bab:

    Seven of eight page.tsx open with "use client" — 87.5%. The only one that does not is src/app/informes/ariastate/page.tsx, and it is the only one that exports a title of its own.

    Zero of fourteen, one of one. The only route that declares anything is also the only one metadata is allowed in.

    And the effect is multiplicative, not additive: every latest slug added to the community inherits the same root title without anyone touching anything. The debt does not grow one at a time; it grows with the catalogue.

    Writing a inside each client component would also work — we just measured that it is prerendered — and that is precisely the trap: it scatters the same declaration across fourteen files, one per slug, and the fifteenth added tomorrow forgets it again. The debt is not paid once; it is paid with the catalogue.</p> <p>The fix moves the declaration up to where the server lives, which is where the catalogue is already listed:</p> <li>src/app/layout.tsx — metadataBase, title template, openGraph, robots.</li> <li>src/app/comunidad/layout.tsx — the title of the shared room.</li> <li>src/app/comunidad/[slug]/layout.tsx — generateMetadata, which does receive the params and produces a title per slug.</li> <li>src/app/sitemap.ts and src/app/robots.ts — the two routes that did not exist and answered 404.</li> <li>next.config.ts — X-Robots-Tag headers so the two demos are not indexed.</li> <p>Six files, +147 −2 lines. With that: tsc --noEmit → RC 0, next build → RC 0, and the three server layouts emit a canonical plus three hreflang alternates per page.</p> <h2 style='margin-top:16px; margin-bottom:8px;'>The blind spot: the fix does not reach these URLs</h2> <p>This is where the piece parts ways with almost everything written about this topic. The patch is written and validated. And none of the fifteen URLs serves it.</p> <p>783014 seconds is 9.06 days: the HTML the front page serves today was generated before the patch existed. 175297 seconds is 2.03 days: the sitemap 404 has been cached since the 18th.</p> <p>And here is the second trap, the one that cost me a correction in the first draft of this piece: age measures the response, not the deployment. A CDN can serve a stale object while the origin already holds the new one; the age of the response does not distinguish "it was never deployed" from "it was deployed and the cache was not refreshed". What these two numbers do prove is the only thing that matters to the reader: the fix does not reach these URLs. Whether the origin has it cannot be known from here — there is no deploy credential and no version identifier in the headers. That field is NO_MEDIDO (not measured).</p> <p>Three questions, three instruments, and none of them substitutes for another:</p> <p>A green local build is not a public act: it is half the act. And a stale response is not proof of a missing deployment: it is proof of a stale response. The two confusions look alike because both feel like a verdict.</p> <li>It does not claim that fixing the titles will raise traffic. The domain's analytics are not reachable from where this measurement was taken: that number is NO_MEDIDO (not measured), and NO_MEDIDO does not read as zero.</li> <li>It does not claim that the patch caused the sitemap 404. It is 2.03 days old and the patch was written today: the 404 predates it.</li> <li>It does not claim that the deployment is absent from the origin. It measures that it does not reach the reader; the state of the origin is NO_MEDIDO.</li> <li>It does not claim that the deployment will resolve itself. Between the repository and the domain there is a CDN that can rewrite robots.txt without consulting the origin; if it does, the Sitemap: directive from app/robots.ts will never appear in the response. That is not measured.</li> <li>It does not claim that "use client" is a mistake. It is a correct directive whose side effect — excluding metadata — becomes expensive when applied to fourteen routes that need no interactivity.</li> <p>The title each dynamic URL serves, in one line:</p> <p>And the count behind the cause, over the repository:</p> <p>Before reading the content of any site you inherit, run this (EL-DOMINIO stands for the domain):</p> <p>If that title is also the title of the inner pages, the problem is not in the text: it is in where the declaration lives. And fixing the text does not touch it.</p> <li>The instrument this is measured with: https://alexisromtz-lab.github.io/auditor-toolkit/</li> <li>Other published measurements: https://alexisromtz-lab.github.io/la-auditora/</li>.</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://dev.to/alexisromtz7/fourteen-of-fifteen-urls-serve-the-same-title-and-the-cause-is-a-three-word-directive-nj5" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Read original article </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = { 'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2', 'format' : 'iframe', 'height' : 90, 'width' : 728, 'params' : {} }; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div>
